name: Access control over Swarm content || András Arányi
description:
Within decentralized public data storage systems like Swarm, where data resides across multiple nodes, ensuring confidentiality, integrity, and availability becomes paramount.
The Access Control Trie (ACT) is a data structure that stores access control information for Swarm nodes. It is used to determine whether a node has permission to access a particular resource.
aiDescription:
The video discusses the application of Web 3 technology to ensure user control over data privacy and access. The speaker explains how their implemented feature, access control trie (ACT), within the Swarm platform allows content publishers to grant or revoke access to specific wallets, ensuring that only authorized users can view or decrypt content. This system aims to address common Web 2 issues such as centralization, data mishandling, security breaches, and censorship. The ACT feature is detailed in terms of its technical implementation within Swarm and its potential use cases, including gated community content, private group chats, confidential data sharing, and monetization opportunities for content creators in Web 3.

A live demo showcases how a publisher can grant access to a member wallet so they can view JSON data, potentially representing NFT metadata. The talk also touches on a partnership with Galaxy XYZ, a platform creating Web 3 communities that will use Swarm for self-serving control over data.

Questions from the audience cover technical aspects of ACTs, such as EVM compatibility and visibility of granted permissions. The response emphasizes the security design where access information does not leak outside intended parties.

The summary is for users interested in decentralized storage solutions, privacy control in Web 3 applications, and the technical mechanisms enabling secure data sharing within blockchain ecosystems.

name: Moving from IPFS to Swarm || Ramesh Pallikara
description: A talk that focuses on what everyone needs to know about IPFS and Swarm, its pros and cons and how to use Swarm instead of IPFS.
aiDescription:
The video features Ramesh, a developer relations representative at Swarm, who has over 20 years of full-stack development experience and has been working with IPFS and Swarm for nearly three years. He discusses the benefits of using Swarm as an alternative to IPFS for certain drawbacks users may encounter. Ramesh clarifies that while he appreciates IPFS, he believes Swarm offers superior solutions for data availability, download speeds, and decentralization without the need for constant node operation or reliance on third-party services.

He explains the technical aspects of IPFS, including its content addressing system through CIDs (content identifiers) and IPNS (Interplanetary Name Service) for mutable pointers to content. Addressing misconceptions about IPFS, he notes that it is not entirely free unless users run their own nodes or use pinning services with limitations.

Ramesh then compares Swarm to IPFS in terms of atomic units, download speeds, censorship resistance, privacy, payment systems, and incentives for running nodes. He clarifies terminology differences between the two platforms regarding pinning and CIDs.

The video also includes a tutorial on migrating from IPFS to Swarm using command-line tools and libraries like BJS for dApps. Ramesh invites viewers to try out Swarm and join their Discord

name: Altruism, reciprocity, and tokens to reward forwarding data: Is that fair? || Vero Estrada-Galiñanes
description:
Decentralized storage networks use different mechanisms to distribute rewards among participants. A caveat is that rewards are often disproportionally concentrated in the hands of a small number of participants, i.e., early adopters or highly-resourced participants.
We notice many design decisions, often poorly understood, can impact in the effectiveness of reward mechanisms.
aiDescription: The video presents a paper on algorithm reciprocity and tokens as incentives for contributing data in decentralized systems, discussed at the IEEE Blockchain Conference. The research, conducted by a team from EPFL, University of Estavangar, and TUDELF, explores combining monetary rewards with other incentive mechanisms to encourage equitable participation and prevent centralization in networks like Swarm. The paper focuses on bandwidth sharing rather than storage and introduces the T4 token model. It examines how different parameters affect the fairness of reward distribution among nodes, using simulations with various settings. Key findings include the impact of gateway distribution on income fairness and the benefits of neighbor shuffling to improve fairness. The presentation concludes with an invitation to review the paper for detailed results and methodologies.

name: Digital integrity of the human person, A new fundamental right || Alexis Roussel
description:
The right to respect for digital integrity is an emerging right to protect people's digital lives.

This talk will introduce this new legal concept, its possible implications for data protection and how this concept is being introduced in the current legal framework. The talk will also be an update of the implementation work with the adoption of the right in the Constitution of Geneva voted with 94% approval rate on the 18th of june 2023.
aiDescription:
The video features a talk by Alex Roussel, CEO of NIM Technologies, on the topic of digital human rights and the concept of digital integrity. Roussel discusses his work on making the idea of digital integrity a recognized right, drawing parallels with physical and mental integrity protected by laws. He shares his success in getting 95% of voters in Geneva to approve a new digital right in 2023.

Roussel explains that digital integrity should be an extension of existing rights, ensuring individuals have control over their personal data and are protected from non-consensual use of it. He emphasizes the importance of anonymity and privacy infrastructure, mentioning that NIM is building a mix net and VPN to support these goals.

The talk also covers how digital integrity can be integrated into legal systems, citing examples from Switzerland where new rights have been added to the constitution. Roussel argues for transparent societal systems where personal data remains anonymous, allowing for private interactions between individuals.

He concludes by stressing the need for decentralized, anonymous systems to protect against misuse by generative AI and other threats. The talk ends with audience questions on how simply adding "digital" to existing rights can effectively convey the necessary protections in legal contexts, with Roussel explaining how jurisprudence would adapt over time to refine these rights.

They discuss concepts like farm-to-table yield, organic versus inorganic yield sources, and sustainable long-term revenue generation methods within the context of stablecoins.

The talk aims to provide insights on applying historical lessons to modern-day currency systems and fostering partnerships within the crypto community.

Each phase has specific quadrants that guide users through setting objectives, choosing funding mechanisms, defining roles and responsibilities, engaging with audiences, determining disbursement strategies, and conducting retrospectives. 

The tool is meant for both new and veteran ecosystem growth leaders and can be used for both new and existing grants programs across various types of organizations. Coach Jay plans to workshop the Define phase in the session using the canvas in a Miro board with audience participation.

In summary, the video presents a hands-on session on how to use a strategic planning tool for grants programs within Web3 ecosystems, aiming to help leaders effectively plan and grow their initiatives.

name: Getting started with Kontrol: a formal verification tool
description: The workshop will be a crash course on Formal Verification with Kontrol. Attendants will leverage their Foundry skills to use Kontrol and get hands-on experience on how to incorporate FV into their everyday development.

name: Enabling Decentralized Networks With DePin and PoC
description: We introduce Proof of Capacity (PoC) that allows on-chain verification of off-chain cryptographic proofs over (almost any) arbitrary hardware commitments to decentralized network. We discuss PoC's role in enabling decentralized network stacks.
aiDescription:
The video discusses the evolution of the term "Deepin" in the cryptocurrency space, which was chosen to describe a particular sector involving decentralized networks and physical work. The speaker notes that Misari, a crypto analytics firm, conducted a Twitter poll in late 2022 to settle on this term, and later published an influential overview of the state of Deepin in 2023. The video highlights that there are over 60 tokens or projects associated with Deepin, indicating its significance.

The speaker explains that Deepin encompasses both physical and digital resources, with a focus on digital resources like computing power. Projects like Filecoin are mentioned for their contributions to digital storage solutions. The speaker emphasizes the importance of proof systems in verifying storage and computing resources, noting the challenges unique to computing power compared to storage.

Fluence is introduced as a decentralized cloud compute platform that aggregates CPU (and potentially GPU) resources for developers to purchase capacity. The platform uses WebAssembly and Docker for deploying general compute tasks. It is governed by a DAO and has its own token.

The importance of supply preceding demand in protocol structure is stressed, with emphasis on creating incentives for resource providers to commit capacity without immediate demand. The speaker warns against protocols incentivizing non-existent capacity as it can be detrimental.

name: Feedback, Cybernetics and Governance
description: Self-regulating systems evolve through continuous input loops, shaping collective decision-making processes. Stepan Gershuni (Cyber Fund), Nick Naraghi (Hats Protocol), Alexander Hicks (Ethereum Foundation), Sofiane Delloue (Newfoundation)
aiDescription: The video features a panel discussion on the intersection of governance, cybernetics, self-evolving systems, and processes within the crypto and AI industries. The speakers include experts from CyberFun, Ethereum Foundation, and HATS protocol. They delve into the concept of a cybernetic economy facilitated by blockchain and AI technologies, emphasizing the transition from traditional bureaucratic systems to automated, digital, peer-to-peer systems. The conversation covers how these technologies enable scalable coordination beyond human cognitive limits and how they can be applied to governance for large-scale coordination. Additionally, the panel explores formal verification of cryptographic models to ensure bug-free systems and the potential of using AI in conjunction with formal verification as a means to create reliable and trustworthy outputs from AI models.

name: Open Models and Interoperability
description: Transparent algorithms and universal standards foster innovation and cross-platform collaboration. Jiahao Sun (FLock.io), Gwen Martin (Ora), Toufi Saliba (HyperCycle), Branimir Rakic (OriginTrail), moderated by Joshua Bate (DeSciWorld)
aiDescription:
The video features a panel discussion on open models and interoperability in the Web3 space with representatives from various projects. Sophie-Anne from New Foundation discusses their work on NewCoin and IPSP, a standard for interoperability and communication. Brandon Mirajoski introduces Origin 12 Decentralized Knowledge Graph, an open-source neuro-symbolic AI system. Gwen from Aura talks about their company's focus on on-chain AI Oracle products and tokenization of open AI models to support open source foundations.

The panel addresses the importance of open models, contrasting the potential risks of centralized AI systems with the benefits of decentralized, pluralistic approaches. They argue that history shows centralized coordination systems often fail, suggesting that a diverse ecosystem of AIs can lead to better performance and innovation without lock-ins or negative network effects.

Concerns about model collapse and the proliferation of misinformation are discussed, highlighting the need for verifiable content and knowledge as valuable assets. The panelists express optimism for a future where decentralized knowledge and AI contribute to an open world model that empowers individuals and enhances collective intelligence. They believe this can lead to a new asset class in knowledge, similar to how Bitcoin revolutionized monetary value.

name: Verifiable Data
description: Cryptographically secured information ensures authenticity and trust in distributed networks.  Kamesh Elangovan (OpenLedger), Josh Benaron (Irys), Branimir Rakic (OriginTrail)
aiDescription: The video features a panel of experts discussing their respective projects and the importance of verifiable data in the blockchain and AI industries. Josh, the founder and CEO of Iris, introduces his project as a scaling solution for Rweave, aimed at increasing transaction capacity to support more projects. Branimir, a founder and CTO of Origin12, talks about their decentralized knowledge graph technology that has applications beyond supply chains and is now implemented across various blockchains. Kamesh, a core contributor to OpenLedger, shares their recent funding success and describes OpenLedger as a decentralized data infrastructure for the AI space inspired by Web2 technologies. The conversation touches on the evolution from Web2 to Web3, the need for verifiable data in AI, and how decentralization can prevent centralized control over AI advancements. The discussion also explores how verifiable data can enable incentives for maintaining up-to-date foundational models in AI, contrasting with proprietary models like ChatGPT. Overall, the panelists emphasize their commitment to enhancing data intelligence through blockchain technology.

name: Economic Primitives in DeAI
description: How can DeAI provide value, monetise, and tokenise decentralized intelligence?   Sofiane Delloue (Newfoundation), Michal Benedykcinski (Arca), Karan Sihota (Mira.ai) , Oak (Valory/Olas)
aiDescription: The video discusses economic models and business strategies in the AI and crypto sectors. Panelists share their personal journeys into the AI space, highlighting the value of decentralized systems, trustlessness, and the potential for broader distribution of ownership and wealth. They explore how AI can shape society and emphasize the importance of open-source infrastructure in this context. The conversation then shifts to business models that are currently succeeding or failing in this naspective field. The speakers note a significant investment focus on infrastructure, with concerns about capital wastage on less authentic projects. Examples include decentralized compute as a major investment area, while consumer applications are still developing. The panel also addresses how funds from AI services can be reinvested into the economy to create new services. Finally, they observe that revenue in AI is concentrated at the application layer or in compute resources, with other areas yet to be monetized effectively.

name: Identity in the Agent World
description: Unique digital signatures allow autonomous entities to interact and build reputations across networks. Evin McMullen (Disco), Kyle Weiss (Gitcoin), Bryce (EAS), moderated by Collin Lowenburg (Dabl)
aiDescription:
The video features a panel discussion with representatives from various organizations in the cryptocurrency and blockchain space, focusing on the topic of digital identity within the ecosystem. The speakers include Evan from Disco, Kyle from Gitcoin, and Mel from DoubleClub. They discuss their current roles, their views on digital identity, and how it's essential for more complex interactions beyond mere financial transactions on the blockchain. The conversation highlights the importance of controlling personal data and how digital identities can facilitate personalized experiences without compromising privacy. They also touch on the challenges of Sybil attacks in mechanisms like quadratic funding and the development of systems that allow users to prove their uniqueness without revealing specific personal details.

The future of digital identities is envisioned as one where interactions with applications become seamless and personalized, akin to the experience depicted in "The Jetsons" TV show. The panelists also consider the role of AI agents in transactions, emphasizing the need for a trust layer to distinguish between genuine human users, beneficial bots, and nefarious actors. The discussion concludes with thoughts on setting industry standards for identification to improve interactions within the broader ecosystem.

aiDescription: The video features a panel discussion on the topic of "proto apps" and the integration of AI with the crypto world. name: A security in depth approach to verifiable offchain computations
description: Hashi and SafeJunction are permissionless abstraction layers to create secure and future proof dapps. Hashi was designed to avoid bridging lock-ins and to enable higher degrees of security. SafeJunction extends this concept beyond cross-chain bridging, to verifiable arbitrary computations.
aiDescription:
The video discusses the importance of security in-depth for off-chain computations, particularly in the context of blockchain scalability and the use of proofs. The speaker explains how layer 2 and layer 3 solutions inherit security from Ethereum's base layer through proofs, which are essential for various applications like scalability, interoperability between layers, and external data verification through oracles. The concept of a "proof layer" is introduced as an abstract idea that is critical for blockchain security but does not yet exist in a concrete form.

The speaker then delves into three main use cases for proofs: improving scalability through vertical integration of layers, decomposability across different systems, and co-processing to offload heavy computations while maintaining transparency and privacy. They also discuss the potential future where everything in the blockchain ecosystem operates via proofs, with layer 1 blockchains primarily verifying these proofs.

However, there are challenges today in achieving this vision due to inefficiencies, fragmentation, trust assumptions, and high costs associated with proof generation and verification. Additionally, there are concerns about large attack surfaces and dependencies on unreliable code libraries.

name: Proof of Humanity DAO Governance Lessons from the Sybil War
description: In 2021 and 2022, the Proof of Humanity DAO faced a governance crisis that led to a fork. This talk will explore several lessons that can be drawn from this drama through the lens of modern political theory.
aiDescription:
The video features Federico, the founder of Kleros, discussing their project Proof of Humanity and its challenges. He explains that Proof of Humanity was created to address the issue of unique human identity on the blockchain, which is critical for applications like one-person-one-vote in DAO governance. The project aimed to prevent Sybil attacks and was linked to a UBI token for fair distribution. However, the DAO faced a crisis due to a lack of shared values and vision within the community, leading to factionalism and eventual collapse.

Federico analyzes this failure by highlighting the diversity in community motivation—some members were focused on technical aspects while others were interested in using the platform for UBI and poverty alleviation. This lack of consensus led to disputes and radicalization among members. He also discusses governance issues like the tyranny of the majority and proposes solutions such as a constitution for DAOs, mechanisms to prevent majority rule, sortition to fight factions, and considerations for voting rights.

He suggests that clear governance rules, separation of powers within DAOs, constitutional panels, and random selection processes could help prevent similar failures in future decentralized organizations. Federico concludes by touching on political theories related to voting rights and democracy versus epistocracy.

name: Benchmarking data for the settlement of crypto derivatives
description: This keynote is an in-depth presentation on the benchmarking data used in the context of crypto derivatives settlement, both on and off chain, specifically diving into regulated use cases and benchmark data provided by independent index providers.
aiDescription: The video discusses the significance of benchmarks in the settlement of crypto derivatives, highlighting their role as reference prices. The speaker explains that benchmarks can be sourced online or from trusted third parties and stresses the importance of using regulated benchmarks to prevent manipulation, drawing parallels to the Libor scandal. The current state of the crypto derivatives market is examined, noting its volume compared to spot markets and the growth in open interest for Bitcoin and ETH futures. Examples of exchanges using regulated benchmarks for settlement are provided, and the requirements for creating reliable crypto benchmarks are outlined, including regulatory compliance, data quality, robust methodology, and a stable platform. The talk aims to convey the maturing process of the crypto industry by adopting best practices from traditional finance.

name: A Lightweight Architecture for Ethereum Archive Nodes
description: The core idea is to maintain compacted, flattened, and fine-grained (i.e., transaction-level) historical states by flattening the minimum state changes of each transaction required for the world state.
aiDescription:
The video features a talk by Andy, the CEO of BlockSec and a professor at Zhejiang University, discussing their research on optimizing Ethereum archive nodes. The research is a collaborative effort between BlockSec, students, and other partners. Andy emphasizes the importance of building real systems with tangible impacts and outlines BlockSec's role in enhancing blockchain security through various products and solutions.

Andy explains that blockchain optimization can be achieved at different layers, including consensus mechanisms, execution layers, and storage engines. Their work focuses on optimizing the storage engine to improve efficiency and reduce costs by modifying the state model within Ethereum's archive nodes.

He provides an overview of Ethereum's storage layer, explaining that it operates as a state machine driven by transactions that change states. The state is an account-based model with each account having its own storage referenced by a storage root. All states are encoded in a Merkle Patricia Tree (MPT) for quick data authentication.

Different types of Ethereum nodes exist with varying capabilities regarding historical data storage. Full nodes only maintain the latest world state for reorganization tolerance while archive nodes preserve all historical states but require significant disk space due to saving all intermediate MPTs at each block.

name: The Prehistory of Blockchain
description: In this talk, we will go over the prehistory of blockchain - the ideas and projects that inspired and guided Satoshi in creating Bitcoin. There were several earlier attempts at a digital currency, such as David Chaum's eCash, Nick Szabo's Bit Gold, and Wei Dai's b-Money.  Proof of work was used in Adam Back's hashcash. And all of these rested on more fundamental ideas, like the very concepts of a blockchain data structure and digital signatures. This talk will cover the groundwork laid by these pioneers that eventually led to Bitcoin and modern blockchain technology.

speakers.name: Bill Laboon
speakers.bio: Director of Education and Governance Initiatives

aiDescription: The video features Bill Laboon from the Web3 Foundation discussing the history and development of technologies that preceded Bitcoin. He explains that Bitcoin's creation was influenced by previous attempts at electronic cash, trustlessness, and decentralization. The talk covers four key areas: the blockchain data structure, proof of work, public key cryptography, and the concept of digital cash. Laboon delves into the origins of blockchain as a decentralized timestamping tool, citing a paper by Haber and Stornetta from the 90s and their company Surety's innovative use of publishing hashes in the New York Times to ensure verifiability. He highlights that these concepts and technologies existed well before Bitcoin's first block was mined, emphasizing that blockchain has a longer history than commonly known and has evolved significantly over time.

name: Gnosis AI: Onchain agents and longtail predictions markets
description: Gnosis AI: Onchain agents and longtail predictions markets talk by @koeppelmann
aiDescription: The video will discuss the role of AI agents in prediction markets and how these markets are used to estimate the likelihood of future events through trading digital assets. It will showcase a live demonstration of an AI agent analyzing a binary question—whether China will invade Taiwan by the end of 2025. The agent will evaluate the question, gather information from various sources, and provide a probability estimate. The presenter will explain that these agents are already operating on blockchain platforms and actively trading in markets, using specialized tools to determine probabilities and make trading decisions based on market discrepancies. The summary concludes with the bold claim that we are close to creating a new form of life through these advancements.

name: The Chain Mail Gaze
description: With their dreams of new ‘Network State’ empires, resource extraction, and colonial domination, today’s tech overlords are the descendants of Europe’s mediaeval Crusaders: well-financed, zealous fanatics remaking the world in the name of their greater good. Through a psycho-political reading of scarcity, chauvinism, and colonialism, The Chain Mail Gaze connects Crusader ideologues’ desire for blood, land, and booty, to emerging ‘frontiers’ mediated by contemporary technologies.
aiDescription:
The video features a speaker named Wissie Malcindy discussing the concept of friction in the context of work and how it relates to a broader spectrum of ideas. The talk delves into various subjects, including rural friction, funding mechanisms, the dynamics of influence and bilingualism, and the evolution of communities over time. The speaker touches on complex themes like anarchy pricing, disappearance of certain elements over years, cultural shifts due to toxic masculinity, and the impact of technological advancements like blockchain and automation.

The narrative also explores Bitcoin's role in this landscape, highlighting its temporal properties and its function as a "chronogenic apparatus" that creates new forms of temporality independent from traditional calendars or clocks. The discussion includes reflections on how Bitcoin operates as a clock, its energy requirements, its perception by maximalists, and its broader societal implications.

Additionally, the speaker examines the concept of petro-masculinity and how it relates to ecological concerns in parts of the UK. The talk concludes by considering Bitcoin's creator Satoshi Nakamoto's disappearance and how Bitcoin enthusiasts communicate within their networks. Overall, the video presents a complex intersection of technology, society, time perception, and environmental issues through the lens of cryptocurrency.

name: From PGP to ZRTP: Decentralized Privacy Protocols in a Centralized Ecosystem
description: Listen to the creator of PGP talking about Decentralized Privacy Protocols in a Centralized Ecosystem
aiDescription:
The video features a speaker discussing their experience in the tech industry, emphasizing a preference for bottom-up design over top-down approaches. They recount working on an automated tape library system in the 1980s and how that project's design philosophy influenced their later work on PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), a cryptographic software. The speaker highlights the challenges faced while developing PGP, including financial struggles and the omission of a trust model in PGP 1.0 due to time constraints. They also touch on the legal issues surrounding PGP, stemming from patent conflicts with RSA Data Security and subsequent federal investigation.

Additionally, the speaker reflects on the early days of email protocols and how they were designed to be decentralized, contrasting it with the siloed nature of modern VoIP services despite using similar encryption protocols. They express skepticism about the necessity of blockchains for achieving decentralization but maintain a strong interest in decentralized systems. The speaker clarifies that when they refer to "crypto," they mean cryptography, not cryptocurrency, and shares anecdotes about their involvement in various projects and protocols over the years.

name: The Public Interest Internet
description: Many of us have spent years imagining a better internet that works for people. But our efforts tend to be scattered, improving one problem or iterating on one technological component, but not considering what global digital architecture should we assemble if we take seriously the idea that the internet should be public interest technology. This talk tries to take on that question. The chances are good that I'm wrong, but I hope to be usefully wrong.
aiDescription: The video features a speaker discussing the concept of accountability in decision-making systems, illustrated by a historical incident involving the mishandling of imported ground squirrels at a Dutch airport. The speaker explains how this event exemplifies an "accountability sink," where no one could be held responsible due to the delegation of decision-making to a set of rules. The talk delves into the importance of feedback loops in governance systems, the challenge of creating autonomous decision-making systems that can adapt to real-world complexities, and the political nature inherent in designing these systems. The speaker emphasizes the responsibility technologists have in shaping rules that govern our interactions and the potential consequences of failing to consider these aspects carefully. They argue that rule-based systems are inherently incomplete due to the unpredictable nature of reality, necessitating human intervention for unforeseen situations. The presentation concludes by highlighting the difficulty in making decisions with no clear right answer and challenges the notion that technology alone can solve complex problems without considering political implications.

name: Making Blockchain Anarchist Again: NymVPN
description: Distracted by short-term financial gain, humanity is finding itself sleep-walking into a universal surveillance state aiming to monitor and control our every action via omnipresent AI technologies. How to fight back? What we at Nym are doing is returning to the anarchist roots of blockchain by enabling two crucial technologies pioneered by the cypherpunks: mixnets for anonymous internet access and anonymous credentials for private payments that give users control over their identity.
aiDescription:
The video features a speaker reflecting on the importance of the Web3 summit in the development and funding of their privacy-focused blockchain project, NIM. The speaker credits the summit for facilitating vital connections and recounts a serendipitous encounter with an investor that led to significant funding for their project. They express concern over political developments, particularly the support some in the crypto community show for authoritarian figures, and criticize those who seek power approval for mass adoption. The speaker emphasizes that crypto-anarchism stands for no masters or authorities, aligning with personal computing's roots in democratizing technology and resisting power centralization.

The speaker also discusses the origins of cryptocurrency in response to financial crises and social movements like Occupy, pointing out the irony of former activists now endorsing establishment figures. They warn against repeating historical mistakes where industrialists supported fascist leaders for personal gain. Instead, they advocate returning to technology's potential to create decentralized power structures and challenge both commercial and state centralization.

Finally, they introduce NIM's mixnet technology, which provides improved anonymity compared to VPNs and Tor by mixing internet traffic to prevent metadata analysis. The speaker plans to demonstrate this technology later in their talk.

name: Ethereum Culture Expanding in the Infinite Garden
description: This talk will look into the cultural aspect of Ethereum through the lens of the Infinite Garden narrative.
aiDescription: The video features Tomoyuki Saito, a designer at the Ethereum Foundation from Japan, discussing the expanding culture within the Ethereum community. He shares his insights on the community's subcultures and ecosystem, drawing parallels between Ethereum events and cultural experiences like Burning Man. Saito reflects on his first impression of the Ethereum community at DevCon Osaka and emphasizes that Ethereum is not just about technology but also about cultural technology. He illustrates this by showcasing his design work, including website visuals and DevCon logos, and by explaining how culture grows and evolves using music as an analogy. Saito traces the origins of club culture to Jamaica in the 1960s to demonstrate how cultures can start from small beginnings and grow over time. The video delves into the importance of subcultures within Ethereum, such as cypherpunk, and their role in shaping the community's identity and future.

name: End of the Ethereum Killer Narrative; The Future of Onchain Businesses
description: This talk will discuss how advancements in scalability solutions are empowering Ethereum to accommodate a vast network of transactions and interactions, fostering seamless operations for onchain businesses of all scales.
aiDescription:
The video features Melissa Kurtcan, founder and CEO of Satoshi21 Venture Studio, discussing insights from the Chain Reaction Incubator in Southeast Asia and her six years of experience in the cryptocurrency industry. She aims to address the fundamental principles and ideologies of blockchain technology, especially in light of the recent FTX incident. Melissa questions the validity of the "Ethereum killer" narrative, suggesting it might be more marketing hype than reality.

She emphasizes that blockchain is ideologically different from other technologies because it solves technical problems with an ideological approach. The talk will cover Bitcoin's value proposition as decentralized digital scarcity and Ethereum's evolution towards programmable decentralization. Melissa critiques the blockchain trilemma (decentralization, security, scalability) and suggests a multi-chain ecosystem for achieving these goals alongside privacy.

She outlines that to challenge an existing layer one blockchain like Ethereum, a new platform must offer a paradigm shift and execute perfectly to gain market penetration. The summary is that technical superiority alone won't lead to mass adoption without underlying ideology, and she argues against narratives that claim established blockchains like Ethereum are outdated.

description: This talk will introduce a tool pack for builders to be equipped with; new models of incentives, and methodologies of entering the market and engage the community.

The video also covers strategies for acquiring attention, activating audiences, engaging users, and generating revenue. The speaker concludes by stressing the importance of giving before asking and building strong relationships with customers rather than exploiting them.

Varun emphasizes that economic audits are crucial as they simulate real-world scenarios under stress to identify potential economic risks that can affect decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols.

He explains that economic audits consider market conditions, ripple effects across protocols, risk parameters, incentive structures, inter-protocol dependencies, and governance weaknesses. aiDescription:
The video features Tino Bredin discussing RPC (Remote Procedure Call) security, the privacy implications of using an RPC endpoint, and how to enhance the privacy of decentralized applications (dApps) for users. He highlights the importance of transport privacy, focusing on protecting metadata such as IP addresses that are often exposed during internet usage. To illustrate his point, he demonstrates a tool called Derp, which mimics an RPC provider and logs requests made through a user's wallet, revealing how easily metadata can link different user accounts.

Bredin then introduces Hopper's solution to this privacy issue, which involves using the RPC-H SDK within a dApp to anonymize RPC requests by unlinking the user's IP address from their on-chain activity. He provides a hands-on example by showing how to integrate RPC-H into a basic blockchain explorer dApp that fetches and displays block data and transaction logs. The video includes a step-by-step guide on setting up DERP as an RPC endpoint in MetaMask, cloning a GitHub repository with the example dApp code, switching between branches with and without RPC-H integration, and installing necessary dependencies to run the application.

description:
ETHBerlin04

Keynote: Puja Ohlhaver, Mikhail Nikulin - The Silent Strings of Proof of Personhood

Experiments in PoP (where each person has a single, unique identity) have increasingly been touted as a mechanism for tracing information provenance, distributing UBI, and facilitating governance over systems of AI. This talk chronicles Idena's experiment in Proof of Personhood from launch in August 2019 to a crisis in May 2022.

ETHBerlin04 - https://ethberlin.org
A Department of Decentralization event - https://dod.ngo
aiDescription:
The video discusses the concept of "proof of personhood" and its implications for democratic governance, economic distribution, and the authenticity of information in the age of generative AI. The speaker shares their experience with a study conducted on Idena, a blockchain protocol that aims to verify unique human identities to enable democratic processes and potentially govern AI. They critique the protocol based on a research paper titled "Compressed to Zero, the Silent Strings of Personhood," highlighting both its ambitions and challenges.

Idena's founder explains that it was the first blockchain with a one-person-one-vote consensus algorithm designed to prevent bots and account trading through identity staking. The goal was to create a decentralized network operated by individuals, countering centralization issues seen in proof-of-stake systems.

However, as Idena grew, suspicious patterns emerged suggesting automation or human farms where individuals were paid to perform validation ceremonies without understanding or controlling their private keys. This raised concerns about the integrity of the proof of personhood concept and whether it can be compromised by such practices.

He emphasizes the importance of high-quality supply for read operations on blockchains and explains how this concept extends beyond Web3 to decentralized social platforms and large language models (LLMs).

The video features a discussion on the current and future state of real-world assets (RWAs) and stablecoins in the cryptocurrency space. Vlad, the founder and CEO of a leading marketing studio based in Dubai, hosts the show, emphasizing the importance of RWAs as a driving force in the industry. The panel includes experts like Mathew Vanikert, who has experience with stablecoins and programmable money; Jack from a Japanese consulting firm leading web strategy; and Nikhil, a blockchain developer from India.

The conversation explores various topics such as the common use cases for RWAs beyond real estate, like tokenizing movies or intellectual property. name: Interplanetary Banking System
description: This talk will talk about lending in the future, if our current infra is sufficient for truly tokenized economy and what is missing to support humans as multi-planetary species.
aiDescription:
The video features a presentation on the concept of an Interplanetary Banking System (IPBS), exploring how lending could operate in the future, including the possibility of mortgages on Mars. The speaker discusses the evolution of banking from face-to-face interactions to blockchain technology, which removes geographical constraints and is enforced by code rather than law. The presentation covers how financial transactions have evolved with communication advancements, from hand-delivered letters to instant global transactions via the internet and blockchain.

The speaker outlines a hypothetical scenario where someone buys property on Mars and secures a mortgage with specific terms, using a tokenized asset as collateral. They delve into various aspects of this futuristic lending system, such as interest rates that could vary based on external conditions like sandstorms, borrower-specific default conditions, and different liquidation processes.

The presentation emphasizes flexibility in lending protocols, advocating for modular designs that can adapt to change and cater to different needs. The speaker suggests that instead of trying to predict future requirements, we should create systems that are responsive and can integrate new modules for functions like interest calculation, default management, and liquidation.

In summary, the video is about envisioning an adaptable and decentralized financial system for an interplanetary future where anyone can engage in financial transactions without the constraints of traditional banking systems or physical borders

name: Panel discussion: Validators and Staking Communities
description: Knowing how to run blockchain nodes is a high leverage skill and highly monetizing. Need to invest time and effort for sure but no prior technical background is needed.
aiDescription:
The video features a panel discussion with Daniel from Kintsugi, Sam aka Stakersaurus, James He from Prism, and Colby from the Ethereum Foundation (EF). They discuss various challenges and topics related to Ethereum staking and validators. Daniel talks about running Ethereum validators and the challenges of incentivization, particularly in developing countries. Sam shares his work on expanding the solo staker talent pool in Asia and his role with Lido's Community Staking Module. James addresses technical issues with validator queues and upcoming improvements in the next hard fork. Colby touches upon execution destruction and the potential conflict of interest for the EF in staking.

They debate issues such as liquid vs. solo staking, capital efficiency, user experience problems, hardware costs for validators, decentralization concerns, OFAC compliance among staking providers, and how it conflicts with censorship resistance. There's also a discussion on the dominance of large staking protocols like Lido and their impact on network centralization.

The conversation highlights ideological differences between maintaining decentralization principles versus practical realities like legal compliance. They conclude that more solo stakers are needed to maintain decentralization and suggest that improvements to Ethereum's core development process could help address some of these concerns. The video aims to provide insights into the complexities of Ethereum staking

name: TLSNotary: Bridging Data from web2 to web3 Using Privacy-Preserving MPC
description: TLSNotary is an open-source project that utilizes MPC-TLS (Multi-Party Computation-Transport Layer Security) to enable users to prove and share their data while preserving their privacy.
aiDescription:

He explains that TLS Notary is part of Privacy and Scaling Explorations, a research lab funded by the Ethereum Foundation, which focuses on programmable cryptography and building proof-of-concept applications.

Chris provides an overview of Transport Layer Security (TLS), emphasizing its role in ensuring secure communication on the internet by confirming data origin and integrity but lacking portability. name: Enter the Portal Network
description: This talk with introduce a decentralized way for all users to access Ethereum in a resource efficient way, but still maintain full access to the state.
aiDescription:
The video discusses the challenges of accessing Ethereum in a decentralized manner due to the high requirements for running a full node, such as significant storage, constant operation, and technical knowledge. The speaker introduces the portal network as a solution that allows nodes to store only the data they need, reducing the burden on individual nodes while maintaining access to necessary information. The portal network operates on a peer-to-peer protocol and utilizes distributed hash tables for data storage, ensuring that data remains accessible and isn't flushed from the network. The incentive model for the portal network is based on low participation costs with high data value. The speaker outlines various networks within the portal framework, including ones dedicated to history, state, and transactions, and explains how data validation works using accumulators and Merkle-Patricia trees.

The timeline for launching different components of the portal network is discussed, with some parts already operational. Portal integration could significantly reduce storage requirements for running a validator or full node. The speaker mentions upcoming improvements like vercal tries and an EIP that would allow offloading old blocks. They also highlight that participation in the portal network requires minimal resources.

name: VDF-Based On-Chain Random Beacon: Practice and Challenges
description: This talk will discuss constructing a VDF-based on-chain Distributed Random Beacon (DRB), introduce two VDF mechanisms, share optimization techniques, and compare applications of Commit-Reveal schemes enhanced by VDF, noting the challenges in blockchain environments.
aiDescription:
The video discusses the development of a distributed random beacon (DRV) for an L2 blockchain due to the lack of support from existing oracle services. The DRV is essential for applications that require secure random numbers, such as leader elections and lotteries. The presenter emphasizes the importance of liveness in DRVs, which ensures that random numbers are generated even if some participants disrupt the process. They introduce the commit-reveal-recover scheme using VDF (Verifiable Delay Function) as a solution to achieve strong liveness, allowing recovery of random numbers if the process is interrupted.

The challenges of implementing VDF on Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) are addressed, focusing on verifying VDF evaluations within smart contracts. Two types of VDFs, Pitchfork and Wesolowski's, are compared in terms of gas costs and implementation complexity. The video also touches on the concept of hash-to-prime functions.

name: Growing The Infinite Garden for Humanity
description: This talk will discuss the challenges and opportunities to play the infinite-game in a self-devouring capitalist environment.
aiDescription: The video features a speaker from the Ethereum Foundation discussing the progress of Ethereum and its impact on local communities, developers, and real-world applications. The speaker highlights the importance of hackathons in fostering Web3 talent and commends the Japanese Ethereum community for organizing such events. They reflect on Ethereum's nearly 10-year history, emphasizing the growth in active contributors and advancements in scalability, user experience, and privacy. The transition from proof of work to proof of stake through the merge is mentioned as a significant milestone for decentralization and environmental impact. The speaker also touches on Ethereum’s educational initiatives, including its integration into Buenos Aires high school curriculum. Lastly, they explore real-world use cases of Ethereum-based solutions like decentralized IDs and voting tools, emphasizing their transformative potential in areas like Latin America.

name: Panel discussion: Deep diving into DAOs
description: Discussing the current state and future of DAOs.
aiDescription: The video features a discussion on Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), their nature, opportunities, and the experiences of two individuals deeply involved in the space. Kazi, an organizer of a DAO-themed hackathon and contributor to a known DAO, shares insights into what DAOs mean to him and their uniqueness in preserving on-chain community activities. Chogo, a developer focused on smart contracts, discusses how DAOs can be applied to real-life communities and projects he's worked on. They explore various definitions of DAOs, including their key components like treasuries and voting mechanisms. The conversation also touches on Bitcoin's relationship with DAO principles and the potential for non-monetary incentive structures within DAO communities. They delve into the technical aspects of smart contracts and how they're essential to DAO functionality. The video also discusses the application of DAOs in business settings, local governance, and cultural preservation, highlighting real-world examples and potential impacts on societal issues like population decline. Fundamental steps for starting a DAO are also briefly covered for those new to the space.

name: Satoshi’s Legacy: Giving AI the sense of space
description: This talk explores how Satoshi Nakamoto's invention of Bitcoin sparked a decentralization movement that is reshaping human organization. It highlights the shift from traditional, centralized models to decentralized networks where AI and individuals collaboratively manage infrastructure and economic activity on a global scale.
aiDescription:
The video features a speaker discussing the legacy of Satoshi Nakamoto, the creator of Bitcoin, and predicting that it will not be Bitcoin itself but rather the foundation for decentralized machine perception and AI interaction with the physical world. The speaker draws parallels between rapid urban development and AI growth, suggesting that machine-to-machine transactions will dominate future economies. They argue that AIs will need to buy collaborative spatial computing resources to navigate and understand the physical world.

The speaker also touches upon how current tech giants are investing in spatial computing, which is crucial for AR devices and autonomous machines but raises privacy concerns due to potential surveillance capitalism. They introduce an alternative concept called Deepin (decentralized physical infrastructure networks), which allows people to deploy large-scale infrastructure projects collaboratively. Specifically, they present their project as a decentralized network for machine perception called PostMesh, which aims to provide an external sense of space for machines.

The project is already being piloted in retail environments to improve inventory management and communication through spatial computing. The speaker announces the launch of their token and a grant program to encourage developers to contribute to this decentralized protocol, aiming to prevent a future where centralized entities like Optimus robots become the primary source of data collection. For more information or involvement, viewers are directed to their website and Twitter page.

description: Demo - Cursive Connections

transcripts.text: Hi everyone, I'm Vivek. I'm presenting on behalf of a five-person team. Rachel, Tessa, and Steven are all here, if you want to raise your hands. And Andrew is coming in a week. But yeah, I want to talk about Cursive Connections, both what is there today and what we're looking forward to over the next few weeks. A little bit about Cursive, we're a research and design lab building cryptography for human connection. We're a research and design lab building cryptography for human connection. So using a lot of different advanced cryptography tools and trying to figure out ways to enable people to connect and coordinate more effectively with them. And Curse of Connections is an app experience that we're hoping to do exactly that. With one sort of key focus being around importing a lot of data about yourself and choosing how you reveal and share that with other people. So what's the tech behind it? Bunch of fancy three-letter acronyms, but the main tools involved are something called multi-party computation and fully homomorphic encryption. All of this is sort of abstracted behind the UI, but all of this enables kind of privacy-preserving sharing of different data. In addition, there's also a lot of ZK stuff going on, but that's not as much of a focus these days. How to use it. So actually, all attendees that have this sort of black wristband can get started with this. All you have to do is take the kind of white chip on your wristband and tap it with your phone. Top of your iPhone, middle of your Android. Two things to catch is that if you have an Android, make sure NFC is on. And in general, airplane mode has to be off, unfortunately, to use this. And yeah, please come talk to me or Steven afterwards if you're having any difficulties. We're happy to debug that. And there's some more instructions here if you're still trying to figure that out. So where is it at today? Basically, there's two simple features. The first thing is being able to share socials on tap. So as you sign up, you basically set up very simple like Telegram, Twitter, and so when you tap on someone else's badge, you can easily share this sort of thing. And you can also basically attach like labels and notes to people as you meet them to remember kind of context for how you met them and see them sort of in like a big kind of like contacts view. The other sort of like cryptographic feature involved is that as you register, you basically can set up some initial set of tags based on how you want to connect with people at the event. And you can use something called private set intersection to when you're sort of both viewing each other's profiles and you click discover, you can do a little computation to see where the overlap is, both in these sorts of interests as well as shared contacts. So all this right now is very minimal. The past few weeks has been focused on backend work so we can add lots of cool stuff during this month. But coming very soon this week, I just wanted to give some highlights. One thing is a flower garden. So we love visualizing all this sort of stuff for people to learn what's going on behind the scenes. And one thing is every single connection you have will be represented as a flower. And as you learn more stuff about each other, as you interact with each other, as you have more shared context, this flower will grow over the course of the event. And it'll give you this sort of like unique kind of artifact of your experience here at the end of the event. Another thing is just adding a lot more data. Right now, the data is very minimal. It's just a few tags because we want our registration to be really smooth, but we want to have people add custom tags. I know that was a feature request from some folks, as well as importing data from other platforms to give you more stuff to connect over. And finally also just being able to edit all the details in your profile. All of it right now is static, but that'll be added in very soon. And I want to give a little bit of a kind of shout out for some of the main kind of themes we're looking to test by the end of the month. The first is something called narrowcasting. So this is the opposite of broadcasting. And the idea here is instead of kind of posting publicly to a big group chat or like on a public forum like social layer, you can instead set private filters for information that you have and get it to the most relevant folks, where only people that sort of match those criteria will be able to decrypt this information. And we think this can enable a lot more efficient coordination and communication between folks in this community and sort of beyond. The second is this idea of super connectors. So as you meet more people and as you do these sorts of private set intersections and learn more about them, we want the app to basically be able to surface to you like, hey, you know, like, these two people, Alice and Bob, and, you know, from what you know about them, they have a lot in common, or they have a lot of complementary things. And you can start basically, like, kind of bringing your social graph together by recommending folks to meet and get to know each other. And finally is this idea of digital pheromones. Pheromone, for those unfamiliar, is, like, this chemical substance that's produced by animals to coordinate with other people of the same species. And we want to build some sort of like digital version of this, where it's kind of a lightweight undetectable signal that you can discover synergy with in a way that you have full control over. It's privacy preserving, but can just enable kind of more serendipitous and synergistic connections to occur at the event. That's all from us. We're funded by Privacy and Scalable Explorations. Shout out to them, and this is some other places to follow us. Thank you.

description: Demo - OHM Wisdom

transcripts.text: Hey everyone, so I'm going to be sharing about decentralized autonomous value accounting with a system that's called Wisdom. And I've gone backwards. There we go. So the question is, how can a community quantify the relative value of diverse contributions and incentivize engagement? And this is the question that I've been thinking about in the context of academia, designing solutions for the last six years or so, and prototyping for the last three. And this has brought me to develop a framework that's called Wisdom, and there's six main stages. The first is for the community to record contributions, which can be any actions, ideas, or resources that they think are valuable, along with some number of dimensions that they think that those contributions should be rated on. Now, reviews are really simple. We just give someone two contributions and ask them to tell us which is more X, where X is each dimension of interest. And the unique part of our model is that we recognize those reviews as valuable contributions in their own right. We award them with one unit of value, and then we include generic representations of reviews in the contribution set to be reviewed themselves. So now we're reviewing reviews. So this is called meta review. And here, it's the same as before, except you're giving someone a regular contribution and asking them to compare that to some number of reviews. So I did embed a little video which is way too little. I'll just keep going. I'll just talk you through it. So basically in this little video, tiny little thing in the corner, there's going to be two regular reviews and two meta reviews and we were prototyping in the context of festivals so we have some festival contributions there the person's just choosing between like a fireflow performance and I think it was some money and then on the the next one you're about to see they're then doing this meta review where they're comparing say a fireflow performance to 100 of these pairwise comparisons and the key thing is that every time someone does one of these, they get their little token counter goes up in the corner. And so they're getting a direct incentive every time they do a review. And they're getting a dopamine button hit to keep on clicking buttons. And so the way we scale this is we include a range of these reviews in the meta review process. And this generates a data set that allows us to fit a baseline. And then we can use that function to automatically calculate the value of any contribution to the community. And so because we can do this for any dimension, we can automatically produce a multidimensional representation of the unique qualities of any contribution to that community. And from there, I think you can see it's relatively simple to then move to an automated reward mechanism. And we can also generate reputation scores that represent the value that someone's added over time so that we can use those for automated governance. And so this is just a flag that we prototyped, like I said, in the space of festivals, but we've now generalized and shown that it can also apply to the space of festivals, but we've now generalized and shown that it can also apply to the space of academia through reviewing contributions to an open science conference. And everything that we're creating is completely open, free, and available for use. So I'd love to meet people that are interested in this idea. We've got some spreadsheet prototypes that anyone can use and explore for their own community. We're also developing or designing at the moment an MVP and we've got a great international developer community but we could definitely use some help with design management and blockchain expertise. And question on my mind is the use of graph databases so if anyone here knows about that stuff I would love to chat with you. And just a flag that we've got interest from the world's largest meta-science conference in June of next year, so we're aiming to sort of really hit the world stage at that one.

So this is cumbersome. It takes time. We have to understand complexity of the markets, but sometimes we have the basic the basic intent to to make money or to save money for particular for particular purpose and I think that's Really the if you simplify it the only thing that matters in the end for the regular person or for any person is You wake up in the morning. name: Should Gnosis Become an L2?
description: The debate centers on whether Gnosis Chain should maintain its position as a Layer 1 blockchain or transition to become a Layer 2 solution for Ethereum. This decision involves fundamental trade-offs between sovereignty and integration, weighing Gnosis's commitment to credible neutrality against potential benefits of deeper Ethereum ecosystem integration. Layer 1 blockchains offer complete autonomy and independent security, while Layer 2s provide scalability advantages and seamless Ethereum interoperability.

description: This talk will discuss my EPF work on Nethermind's IL-EVM project, which included developing tools to analyze EVM execution patterns, writing  (optimised) opcode and top pattern implementations, and conducting and writing tests.

name: Control or Convenience: The Clash Between Local Apps and Cloud Services in the Future of Blockchain
description: The debate between local apps and cloud services centers on trade-offs between security, decentralization, performance, scalability, and user experience. Local apps offer greater control, security, and alignment with blockchain's decentralized ethos, but they may face challenges in scalability and user accessibility. Cloud services, while offering scalability, performance, and ease of use, introduce concerns about centralization, data privacy, and regulatory compliance.

name: Ethereum's Crossroads: Maximize Capacity or Prioritize Participation?
description: The "Larger Blockspace vs. Ability to Run Chain on Lower Spec Devices" debate is a fundamental discussion about the direction of blockchain development. It revolves around the trade-offs between increasing a blockchain's capacity to handle more transactions (through larger block sizes) and maintaining accessibility by ensuring the blockchain can be run on less powerful, lower-spec devices. It addresses the trade-offs between enhancing the network's capacity and performance versus ensuring it remains accessible and decentralized.

name: Navigating Adoption: Can Blockchain Scale Without Sacrificing Its Values?
description: The "Onboard the next 1B vs. Onboard the next 1M" debate is fundamentally about growth strategy. Should the focus be on building a massive, mainstream user base as quickly as possible, potentially at the cost of some blockchain ideals? Or should the effort be on cultivating a smaller, more engaged community that will ensure the technology’s integrity and long-term success? The answer often depends on the specific goals of the blockchain project and its vision for the future.

name: Should MEV be Tackled at Application Layer or Protocol Level?
description: The debate focuses on the optimal level at which to address Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) in blockchain systems - whether at the foundational protocol level or through application-layer solutions. MEV represents value that can be extracted from blockchain systems through transaction ordering, front-running, and sandwich attacks, affecting user experience and fairness. This conflict explores where in the blockchain stack MEV should be primarily addressed to maximize effectiveness while maintaining system efficiency.

In that case, that means that in equilibrium, 99% of the MEV ends up going to the smart contract instead of the sequencer. And you can actually make this arbitrarily large. You can make it 99.999% ends up going to the smart contract rather than the sequencer. Now, what is this ultimately? I think the best way to think about it is an auction. The smart contract is auctioning off the right to interact with it first, but normally this is an auction that's happening for the benefit of the sequencer, and MEV taxes means that it happens for the benefit of the application. And ultimately the application is in the best position to give it back to its users and properly allocate it to the users. The searcher is making the exact same amount of money that they were before. So before, there was some amount of profit that the sequencer was going to make. That's the little green bar there. But most of the MEV was going to be paid as part of the priority fee, which basically just currently goes to the sequencer. Once you've added MEV taxes, the green bar stays the same. The searcher isn't paying anything different because they're changing how they bid. They're changing the priority fee that they pay because of the MEV tax. Instead of paying the full amount of the MEV or the MEV minus their profit to the sequencer in priority fee, instead they're setting a much lower priority fee because they know they're going to need to pay this 99 times larger Mev tax. So searcher changes their behavior. They still pay the exact same amount, make the exact same profit total. What happens is the proposer, the sequencer, gets less in priority fees and the application gets gets all of it. So I think this is a very powerful primitive. It actually covers a lot of what we think about when we think about MeV. So one example is automated market makers that capture MeV for their LPs. So this is this famous problem of loss versus rebalancing. If you can auction off the right to interact with your AMM first in the block, then you can capture that MeV for yourself and give it to your LPs. case, and I think in my view the motivating case for MevTax is order routers like Uniswap X. This is a case where searches are optimally routing users. Basically you put an order in and you say I want whoever is able to fill this order at the best price. A user is trying to sell 1 ETH. Whoever is able to give the most USDC in exchange for that 1 ETH gets to fill the order. And the way the MevTax is with the Uniswap X work, and this is in test right now. It's actually been prototyped and running live on base right now, is searchers are bidding to pay the most USDC possible to that user. And that gets them actually included first in the block. So it's a way to have this auction for Uniswap X happen on-chain, which used to be an off-chain auction for order routing, now it's happening on-chain as part of this priority auction. Another example is oracles that capture value that is created by their updates. So example, suppose you have an on-chain order book and you just want applications that interact with it, you want users when they interact with it to be able to cancel transactions before anyone is able to fill orders on that order book. Again, I'm not sure this is necessarily the best design for an on-chain order book, but it's one kind of thing you might want to do with a sequencing rule. And you can do this, actually, with just priority ordering. What's cool is people have talked about ways to do this, build in different lanes into the end of the blockchain itself, but you really don't need that. the transactions are ordered by priority, and you could build application-specific sequencing on top of it. So here we say, if you're going to cancel an order, you have to include it in a transaction that has priority greater than some number n. And if you're going to fill a transaction, you have to include it in a transaction that has priority less than that number n. And so that gives us blocks where all cancels end up preceding all fills. And so market makers who want to cancel their orders because the prices have moved, they get the right to do that. And they're not competing for MEV with the users who are trying to fill. You don't have to run your own relayers or anything. This just works. And searches can just follow it and obey it. Another benefit is that applications remain composable and atomic with on-chain liquidity to what I think is about as well as it can do. We want on-chain liquidity to be competitivections on-chain. And that's what Uniswap X with MEV taxes does. It's particularly useful, I think, for complex auctions, like Uniswap X order routing. And the nice thing here is with Uniswap X, in addition to making on-chain liquidity competitive, it also means that you get these fillers who are able to now search the chain and find the most compelling routes to find the best prices for users and fill them on chain. And I think that's just always going to be more sophisticated than just any order router that Uniswap or anyone else could try to write, because it becomes a competitive process. So there are some challenges to priority ordering. I think the biggest one is it requires the block reposer, or in the L2 case, the sequencer, to obey these rules of competitive ordering. And that could potentially help make these auctions more fair. And then the other line of research that's going on in this is Rollup Boost, which is the work being done by Flashbots as a TE builder for L2s being prototyped for the Unichain. name: Reimagining Layer 0: New Worlds and Ancient Philosophies
description: Where the early internet was an expression of freedom, liberty, and democratising virtual spaces, etc. Today, our digital spaces are breaking and have not met that promise. The Web3 space also faces scams, degen behaviour, and capture by centralised actors.  How do we guide Ethereum to stay aligned with human values as we build a new world?  Revisiting ancient Asian philosophies can help us reimagine a new world from Layer0.

speakers.name: Dev Lewis
speakers.bio:
Dev is a researcher & public speaker, workshop designer/facilitator, and community builder at the intersections of digital tech, law and policy, geopolitics, and asian philosophy. 
His podcast Light Forest traces the roots to global crises through Asian philosophical lens. As a founder of digi-cnx he is building a network of Web3 and digital technology focussed change makers in Chiang Mai.

name: What’s Going Into the Pectra Upgrade?
description: A talk explaining the core EIPs going into the Pectra upgrade and the core EIPs still TBD for inclusion in Pectra. The talk will also touch on Pectra timing and fork scoping for the next hard fork after Pectra. Finally, the talk will share insights about the governance process of Ethereum in light of Pectra and takeaways about the priorities of Ethereum protocol developers.

speakers.name: Christine Kim
speakers.bio: Christine Kim is a Vice President on the Research team at Galaxy Digital. Prior to joining the firm, she worked for three years at a crypto media company called CoinDesk as an analyst and tech reporter, mainly covering developments on Ethereum. She holds a BA in Economics and International Relations from the University of British Columbia.

name: Why VPNs are scams and what to do about it
description: Existing VPNs are essentially scams. Free VPNs and most centralized VPNs (such as ExpressVPN, owned by Kape) are effectively data harvesting companies.  Decentralized VPNs usually have a few large servers and offer barely any more privacy than centralized VPNs. What is missing is 1) onion-routing packets like Tor 2)  adding noise (fake traffic) 3) censorship-resistance and 4) mixing packets from different users together. We'll explore how technologies work to defeat even AI adversaries.

name: Introduction to Multilateral Trade Credit Set-off in MPC
description: Multilateral Trade Credit Set-off is a process for collecting outstanding invoices from a network of firms and detecting cycles. A cycle is a circular pattern of due payments that connects businesses. Removing a cycle yields liquidity savings for the firms involved. This process is done by a central agency that collects the invoices and performs the netting. Instead, we leverage MPC to perform the set-ff while preserving the privacy of sensitive financial data of the firms

name: Mopro: Make Client-side Proving on Mobile Easy
description:
Mopro is a toolkit for ZK app development on mobile. Mopro makes client-side proving on mobile simple. Mopro aims to connect different adapters with different platforms. In this talk, we will share:
- How to use Mopro to develop your own ZK mobile app.
- What is the current development progress, including the current supported proving systems, supported platforms, and mobile GPU exploration results. 
- Moreover, we will share the challenges that Mopro faces and our future roadmap.

name: Understanding EIP-7002 and EIP-6110
description: The first part will be an overview of EIP-7002, explaining how it works, why adding this extra option to exit validators is important, and addressing some of the UX challenges of this approach. The second part will be a technical overview of EIP-6110, explaining the UX improvements for validators depositing on the beacon chain, the removal of pre-merge technical debt as well as a quick look at the EIP implementation in Teku.

speakers.name: Lucas Saldanha
speakers.bio: Lucas is an Ethereum enthusiast and passionate about protocol development. He has been working at Consensys for the past seven years as a protocol engineer. Lucas has worked both on Besu, an Execution Layer client, and Teku, an Consensus Layer client.

name: Bridging TradFi and DeFi through Ethereum and EVM: A Pathway to Innovation
description: This workshop will explore how Ethereum and EVM-based environments are becoming the critical intersection between traditional finance (TradFi) and decentralized finance (DeFi). It will focus on Ethereum’s maturity for real-world use cases, the role of EVM in regulated environments, and how  institutions, governments, and central banks can foster innovation by leveraging permissionless blockchains while maintaining compliance with regulations.
