name: Oracles for number values
description: We will overview the history and state of research on how to design a cryptoeconomic oracle that outputs a number value. One wants such tools for price oracles, but also for bringing other information on-chain, e.g. the damages to award from an on-chain insurance contract. We will look at approaches ranging from Vitalik's 2014 SchellingCoin proposal to ideas drawing from social choice theory, including based on recent research. We will explore tradeoffs including resistance to several attacks.

speakers.name: William George
speakers.bio: William George has a PhD in mathematics from the University of Toronto. His thesis was on number theory problems related to elliptic curve cryptography. William began actively researching problems related to blockchains during postdoctoral fellowships at the University of Toronto and at École Polytechnique (Palaiseau, France). William has been doing crypto-economics research for the blockchain-based dispute resolution platform Kleros since 2018.

name: Clookup - Composite Function based Lookup Argument
description: Presenting Clookup, a novel lookup protocol that enhances efficiency in verifiable computations. By using a composite function approach and multivariate polynomials within the sumcheck protocol, Clookup achieves optimal time complexity \(O(m(m+n))\) when processing \(2^m\) witness elements against a \(2^n\) table. This method eliminates the need to compute coefficient forms of composite functions.

name: Anon-Aadhaar Protocol using Halo2 and Noir

name: How to Audit Smart Contract Languages: Brief Intro
description:
In this talk, we’ll dive into the unique challenges and considerations when auditing a smart contract language, as opposed to auditing individual smart contracts. We’ll cover:

- Things to Look For: Key aspects of a smart contract language that need review.
- Mindset Difference: Shifting from a contract-centric to a language-centric perspective, focusing on broader systemic issues rather than isolated contract logic.

name: Double entry point issues - From breaking Compound to Uniswap v4
description: A short explanation of a critical-severity vulnerability we found in the Uniswap V4 core contracts that would have caused a ~$15M loss in Uniswap's pools. name: Blockchain for humanitarian aid disbursements
description: This panel will discuss learnings from a UNICEF Nepal pilot using blockchain to create an efficient, transparent, and accountable aid distribution system. We’ll cover collaboration between UNICEF Nepal, Local Government and Rahat to develop and implement the technology for underbanked and unbanked communities. Additionally, we’ll explore expanding smart contract use in anticipatory action for preemptive climate disaster responses.

speakers.name: Rumee Singh
speakers.bio: Rumee, CEO of a UNICEF Innovation Fund portfolio startup, leads Rahat, a financial access platform focused on cash assistance and building financial resilience for the most vulnerable against climate shocks. With over 20 years of global leadership, Rumee Singh is celebrated among Nepal's leading women in tech; a 2023 MIT Solver and is featured in the Women for Change 2024 global campaign. Rumee is an electronics engineer and also has a journalism degree from Boston.

name: Keynote: Lessons learned from Tor
description: I will share lessons learned during Tor's twenty years as free software fighting for privacy and human rights. We'll talk about distributed trust and privacy by design, how to help people understand the good uses of your tech, getting allies in both cypherpunks and government, why transparency and community-building are so essential to trust, and successes from other spaces. It may seem like the crypto wars never really end, but we all have a part to play in saving the world.

speakers.name: Roger Dingledine

Roger works with journalists and activists on many continents to help them understand and defend against the threats they face, and he is a prominent researcher in the online anonymity field. EFF picked him for a Pioneer Award, and Foreign Policy magazine chose him as one of its top 100 global thinkers.

name: Keynote: How to Properly Open Source Software:  Lessons Learned from the Linux Foundation
description: It can be challenging to properly open source software:  there are licenses, IP, security reporting, and many other issues that need to be addressed.  In this talk, we will discuss the best practices for open source software development learned from almost 25 years of experience at the Linux Foundation.  Attendees will learn about how to set up their projects for a variety of potential goals, including things like maximizing security and community building.

speakers.name: Hart Montgomery
speakers.bio: Hart Montgomery is the CTO of Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust and serves as the ED of the Post-Quantum Cryptography Alliance. Hart previously worked in blockchain and cryptography research at Fujitsu where he helped lead Fujitsu’s efforts in Hyperledger. Prior to Fujitsu, Hart received a Ph.D. in cryptography at Stanford. Hart has numerous academic publications and patents in cryptography and blockchain and brings a wealth of experience in these areas to the LF.

speakers.name: Nicholas Paul
speakers.bio: Nicholas thinks about thinking. He is currently researching and realizing a new project focused on the ‘thinking’ part of ‘long-term thinking’. Before this, Nicholas helped run The Long Now Foundation—the storied nonprofit fostering long-term thinking at the timescale of 10,000 years—where he served as both Director of Development and Director of Strategy for many years. His background spans systems engineering and philosophy. He is currently a fellow at The Institute in San Francisco.

name: Public epistemics and futarchy
description: 35 years ago I began outlining a vision of how betting markets could offer informed credibly-neutral estimates on far more disputed topics. I elaborated 25 years ago on how decision markets could support neutral governance, and 21 years ago on how combinatorial markets allow estimates on all possible combinations for existing topics. Now in the last year, we are seeing substantial crypto-based trials, especially re governance. In this talk, I’ll paint a picture of where all this could go.

So this happened. In the last few years, as I mentioned, we've had a number of efforts to apply this concept of conditional markets to governance. First, there is a secretive India-based government medical organization that's done roughly a half a dozen markets where they've asked hundreds of thousands of their customers to bet on various health policies that they've adopted or not. I think they adopted five out of six. A little bit later, we have the MetaDAO, which has apparently now done 23 proposals for governance of the MetaDAO, and only six of those were rejected. They have some customers now. 14 proposals, three rejected. You know, a lot of volume in trade. MetaDAO is now apparently focusing more on using governance to advise, say, MetaDAO grant proposals. Estimating the consequence of a grant proposal and seeing which ones to fund. There are some other organizations in this space. And I apologize if I don't know about yours and not mentioning them, but one that I do know about is called Buttery, and they're also focusing on this idea of funding projects in terms of estimating the outcomes for the projects. And I'm advising lots of these efforts, and in particular, I am chief scientist here at Futarki.fi, which was previously named Quiver. We have at least one customer, which is Gnosis, to do governance for them. We'll do it for ourselves. And we are interested in the question of how to do governance for organizations without bothering the bosses who don't want to be replaced. And one promising application there is the relationship between investors and managers. Often they're in dispute about when to raise more money and maybe a future arching mechanism can sit as an intermediary there to help them make that decision. All right, now, but I warned you about social dark matter. Key thing is that I've been describing a simple, elegant idea. There are a bunch of issues that we've worked through in a talk yesterday. I went through a number of the technical issues and problems. But just in general, all real-world things are not just simple, elegant ideas. They have a lot of messy details. And so we just need real- world experiments to work out those details because in some sense we don't fully understand human behavior. There's a lot of social dark matter. There's a lot of ways in which we make simple theories that should work and they don't. So we just need to try things. Let me elaborate a bit. Imagine we put an autistic person in the C suite of a typical corporation. They are a person who knows the business very well. They are very knowledgeable and informed about key decisions, but they have no social savvy. Whenever a topic comes up, they just blurt out whatever they think the truth is without having any idea whose agendas might be squashed by that. Such a person will just not last in the C-suite. they might become a trusted advisor of somebody else nearby but they won't be sitting there but that's in essence what prediction markets are they are very smart and knowledgeable things that speak the truth without knowing who's bothered by that and that highlights the fact that modern organizations a lot of what they do is politics and massaging and messages and so we need to search in the space of how to place these things in organizations. And 20 years ago, there was a wave of prediction market applications, and hundreds of firms tried them. But even though they typically had more accurate estimates, satisfied users, the experiments didn't continue, largely because of objections from managements who really got pissed when the market disagreed with them and the market was right. And so we need to deal with that. So a more concrete example, even, think of a project manager who has a deadline. They want to know what the chance of making the deadline, but they also want to have a good excuse if they fail. How will they do that? Well, their favorite excuse if they fail is to say, well, we were going along just fine until the last minute when something came out of left field, some weird thing, it's so rare and it'll never happen again, so let's just forget about it. And the problem is the prediction market gets in the way of that because it tells you a long time before, you were going to fail, you're going to fail, and you can't say we didn't know that until the last minute. So you can see we need to overcome this sort of a problem in organizations in order to be able to field them. And that's why we need to be doing these experiments, which I'm excited to be doing. And that's my talk.

name: How crypto is used in Africa today? Hear from leading builders
description:
How are Africans using crypto at scale, and what has been the impact on society? Last year Africa saw close to $120B onchain transactions, and 10%-20% of major countries' populations used crypto. 

What problems are the top African founders solving for retail and businesses? What are the technical + non-technical friction points they face in building for the fastest growing markets in the world?

Hear African founders share lessons, nuances, and user behavior from the front lines.

speakers.name: Yoseph Ayele
speakers.bio:
Building an open, permissionless, and borderless economy for the African market, powered by Web3. Founder, Borderless Africa and magma: a coordination point for Africa's leading founders. 
General Partner, LAVA, investing in early stage Africa focused startups that are building utility-driven and scalable applications for the fastest growing market in the world.

speakers.name: Yele Bademosi
speakers.bio: Co-Creator of Onboard, a digital money app for creators and dreamers.

speakers.name: David Nandwa
speakers.bio: David Nandwa is a serial entrepreneur as well as CEO/CTO & Founder @ HoneyCoin, before HoneyCoin he's worked as a software engineer at or with leading companies like Flutterwave and Andela. He's started, scaled, and exited two ventures prior to HoneyCoin and has a passion for finance and building real-world solutions to hard problems on the continent.

name: Debunking Myths about Building out of SEA
description: South East Asia is home to a burgeoning community of builders and some of the most influential projects in Ethereum. Listen in as SEA founders share their experiences and answer your questions about building out of this corner of the world.

speakers.name: Harith Kamarul
speakers.bio: Product at Etherscan & Organiser at ETHKL

name: Wtf are based rollups and preconfs?
description:
The rollup-centric roadmap is critical for scaling Ethereum but has introduced fragmentation of users, developers, and liquidity. But don't worry, based rollups are here to save the day! But wtf is a “based rollup”? And wtf are these “pre-confs” that usually get talked about together?

The focus of this talk is to demystify these concepts and try and get more people engaged in the based rollup ecosystem, which has the potential to heal Ethereum’s fragmentation problem.

name: Based Preconfirmations with MR-MEV-Boost
description: In this talk, we will analyze a simple strawman setup of based preconfirmations to highlight its challenges, such as supply chain centralization, the lack of pricing mechanisms, and latency/spam races. We will then introduce MR-MEV-Boost, a preconfirmation solution that runs multiple rounds of MEV-Boost auctions within a single slot. This solution addresses the mentioned challenges by preconfirming batches instead of individual transactions and better integrating with the L1 PBS pipeline.

name: Defcon at Devcon: A table top experience
description:
It's 3am and your phone is blowing up—Telegram, Signal, Discord, X—all are saying your project just got rekt. Your team is panicking and begging you to sign off on a quick protocol upgrade. What do you do?

Join our workshop to get hands-on with crisis management in web3. Learn to handle attacks, keep cool under pressure, and manage your stakeholders. By the end, you'll turn this crisis into manageable challenges, protect your project, and keep building.

speakers.name: Heidi Wilder
speakers.bio: Heidi Wilder is a part of the Unit 0x team at Coinbase, where she focuses on identifying and preventing on chain threats. Besides on chain analysis, one of her passions is protecting people and teams from becoming victims of hacks, thefts, and scams and making the crypto space safer for everyone.

speakers.name: Peter Kacherginsky
speakers.bio: Peter Kacherginsky is one of the most respected blockchain security researchers in the industry. He founded first of their kind Blockchain Security and Unit 0x teams at Coinbase to make ecosystem safer for all. Peter also publishes a weekly BlockThreat newsletter where he advises 10k+ subscribers on the latest developments in the blockchain security industry. He is passionate about using his extensive knowledge of past hacks, threat actors and their tactics to educate the DeFi community.

name: How I Audit
description:
Dom, a former lead auditor at Trail of Bits, is going to give a peek of what it's like to be an auditor in 2024. Some of the techniques and tools discussed:

* How to prepare for an audit?
* How to hand over the resources?
* What is the first thing auditors do?
* How to communicate with auditors?
* How I use the following tools, and their evaluation:
  * Codebase visualization with Wake and Neovim
  * Static analysis tools
  * Fuzzing (and debugging)
  * Manual review

speakers.name: Dominik Teiml
speakers.bio: Dominik Teiml studied Maths & Computer Science at the University of Oxford. He got into blockchain with Gnosis, where he focused on decentralized exchanges and formal verification. Later he transitioned to security assessments, first at Certik and later at Trail of Bits. He was part of the founding of Ackee Blockchain, where he focused on employee training and auditing. Dom is the author of the Yellow Paper Course on Youtube and the creator of Wake, a security-first Solidity framework.

name: Agent-based modeling of Execution Tickets
description: Execution Tickets are currently debated as one of the most promising approaches to streamline incentives at protocol level. We created a holistic overview of potential mechanism designs and implementing an agent-based model to realistically compare different mechanism designs and identify potential drawbacks early on. The agent-based modeling approach is presented together with the results. In the second part, we will guide through running the simulation in the workshop.

speakers.name: Pascal Stichler
speakers.bio: I am doing research on Ethereum protocol-level economics and incentive design. Currently, I mainly working on APS (esp. Execution Tickets) and multi-block MEV. Previous work included data analysis on blobs and the effects of EIP-4844 on Layer 2s. In my former life I co-founded a tradFi business automating the M&A process for SME companies.

name: Discovery - the tool at the core of L2BEAT
description: Hands on workshop about how to use an L2BEAT tool called discovery for mapping, researching and monitoring all the contracts involved in a project. We'll start by introducing the problem that discovery tries to solve and after that we'll get into trying to understand the architecture of a real world project by using the avenues this tool gives us. After this session the participant should feel empowered to use discovery to deepen his knowledge about all on-chain deployments.

name: Building FullStack apps on Ethereum - SpeedRunEthereum3
description: In this session, we’ll build a fullstack app on Ethereum using Scaffold-ETH v2. We’ll follow along SpeedRunEthereum, a set of challenges that helps you quickly get hands-on with building on Ethereum. Together, we’ll create a simple Decentralized Staking App—an app that lets users lock up their tokens & earn rewards. This session is great for both beginners and more experienced devs looking to level up their skills and get practical with Ethereum.

speakers.name: Eda Akturk
speakers.bio: Developer & Educator. I'm part of BuidlGuidl, where I work closely with Ethereum developers to build tools and educational content for the Ethereum ecosystem. I'm also a Developer Advocate at Hyperlane, where I focus on cross-chain messaging and interoperability. You can check out my blog for the topics I'm interested in and some of my writing: https://mirror.xyz/edatweets.eth

name: How to do something to some state in some contract
description:
Smart contracts are changing. 

So far, they needed every transaction to be public in order for nodes to agree. Zero-Knowledge came in to change things a bit: you can actually make your transaction client-side and just broadcast a proof.

In this workshop, we will use Noir and write a simple Aztec and/or Ethereum contract that allows for most of the execution and state to remain private.

speakers.name: José Pedro Sousa | zpedro
speakers.bio: Music teacher turned self-taught software developer. I've been in the space for some years, coding everything from C++ smart contracts to Noir circuits. I talk about zero-knowledge and how interesting they are when paired with distributed systems.

name: Native Account Abstraction in Pectra, rollups and beyond: combining EOF, EIP-7702 and RIP-7560
description:
Account Abstraction has rightfully become one of the most discussed topics in the Ethereum ecosystem.
The upcoming Pectra upgrade is set to be the first one to improve EOAs by including EIP-7702.
But can EIP-7702 alone achieve "Account Abstraction"?

We will discuss the challenges and benefits of EIP-7702, and break down the team's vision for achieving "complete" Native Account Abstraction with RIP-7560/EIP-7701 and how it differs from ERC-4337 + EIP-7702.

speakers.name: Alex Forshtat
speakers.bio: Account Abstraction core team developer. Co-author of ERC-4337, RIP-7560 and more.

name: Designing an End to End Solution for Based Preconfirmations
description: This workshop provides the audience with a foundation for building an end-to-end solution to deliver fast preconfirmation of transactions on a based-rollup like Taiko. In addition to understanding the basics of based sequencing and preconfirmations, attendees will learn about settling these preconfirmations as an Eigenlayer AVS, designing the AVS client, syncing L2 state using preconfirmed blocks, preconfer election, and managing a proposer lookahead using Beacon state within smart contracts.

name: RIP-7755: Empowering Cross-Chain Interactions
description: Cross-chain interactions are becoming essential as Ethereum Layer 2 solutions multiply. RIP-7755 changes the game by trustlessly bridging the gap between L2 chains, allowing new use cases that rely solely on Ethereum and its rollups. In this workshop, we’ll explore RIP-7755 by building a cross-chain NFT minting app, focusing on nested storage proof implementation details to eliminate trust assumptions.

speakers.bio: Proud to be a Base builder! I'm leading the research initiative for developing RIP-7755 and advancing interoperability within the Ethereum ecosystem.

name: Demystifying Smart Contract Security: Facts & Fallacies
description:
Smart contract security is of critical importance as the Ethereum ecosystem rapidly expands across different infrastructures & applications. However, there exist serious gaps and misconceptions about security as it relates to smart contract design, development, validation, tooling, offchain components, audits, bug bounties, monitoring & incident response.

This panel brings together six recognized researchers within the Ethereum security ecosystem to help demystify facts from fallacies.

speakers.name: Josselin Feist
speakers.bio:
Engineering director at @trailofbits.

Working on blockchain security & program analysis

speakers.name: 0xRajeev
speakers.bio: Rajeev is a security researcher and the founder of Secureum & TrustX. Having spent ~25 years doing security research, he dedicates his time to scaling Ethereum security by collaborating with leading initiatives in this ecosystem.

speakers.name: Matthias Egli
speakers.bio: Matthias Egli is a co-founder and the CTO of ChainSecurity. He holds a master’s degree in electrical engineering from ETH Zurich. Before ChainSecurity, Matthias had a prolific IT career both in the Silicon Valley as an expert data scientist, and in Switzerland as a software engineer and C-level executive. During his time at ChainSecurity, he has worked on many audits and contributed to responsibly disclose vulnerabilities in the Ethereum protocol itself.

speakers.name: Mehdi Zerouali
speakers.bio:
Mehdi Zerouali is a co-founder and Director of Sigma Prime, a leading Sydney-based blockchain security company. Mehdi has been in the information security industry for 13+ years and has performed hundreds of security assessments targeting critical infrastructure. 

With Sigma Prime, Mehdi applies his skills to the Blockchain space, helping prominent projects secure their decentralized protocols.

speakers.name: Mooly Sagiv
speakers.bio: Shmuel_Sagiv is a professor and chair of Computer Sciences at Tel-Aviv University and a CEO and co-founder of Certora. He is a leading researcher in large-scale (inter-procedural) program analysis and one of the key contributors to shape analysis. His fields of interest include programming languages, compilers, abstract interpretation, profiling, pointer analysis, shape analysis, interprocedural dataflow analysis, program slicing, and language-based programming.

speakers.name: Harikrishnan Mulackal
speakers.bio: Hari is a co-founder of Spearbit and Cantina. He was previously part of the Solidity team at the Ethereum Foundation.

name: Visual code of cypherpunk and lessons from subcultural aesthetics we should remember
description:
I want to take builders on the turbulent ride through how subcultural and social movements used their visual codes when spreading globally, and what design tasks are still ahead of us on the way to making Ethereum cypherpunk again and onboarding the next billion users to Web3 at the same time.

This ride will include three stops:
1. waving one's emotional state into the collective identity
2. using shared aesthetics as a signal of belonging
3. coordinating a collective design process.

speakers.name: Ira Nezhynska
speakers.bio:
Ira is an independent designer specializing in branding and visual design strategy. After years in the consumer and fintech branding realms, she joined Web3 in early 2018 and has since served as a Creative Director at companies big and small, helping founders win hearts and minds of early adopters and funders. 
These days, she runs her own design practice and conducts DIY (design-it-yourself) workshops for pre- and seed-stage companies.

name: Beyond Multidimensional Fee Markets
description: We study TFMs in the presence of heterogenous transactions and computational nodes. Our first set of results show that multidim fee markets (such as EIP-4844) fail to achieve good guarantees as heterogeneity increases. We complement this result by introducing the Broker Mechanism, which works in the fully heterogenous setting. This mechanism is suitable as a market for sharding computation, delegating computation to off-chain nodes (prover markets and coprocessors), and allocating preconfs.

name: Unlock Web2 Data with TLSNotary: Hands-On Workshop
description:
Join our hands-on workshop to master **TLSNotary**! Dive into multi-party-TLS and learn to prove and verify online data authenticity to a third-party verifier while ensuring privacy. We’ll start with small examples in Rust and build up to custom browser extensions in TypeScript to collect and verify private user data.

Bring your laptop, bring a friend, and learn together. Get ready to unlock and compose Web2 data in innovative ways.

speakers.name: Hendrik Eeckhaut
speakers.bio: Hendrik holds a PhD in computer science and is the founder of Sigasi, a software company that develops tools for chip designers, focusing on VHDL and SystemVerilog. He supports the TLSNotary team at the Ethereum Foundation's Privacy and Scaling Explorations research lab, working on software for privacy-preserving data provenance. In his free time, he enjoys running, climbing, and exploring the world.

name: Maximum Viable Security (MVS) – a new issuance framework
description: We derive a new framework for analyzing Ethereum Issuance, based on Ethereum's core values: security and neutrality. Upon discussing various attacks on Ethereum, we study future growth projections and the importance of diverse validator set, and conclude that Ethereum's defendability is the key factor for issuance policy evaluation. Via MVS, we show how the current issuance reduction proposal is dangerous, based on the future staked ETH concentration with CEXs & impact on solo stakers.

speakers.name: Artem Kotelskiy
speakers.bio: For 2013-2023 period I was a pure mathematician, studying low-dimensional topology and symplectic geometry in Princeton, Indiana and Stony Brook Universities. I got interested in crypto as early as 2015, and did some investments and research in Ethereum ecosystem on the side. In 2022 I also taught a course on blockchains in Stony Brook (artofkot.xyz/blockchain-course), and in 2023 move into the space full-time, as a research lead in cyber.fund.

name: Practical endgame on issuance policy
description: A practical endgame on issuance policy stops the growth in stake while guaranteeing proper consensus incentives and positive regular rewards to solo stakers. Viable reward curves for this endgame are presented. Motivations, impacts and potential downsides of an issuance reduction are in focus. A tangible framework is also introduced: never exceed an issuance rate of 0.5%. A stringent cap on issuance caps the inflation rate, solidifying ETH as trustless sound money with robust economic security.

speakers.name: Anders Elowsson
speakers.bio: Anders Elowsson is a researcher at the Ethereum Foundation working on staking economics with a specific focus on issuance policy.

name: Unpacking EOF: Applications in Developer Infrastructure and Tooling
description:
In this talk, we will delve into the Ethereum Object Format (EOF), a pivotal component of the upcoming Pectra hard-fork, focusing on its profound implications for development infrastructure and tooling. EIP-7692 introduces a new execution environment and a structured format for executable code, bringing extensive changes to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM).

How will it affect developers? What will make their lives harder and what easier?

speakers.name: Nebojsa Urosevic
speakers.bio:
Co-founder & SVP of R&D of Tenderly. Before Tenderly, Nebojsa was a blockchain engineer at Decenter and a software engineer at GoDaddy. He has experience building, scaling, and maintaining large-scale distributed cloud systems. 

In Tenderly Nebojsa leads a diverse and experienced team of engineers and is one of the engineering leads. He has in-depth knowledge of the blockchain and EVM.

name: The Future of EOF: Layer 1, Layer 2, and Beyond!
description:
While the EVM Object Format provides a mechanism to modernize the EVM, the container format itself provides a stable path for innovation and experimentation within the base and rollup layers of ethereum, as well as rollup layers, and even chain free execution.

In this presentation we will show how the structure of the EOF container may be adapted to support these potential use cases.

speakers.name: Danno Ferrin
speakers.bio:
Danno Ferrin is a seasoned Ethereum core developer with a deep-rooted passion for the technology.  He has been focused  the evolution of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM), contributing significantly to its ongoing development and optimization.

With a background spanning roles at Oracle, Google, and ConsenSys, Danno brings a wealth of experience to his work on Ethereum. He is currently an independent contributor to the ecosystem.

name: Changes to the L1 EVM versus L2s
description: The EVM has long been a target for improvement, but major changes have been postponed due to other priorities. As Ethereum's core, EVM modifications could significantly affect network stability, security, and performance, or add complexity. This necessitates lengthy approval and implementation processes. Panelists will explore new initiatives to implement EVM upgrades such as the EOF on L2s before L1, discussing their pros and cons.

speakers.name: Eniko Garam
speakers.bio: Building communities and organizing events like the EVM Summit

speakers.name: Mark Tyneway
speakers.bio: Mark is a cofounder of Optimism and is interested in building the institutions of the future on top of Ethereum

name: Scalable and sovereign EVM data: modern data engineering best practices
description: Collecting and analyzing large historical EVM datasets can pose a significant challenge. This has led many teams and individuals to outsource their data infrastructure to commercial 3rd-party platforms. However, over the past year a new style of data workflow has emerged, using entirely open source software and local-first processing. This new ecosystem of tools allow anyone to cheaply, easily, and robustly collect and analyze any EVM dataset from the comfort of their own laptop.

name: [CLS] Ethereum Magicians Infinite Endgames: Ethereum Execution
description: A fishbowl-style discussion with core Ethereum contributors and community to publicly discuss the "endgame" of execution on Ethereum. We will discuss what the evolution of Ethereum’s execution layer will look like, L1 vs. L2, settlement vs. execution, enshrined rollups, consensus changes vs. client performance improvements, etc.

name: [CLS] Ethereum Magicians Infinite Endgames: Block construction
description:
Once again, Devcon will host Ethereum Magicians gatherings for the community to come together and discuss the most important topics in Ethereum’s roadmap. Join us here to discuss the “infinite endgame” for block construction. We'll cover PBS, MEV, role of validators vs. builders, centralization risks, and more!

For more context, see: https://bit.ly/ethmag-sea

speakers.name: Alex Stokes
speakers.bio: Researcher at the EF. Focused on making Ethereum secure, scalable, and sustainable.

transcripts.text: I don't have any slides prepared for this event, but I have some from a past talk that I can use to kind of kick off the discussion. And I think that's more the framing is just to have a conversation with the people here in this room. But yeah, I can tell you a bit about the state of things now in Ethereum with MedBoost and PBS and things like that. And yeah, then maybe that will seed off the conversation and we can go from there. So, yeah. I guess, uh, one question is just, like, has everyone here heard of MedBoost? Does this mean anything? Yeah? Okay. There's, like, maybe a few nods. So, anyway, uh, maybe I'll just start from the beginning then. So, we have Ethereum. We all, we all know and love Ethereum. And Ethereum's cool because it lets you send transactions, which can do all sorts of types of things with all these decentralized applications. It turns out that you can basically, you know, craft the blocks of Ethereum in a certain way. And in this certain way, it turns out that, like, a builder of the block can get more, you get more revenue or profit compared to other ways. We generally call this thing MEV. And point being is this poses a concern for the protocol because, yeah, essentially if you're better at MEV extraction than someone else, then you now kind of have this flywheel where you can reinvest in your operations and you just get bigger and bigger. What this could even look like right now is offering better returns to validators. And then you have this flywheel where like all the stake ends up with you and Ethereum is no longer decentralized. So this is very bad. And, you know, I think the way we generally think about this in terms of at least protocol research is with PBS. PBS here is Proposer-builder separation. And it's thinking about ways to separate off this building role of these very valuable execution payloads in the protocol from these validators. So what you could imagine is there's this very even light layer of validators that are, again, sort of attesting to the validity of the network, but then you entirely fire off these concerns of this MEV stuff. And the point here is that even if you do end up with a very centralized builder or block builder world, I mean even nowadays we talk about transaction supply chain, so it's very much professionalizing and operationalizing. Even if that does become more centralized than we would like, you still have this very robust validator set that attests to the truth of the chain. So, is there a question? Oh, sorry. You can either do it, I guess, like one high decision point is like, is your PBS on-chain or off-chain? We'll talk about on-chain flavors in a bit. But given that, like an on-chain setting would be a protocol change. It's probably going to take a while to even come to an agreement around what the best way to do this. And even right now, maybe I'll talk about this in a little bit, but even right now, there's still, like, big open questions around the best way to do PBS in the protocol. So what can we do? Well, in the meantime, we can essentially do PBS off-chain, and the implementation we have that has the most adoption at this point in time is MedBoost. And I think that'll tee me up for these slides. So the way you can think about this working is that it's almost this, like, rendezvous service between, again, builders and proposers. So these proposers, you know, as you go to, like, validate the chain as a validator, you then also have the opportunity every so often to propose a block. This is building the consensus block, and then also this execution payload. And now this is where the PBS comes in, as you can think about carving off the task of building this execution payload, the execution part of the block where all this juicy MEV is, and handing it off to someone else. And MevBoost, again, is a software stack and a protocol that implements this. And one way to think about it is, yeah, you have this green sort of rectangle over here is the execution payload. The gold is meant to represent the MEV around it because it's this nice money everyone likes to fight over. And then you have this blue block on the right, and this is the consensus block that the proposer wants to, you know, send to the network. And the question now is, like, how do you have, like, this, you know, secure exchange between these two parties who might not trust each other, and in fact we don't want them to trust each other. Because otherwise, again, you kind of fall back to the status quo I was talking about, or not the status quo, but, you know, a failure mode, I was talking about a minute ago where you have a very small validator set that all works with these one or two builders and things like this. So in any case, we now have to think about how to get this block, the extrusion payload into the block and make this all work well. And at a high level, the way to think about MedBoost today is that it's like this commit reveal protocol, meaning you like commit to something and then once you've committed to it, it's, you know, the person committing now is the proposer, but once they've committed to it, then the builder is free to like release their block with no worries. And, you know, diagrammatically, you can imagine that the builder then has their like nice, nice screen execution payload. It has, like, some juicy MEV with a gold border. And then the, like, shaded thing on top of it is meant to represent that it's blinded. And the reason why you want this is because if the builder sends the payload unclear, then the proposer basically could, like, copy the builder's work, take all the sort of, you know, rewards from that work for themselves, and the builder would be unhappy. What this means then is that the mechanism itself is not sound, and then no one would use it, and it would be bad. Because proposers would just fall back to, like, these backroom deals and God knows what. So the way to get around this is basically you need some way for the proposer to commit to the block. This is the commit step, and so they get a blinded payload, which goes into the block. The way this works is that, you know, sort of like zooming away into the details, the proposer signs over this block in a compatible way with what's actually the thing that ends up on chain. And, yeah, basically they do this, and then they can show the builder kind of as proof that, like, they've committed to this particular payload, say including one that pays the builder for their work. And then once the builder sees that, they can release it to the wild. And this bottom right square is what would go on chain. And yeah, so the thing to consider here is this sort of mev stealing issue that I was just trying to describe. You can imagine that there's a block with some MVV. The builder takes some amount of funds to that address and wants to pay the proposer this. If there isn't this commit to reveal step baked into the protocol, then the proposer basically could just take the block, say thank you very much for all this hard work. They could rewrite the payment transaction, for example, that sends all the revenue to the proposer, and then builders don't want to use it. name: [CLS] Ethereum Magicians Infinite Endgames: Ethconomics
description:
Once again, Devcon will host Ethereum Magicians gatherings for the community to come together and discuss the most important topics in Ethereum's roadmap. Join us here to discuss the "infinite endgame" for Ethereum's economic model. We'll cover the role of Ether in the network's security, issuance proposals, out-of-protocol economic influences, and more! 

For more context, see: https://bit.ly/ethmag-sea

name: [CLS] Programmable Cryptography
description: The Programmable Cryptography CLS hosts a series of talks exploring how advanced cryptography can reshape digital infrastructure beyond blockchain and trust infrastructure.

speakers.name: gubsheep
speakers.bio: gubsheep is co-founder of 0xPARC and creator of the Dark Forest game.

speakers.name: Barry
speakers.bio: I do pgor crypto r and d :)

speakers.name: Albert Ni
speakers.bio: I work on understanding what Ethereum is, and realizing what it can become.

name: Multi-Party Fully Homomorphic Encryption (MP-FHE) in Practice
description: In this session, we will break down the FHE game Frogzone, which required advancements at every layer of the cryptographic software stack: cryptography libraries and tooling, circuits, software infrastructure, and even DevOps. We will also cover additional use cases for FHE at a technical level.

speakers.name: gubsheep
speakers.bio: gubsheep is co-founder of 0xPARC and creator of the Dark Forest game.

speakers.name: riley wong (they/them)
speakers.bio: Riley Wong (they/them) is the Principal of Emergent Research, investigating privacy, governance, and data. Interests include applied cryptography, consent interfaces, p2p networks, and cooperative infrastructure. Their work is rooted in community practice and guided by collaborative work in solidarity economies, public goods and the commons, and interdependence. They have previous lives in machine learning, investigative journalism, and community organizing and are based in NYC.

speakers.name: Eduard Sanou
speakers.bio:
Currently working at PSE (EF).
I worked for two years on the zkEVM and I'm currently doing research and exploration in multiparty FHE

name: Building Consumer Apps with Programmable Cryptography
description: 0xPARC community developers will present apps built on top of the Programmable Cryptography stack, including FROGCRYPTO, Zupass, Meerkat, and many more. This session will also include a live workshop where you can learn to build your own, and there may be a cryptographic prize for those who complete the challenges…

speakers.name: Richard Liu
speakers.bio: Richard works at [0xPARC](0xparc.org) and is a core contributor to the [Zupass project](https://x.com/zupassproject).

speakers.name: Rob Knight
speakers.bio: Rob Knight is an engineer and contributor to the Zupass project.

speakers.name: Veronica Zheng
speakers.bio: Veronica currently works with 0xPARC on various programmable cryptography applications. Previously, Veronica was a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Coinbase.

name: L2 DAOs - biggest challenges we face to make L2s sustainable long term
description: Today L2 DAOs are mostly focused on growth and supporting their ecosystem builders. But long-term they will be responsible for the management and maintenance of their chains from all perspectives - ecosystem growth, software development, security, chain economic parameters management, and others. In this talk, I will explore what DAOs need to figure out and fix before they will be able to take this responsibility in the coming years and why we should be addressing those issues already today.

speakers.name: Krzysztof Urbański
speakers.bio: Governance Lead at L2BEAT, long-time governance, and public goods nerd.

name: Superliquid Mechanisms for Decentralized Stablecoins
description: USDC and USDT outpace decentralized stablecoins in large part due to their liquidity. This talk covers the theory, data, and risks of stablecoin liquidity innovations. This will include mint/redemption mechanism design, liquidity pool design, rehypothecation, and protocol-owned liquidity. The analysis will distill how the flexibility of decentralized stablecoin issuance mechanisms can safely be used to their advantage over centralized stablecoins, which Gyroscope v2 is putting into practice.

speakers.name: Ariah Klages-Mundt
speakers.bio: Ariah designed and built key parts of Gyroscope’s GYD stablecoin and liquidity pools. He is a DeFi researcher with a track record of predicting design problems in stablecoins, including issues that manifested in Dai’s Black Thursday crisis and in Terra’s collapse, and holds a PhD from Cornell University.

name: Degen incentives for Regen outcomes
description: Degens (financial speculators) and Regens (blockchain altruists) don't like each other. But there's a lot that can be achieved if both tribes work together. In this panel we'll explore those projects that embrace both energies to find balance in the force and unlock Ethereum’s potential.

speakers.name: Griff Green
speakers.bio:
Trying to build something better than governments.

Co-founder of Giveth, q/acc, Unicorn.eth, Pairwise, General Magic & DAppNode

Top Steward in Arbitrum, ENS & Optimism, TEC as well as many other Ethereum community projects. 

Been DAOing my heart out since 2015.

speakers.name: Nico Gallardo
speakers.bio: Uniting degens and regens through OttoDAO / LottoPGF. Compulsive builder. Initiator of AFK communities Ethereum Bolivia and W3b Lab.

speakers.name: Lauren Luz
speakers.bio: GIVeconomy Product Lead at Giveth. Passionate about using evolving public goods funding mechanisms using web3.

name: Building a Cross-Chain DEX with Chain Abstraction & Intents
description: In a multi-chain world, creating a user-friendly DEX is challenging. This talk explores how a DEX can leverage intents and chain abstraction to offer seamless cross-chain trading. We'll discuss the implementation of ERC7683 and integration with Across Protocol to enable trading across multiple chains.

speakers.name: Shao
speakers.bio:
Shao co-founded Perpetual Protocol (perp.com)—the first AMM-based on-chain perpetual exchange, launched in 2019, which has served over 500,000 users with tens of billions in trading volume. 

This year, he’s focused on Nekodex (under PERP), a mobile-first DEX that lowers entry barriers by abstracting blockchain complexities, making crypto accessible to a broader audience.

name: Memecraft: Effectively Communicating Crypto Concepts
description:
Memes have been crucial to the proliferation of various concepts and ideas within the crypto space (ultrasound money, (3,3), regen/degen, QF) which has led to real capital being allocated toward impactful outcomes. The downside to some of this memeing however has been misleading narratives and misunderstandings. How do we leverage memetic power for education and tacit understanding of complex concepts?

The workshop will include 1) Scene Setting 2) Structured Discussion and a 3) Group Activity.

speakers.bio:
Beth McCarthy is a Berlin-based strategist, researcher & experience designer. She is a Program Director at Funding the Commons, an organization exploring new models & mechanisms for open source & public goods funding. 

Formerly building ecosystem & culture at projects including Centrifuge, Toucan, Gnosis & Ocean Protocol, Beth is passionate about the lunarpunk potential future of blockchain & enjoys geeking out at the intersection of art, philosophy, law & computational systems of behavior.

This transcript is from a presentation about VANA, a platform that allows users to control and monetize their data. The speaker starts by introducing themselves and VANA, explaining that they got into crypto through mining Ethereum in 2015 and into AI because they wanted better data for their econometrics models. They then discuss the data wall, which is the problem of AI models running out of data to train on. They explain that most training data is private and that companies are increasingly monetizing and restricting access to their data. The speaker argues that users legally own their data and can take it back from platforms. They give examples of exporting data from Instagram and 23andMe. The speaker then introduces VANA, which allows users to control their data using their wallets and pool their data with others to increase its value. They discuss two core concepts on VANA: non-custodial data and proof of contribution. They then go through a bunch of different applications that can be built on VANA, including data DAOs, Datify applications, data access, and data portability. They explain that data DAOs are the most self-serve application and that they allow users to pool their data and govern it together. They also discuss proof of contribution, which is a way to validate data on VANA. Finally, they talk about data tokens, which are used to reward contributors and allow companies and researchers to buy access to data.
This transcript discusses various aspects of VANA, a platform for data ownership and monetization. Users can create and join DataDAOs (Decentralized Autonomous Organizations) to pool and manage their data collectively.  They earn data tokens for contributing and verifying data quality.  The platform supports building applications like DeFi apps with data tokens, AI applications with data access, and personalized AI agents using data portability.  VANA facilitates data access through a manual approval process, with plans for automated API access in the future.  Data storage is user-controlled and agnostic, allowing integration with various storage solutions. The platform emphasizes data privacy and security, using techniques like TEEs (Trusted Execution Environments) to prevent data leakage and ensure responsible usage. A key aspect is the shift from one-time data payments to ongoing ownership and control, empowering users and aligning incentives with AI development. The transcript also highlights the importance of go-to-market strategies for DataDAOs, citing examples like influencer marketing and community building.  Finally, it mentions upcoming developments like the VRC-13 upgrade and a global hackathon to further the VANA ecosystem.  Key individuals involved in the project are also identified for follow-up discussions.

transcripts.summary: This transcript features a discussion between Chris, Yush, Dan, and an unnamed speaker about data privacy, sovereignty, and security in Web3.  Chris, head of engineering at Vana, emphasizes Vana's focus on user-controlled data usage within applications.  Yush, working on ZK email, highlights their work on data authentication and validation for model training. Dan, from Flashbots, advocates for privacy in efficient markets, focusing on block building within TEEs.  They discuss trust in decentralized systems, emphasizing the architectural approach of distributed key generation and the use of TEEs for enhanced security. The conversation then delves into the vulnerabilities of the decentralized data space, focusing on potential hardware and supply chain risks associated with TEEs, and the need for robust user experience to mitigate common wallet vulnerabilities.  They explore the definition of data sovereignty, emphasizing user control, ownership, and verifiable data usage. The transcript concludes with a discussion on breakthroughs needed for full data sovereignty. They see the growing use of LLMs combined with user-owned data as a potential catalyst.  Practical advancements in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), user-friendly experiences, and potential legal frameworks are highlighted as crucial for the future of data sovereignty.

transcripts.summary: Michael Casey, chairman of the Decentralized AI Society, believes decentralized AI is in its early stages, similar to Bitcoin's beginnings. He emphasizes the need for a new token design framework that avoids the speculative nature of traditional VC-backed projects to foster broader ownership of decentralized AI infrastructure. Victor from Zubu highlights the potential of decentralization to parallelize AI development, moving from siloed development to a collaborative ecosystem. JB from Tenfold expresses concern about the lack of decentralized compute for AI training and promotes agent swarms as a promising area for decentralized protocols. The panelists discuss the overhyped nature of AGI and deep research, emphasizing the importance of data quality and the potential of agent swarms and System 2 thinking. They also discuss the blockers to progress, including the current funding model, the concentration of compute resources, and the need for better incentives and reputation systems. Decentralization is presented as a solution to these problems, enabling a commons-based approach to AI development and management. The panelists conclude by emphasizing the importance of long-term utility over short-term hype and the potential of decentralized mechanisms for verifying data and research.

transcripts.summary:
This transcript discusses data as an asset class, focusing on its financialization and the infrastructure needed for it to become tradable. Speakers explore data's inherent value, drawing parallels with commodities like oil and gold.  They discuss the importance of data quality, privacy, and programmability for its effective use and monetization.  The rise of AI and machine learning, especially unsupervised learning, is highlighted as a key driver of data's increasing importance.  Data DAOs are presented as a promising example of data financialization, allowing collective ownership and monetization of data pools.  The conversation also touches upon the challenges of data valuation, the potential role of ZKPs in preserving privacy, and the evolving relationship between the cost of physical versus digital experiences.  The transcript concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of data commoditization and the need for economic incentives to encourage data sharing.
A discussion about the future of privacy, data, and AI. The speakers express concerns about the erosion of privacy in the digital world, the potential for AI-generated data to surpass human-generated data in value, and the implications of increasingly realistic and accessible AI companions. They also discuss the ease with which journeys and experiences can now be created, and the potential for this to lead to a loss of fulfillment. The conversation concludes with speculation about brain-to-brain communication and the dissolving of language.

transcripts.summary: This panel discusses the value of data, featuring experts who have experience buying and selling data. They discuss how private data is more valuable than public data, the strangest datasets they've encountered, and their dream datasets.  The panelists emphasize the importance of data aggregation and the potential of data DAOs to empower individuals to control and monetize their data.  Specific examples mentioned include selling Facebook user data back to Facebook due to privacy restrictions, the challenges of using medical data due to privacy regulations, and the potential value of biohacking and Amazon purchase data.

transcripts.text: Hey folks, so the most valuable systems in our economy today are built on this kind of fundamental asymmetry, right? Whoever can aggregate the most data essentially wins, but what if we could radically change that equation? What if we could enable institutions, individuals, and agents to collaboratively compute over sensitive data without introducing information asymmetries, without giving up control of their data? So today I want to explore an emergent class of computational primitives, of cryptographic primitives that is not just creating new technological capabilities, but also reshaping how value gets created and distributed in these multi-agent systems. So we call this collaborative confidential compute. What excites me about collaborative confidential compute is this potential for it to be a disintermediate force. It has this capacity to become another step on a kind of global progressive disintermediation journey. What I mean here is, so the internet was this radically disintermediating force for access to information. Blockchains like Ethereum are this disintermediating force for access to finance, and I see collaborative confidential compute as this radically disintermediating force for access to an interaction with systems that aggregate information, multi-agent systems that create value from large-scale aggregation. Large-scale aggregation like this has historically been the purview of large-scale organizations that have the capacity and willingness to aggregate and hoard huge amounts of user data. And I think collaborative confidential compute will enable essentially a whole new class of applications that deal with shared secret space and the value that it creates. So looking at some of the most valuable companies today, Facebook and Google make huge amounts of profits by aggregating shared, by aggregating secret data from, sensitive data from users. Their web traffic, their social interactions, their purchasing, and their search data. The pattern is fairly clear here. Being able to aggregate large amounts of information, particularly large amounts of private information, lets you win. And this creates this fundamental dilemma for builders building systems that aggregate information. Either take custody of user data or miss out on the insights that you can gain and the value that you can create from aggregating that data. And then a corresponding dilemma for users of these systems, for participants in these systems. Either give up custody of your data or miss out on access to the benefits that those systems create. Every current attempt to solve for this set of problems has come bundled with a handful of fundamental flaws. Either privacy is temporary or it rests on some essentially trusted operator or trusted hardware. But here's what's changed. So we have three cryptographic technologies that are kind of maturing in parallel, maturing simultaneously, that can be composed in a variety of different ways to enable really interesting novel systems. Zero-knowledge proofs allow you to prove, succinctly prove statements of knowledge without revealing the inputs. It's the theory, the tooling, and the performance around ZKPs has improved dramatically over the last few years. Multiparty computation allows you to distribute secrets across an arbitrary set of parties such that none of them have direct access to the secret but can use it in a way that does not reveal access. And so some use cases here are things like distributed key generation and threshold decryption allowing you to distribute, control, or solve for key management in these kind of multi-agent systems. And then lastly here, fully homomorphic encryption, FHE, allows you to compute directly over encrypted data and produce an output that when decrypted is equivalent to if you had to run the same computation on plain text. FHE has, the performance for FHE has improved dramatically over the last few years, taking it from possible in theory to usable in practice. And the kind of real breakthrough here is that these combinations of technologies let us embed privacy at the system level, making it possible to run arbitrary computations over encrypted inputs with very strong guarantees around the inputs and intermediate states from any private while the outputs being verifiable and trustworthy. All without necessarily creating individual points of trust or failure. So before we dive into, or further into the kind of technical side of things, I just want to establish some of what's at stake here. So again, I mentioned hundreds of billions in revenue generated by digital platforms that rely on harvesting user data. And users rarely, if ever, if ever compensated with anything other than access. And often users are harmed by the misuse or mishandling of the sensitive data that they ultimately hand over to these platforms that are harvesting their data. This asymmetry is a really defining feature of today's data economy. But it's not just about money and access. We also have things like life-saving medical research slowed or halted because of data silos between institutions or regulatory hurdles. We have things like systemic financial risk that are hidden or not discovered because of competitive secrecy between financial institutions. And things like AI models that are biased due to, that are distorted, sorry, because of biased or incomplete training data. And I think, yeah, the difference now is that with this combination of cryptographic tools, we can take, again, this private data and aggregate in such a way to produce verifiable outputs without revealing inputs. And essentially this class of applications that were once theoretical are now becoming practical. The basic patterns for collaborative confidential compute look something like this. Essentially you have some data sources that will encrypt their inputs, compute will happen confidentially somewhere, we'll get to that in a minute, and then outputs are decrypted, again, with kind of strong guarantees around inputs and intermediate states remaining private and outputs being trustworthy, verifiable. There's multiple technical approaches to this, each combining some mix of kind of five-ish key ingredients, trusted execution environments, zero-knowledge proofs, multi-party computation, FHC, and then some form of game theory. And they each have a different set of trust assumptions, trade-offs across privacy, scalability, cost, and throughput. The key insight, though, is that we have multiple viable technical paths to achieving collaborative confidential compute. And so this creates a completely new design space for builders. You have new constraints around your computation costs, economics, trust models, and user experience that you need to consider, but alongside of that you get these kind of powerful new affordances. You can enable competitive collaboration between otherwise distrusting parties, you can reduce viability from the data that you might have to take on in order to produce insights, you can prove that systems and their outputs are fair without revealing inputs, and you can implement dynamic value distribution based on contributions without revealing the contributions. And these are fundamentally new capabilities for system designers. So let's take a quick look at how these ideas kind of work in practice, starting with a surprisingly unsolved problem, digital voting. So there's a good reason why every worthwhile democracy in the world uses a secret ballot. Open ballots enable collusion, corruption, bribery, coercion that ultimately distort their outcomes. The state-of-the-art for secret ballots is writing a vote on a piece of paper, dropping it into a big box with everyone else's votes, and shaking the box. And there's a reason that digital voting has not kind of widely displaced paper ballots. It turns out that it's really, really hard to cast a digital ballot in such a way that you don't leave a traceable footprint. And in doing so, it creates an avenue for bribery, coercion, collusion, and the corresponding negative outcomes. So digital voting isn't broken because we can't tally accurately or we can't produce voter registries or any of the kind of technical challenges there. It's broken because its fundamental flaws enable corruption, enable collusion, and again, ultimately distort its outcomes. But with careful design choices, collaborative confidential compute can enable voting systems that are legitimately receipt-free, enable us to build verifiable, censorship-resistant, receipt-free voting. And that last property, receipt-freeness, has been really, really challenging, if not impossible, to build to date in digital voting systems without taking on untenable trust assumptions—trust assumptions in individual operators or trusted hardware and their corresponding complexity and attestation chains. Beyond voting, though, these patents kind of enable a whole class of new applications—medical research that can happen across institutions without revealing institutional data, without revealing patient data—say, custody by different healthcare institutions, different medical institutions, different research institutions. You can have collaborative analytics across competitive financial institutions, and you can have feel-good auctions where you don't reveal any of the bids or bidders but have a verifiable outcome, just to name a handful of these cases. The pattern's the same for all of these. You have inputs, secret inputs, that users submit encrypted to some execution environment, some encrypted execution environment. Computation happens in a verifiable way, and then an output is produced without revealing any of the media states. Performance-wise, collaborative confidential compute is practical today for moderate complexity, high-value use cases, where this kind of privacy premium is justified by the value of the output. But the cost and performance of collaborative confidential compute is improving radically year over year, and so I think the floor on what's a justifiable use case is radically dropping. So I just want to talk quickly about the kind of design space here. Security in these systems requires thinking across a handful of different layers—the cryptographic assumptions, the economic incentives, the protocol implementation, nuances, and a handful of other layers. Different approaches have different sets of trade-offs. So, for example, trusted execution environments, they're the kind of de facto standards for a lot of these types of use cases currently. They're relatively performant but bundle in a whole bunch of complexity along with trusted hardware and trusted manufacturer and supply chain assumptions. MPC allows you to distribute secrets such that you can arbitrarily compute with them without revealing the secrets to any of the parties or revealing the secret publicly, and this is really great for things like distributed key generation and threshold encryption, allowing us to solve for distributed key management in these type of multi-agent systems. Zero-knowledge proofs, CKPs, they allow you to succinctly prove statements of knowledge about some data without revealing the data itself. There's this kind of moderate overhead, and they're super useful for a handful of different scenarios. They're not great in scenarios where you want to aggregate information about multiple users because you must know the data that you need to prove in order to be able to generate a proof. And then the last one here, oh, I'm sorry, it's not on the table, but FHE allows you to compute other sensitive, compute other data while it's encrypted, produce a ciphertext that when you decrypt it will give you the same output as if you had to compute it over the plaintext data. The key here is to choose the combination of technologies that make sense for your use case, and obviously to take into account the kind of performance, privacy guarantees, trust assumptions, and all this good stuff. In my opinion, the combination of FHE, ZKP, and MPC is one of the holy grails of cryptography. It gives you verifiability, allows you to compute over encrypted data, and to distribute trust in the decryption keys as broadly as you like. Caveat with scaling constraints there. So I think this technology has some pretty profound economic implications. Currently data aggregators like Facebook, Google, OpenAI, they capture this disproportionate value based on their capacity to aggregate private information, but collaborative confidential compute will challenge this. It will allow participants to engage in these kind of aggregation systems without giving up their data, which ultimately gives them leverage and should help to force more equitable value sharing in these types of systems. We can build data cooperatives with cryptographic guarantees that enable competitive collaboration in previously zero-sum environments and implement merit-based application without revealing private information. So for builders ready to start, there's several emerging tools. Enclave, the tool that we're building at Gnosis Guild, provides a substrate for FAT-based encrypted execution environments. Sunscreen has a really performant TFAT library. Primus, they've got a fantastic ZKTLS library as well as some promising research on threshold TFAT and also another TFAT implementation. Aztec has this awesome ZKDSL, which has really made it much more accessible to write ZKPs. Risk Zero, for example, has a great ZKVM, a RISC-V-based ZKVM that makes it really easy to prove correct execution of arbitrary codes that can compile down to RISC-V. And so with tools like these in hand, developers, builders now have everything they need to be able to build these systems leveraging collaborative confidential compute and ultimately create aggregations of information without leaking sensitive information. So this is bigger than any one project, right? We collectively are building infrastructure for a more equitable digital economy. For researchers, there are fascinating open problems in optimization, in encryption schemes, in mechanism design. For builders, we need people pushing boundaries, breaking these things, and ultimately discovering how they work and where they're useful. And then for organizations, there's a really great opportunity to, again, get a push for boundaries here and pioneer privacy-preserving initiatives that still enable you to gain access to the insights you ultimately want from data that you would otherwise have to aggregate and take custody of. This is a vision of the future where data producers control their data and share in the value that they create, and where cryptography enables the collaboration between competitive institutions to their mutual benefit. So I'll wrap up here. As I was saying, we're building towards this future where people who produce data actually control and share in the value that it creates, where insights from large-scale aggregation don't require giving up data, giving up custody or autonomy over your sensitive information, and where cryptography enables collaboration between competitors to their mutual benefit rather than just competition. So this is collaborative, confidential compute, and it's going to reshape how we think about data, how we think about privacy, how we think about value creation in these multi-agent aggregation systems. If you're interested in building this future, our team at Gnosis Guild is developing an open-source protocol called Enclave. It combines ZKPs, FHE, MPC, and obviously economics and game theory to enable encrypted execution environments. Yeah, that's it. We'd love to hear your thoughts. If you want to chat about CCC, Enclave, or anything related afterwards, then yeah, come find me. I'd love to chat. Thank you. Thank you, Oren. We have a moment for a few questions down here up front. We have someone with a question. Thank you. So at the moment, there are mainly two paths to build applications with private shared states that are, like, because FHE is so slow compared to MPC. So either you build, like, co-SNARKs. So this is the approach on NOIR, like on Aztec, for instance, where you prove your SNARK inside an MPC setup. Or the other one would be more like doing everything in MPC, no ZK. I think Archium is building that on Solana. And so, yeah, on top of existing L1s. What do you see? If there is a dark pool in two years, which one do you think would be where it would be? Yeah. I mean, in two years, I think a lot can happen in terms of acceleration of and kind of improved efficiency on both MPC, on co-SNARK, and on FHE. And so I think it's hard to pick right now which one is going to be most viable that far out. I'd say if you're trying to MPC is the best solution for that, just like in a purely MPC-based solution. The challenge there, obviously, is that you give up some of the verifiability. It's a more trust-based system. I tend to think that the smaller, the complexity compute tasks are the things that are more accessible right now. So voting, the reason voting is the example there is that it's a similarly lightweight computation that's very high value. And so that's where we are initially focused. And I think where the team's building this should probably be focused is in those kind of lightweight aggregations that unlock a tremendous amount of value. Out of the two options that you suggested, my preference is obviously for co-SNARKs. I would much prefer it to be cryptographically verifiable. And then, obviously, the architecture that we're going to be pioneering is this combination of ZKPs for input validation, validating things like DKG and threshold encryption, FHE for the computation itself, and then MPC to distribute key shares. And I think by segmenting, particularly by pushing input validation to the edges, even on relatively complex computations, you can move a lot of the complexity to the edges and have users prove the validity of their inputs as opposed to doing that part of the computation in FHE. And so it can offset or reduce how much of that FHE overhead you have to take on.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses collaborative confidential compute (CCC), a class of cryptographic primitives that aims to reshape how value is created and distributed in multi-agent systems. CCC enables institutions and individuals to collaboratively compute over sensitive data without information asymmetries or loss of data control. It's presented as a disintermediating force, similar to how the internet disintermediated information access and blockchains disintermediate finance, but for systems that aggregate information. The current data economy is characterized by large platforms like Facebook and Google profiting from aggregated user data, creating a dilemma where users must either give up data custody or miss out on system benefits. CCC addresses this with technologies like zero-knowledge proofs, multi-party computation, and fully homomorphic encryption, allowing computations on encrypted inputs with strong guarantees and without central points of trust. Applications include secure digital voting, medical research across institutions, collaborative analytics among financial institutions, and feel-good auctions, all without revealing sensitive data. While currently practical for moderate complexity, high-value use cases, the cost and performance of CCC are improving. Security requires considering cryptographic assumptions, economic incentives, and protocol implementation. The speaker suggests that data aggregators currently capture disproportionate value due to their ability to aggregate private information, but CCC will challenge this, allowing participants to engage without giving up data, forcing more equitable value sharing. The talk concludes with examples of emerging tools and a call for researchers, builders, and organizations to explore CCC's potential for a more equitable digital economy, where data producers control their data and share in the value created.

transcripts.summary: The speaker begins by outlining three caveats: the talk's title, 'Radical Crypto Imaginaries,' was not their own, the talk isn't really about Enoma, and it's also not really about Web3 privacy. The main question posed is: what is the crypto industry? The speaker compares the crypto industry to the automobile industry, analyzing what each consumes, produces, and needs to sustain itself. Initially, they thought crypto consumed skilled labor and produced distributed databases with a culture of knowledge sharing. However, they now believe crypto primarily consumes skilled labor for marketing tokens, rather than building better databases. Tokens are the primary product, with databases serving to legitimize them. The speaker questions the sustainability of the crypto industry, suggesting that it boils down to whether people want new tokens, given that most tokens don't perform as well as the S&P 500. They propose three paths forward: becoming Finance 2.0, collecting paychecks while the world burns, or exploring alternative options like financial engineering for the public good (e.g., Ansari X Prize), a non-dystopian WorldCoin, or vertical integration with centralized control to build and market consumer applications effectively, referencing Moxie Marlin Spike's defense of Signal's centralized approach.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the dangers of relying on closed-source AI like ChatGPT, arguing that users become the product and risk their data being used for training purposes. They highlight the importance of privacy and control over AI, drawing parallels to historical privacy breaches and the Stasi. The speaker then introduces three imperfect solutions: private solutions (which they deem untrustworthy due to TEE vulnerabilities), local solutions (like LM Studio and Ollama run on personal devices or Dappnotes, but limited by hardware), and distributed solutions (which are still in development and currently lack privacy). They promote Dappnotes as a free, open-source platform to run AI models locally, offering an ecosystem for self-sovereign individuals. They invite the audience to join the Dappnote AI early adopter community to experiment with private AI, acknowledging hardware limitations but emphasizing the potential for local AI to become a valuable tool. They briefly touch on future developments like AI agents and distributed AI inference networks with privacy layers, advocating for local-first AI solutions to enhance user control and privacy.

transcripts.summary: Zach Williamson, CEO and co-founder of Aztec, discusses the importance of privacy for Web3 to interact with real-world assets and identities. He argues that privacy is not just an addition to Web3 but a core value, enabling trustless oracles and identity technology. He points out that the fundamental value in Web3 currently comes from dollar-backed stablecoins and economic consensus, missing real-world assets and obligations. To solve this, Web3 needs to interface with Web2 meaningfully by proving real-world attestations on-chain securely, linking accounts to identities in a holistic way, and establishing digital sovereignty. He introduces Noir, a programming language adapted to zero knowledge, and the Aztec network, a privacy-focused blockchain designed to enable secure and decentralized applications. The Aztec testnet is live, featuring end-to-end encrypted Web3 transactions with client-side proving. He envisions privacy technology making Ethereum cyberpunk again, enabling self-sovereign money, advanced financial primitives, and decentralized autonomous organizations, emphasizing individual autonomy and data ownership.
