transcripts.text: Hello, TAPCORN, hello, Berlin. When I walk over to the audience here, I see a room full of builders and founders, and I think I can honestly say that we share the same enthusiasm for building the next generation of FinTAP applications and change the world while we're at it, right? So I bring good news. I think, you know, at least from the stablecoin market, things are really accelerating with new entrants like Stripe, with the acquisition of Bridge, and it really seems like things are going to happen. I've been coming here for the past few years as the CTO of Monerium, mostly talking about the products that we've had, the integrations, and some of the partners that we have in this very audience, but there have also been some internal changes within Monerium. So we, the founders, so our ex-CEO, Sweden, who is here in the audience, is now the chair of the board, and I've superseded as the CEO. So, when creating this presentation, I put the CEO hat on and created, I think, a very good presentation. It had all the hype in it, it had the graphs that went to the right and up. I was pretty proud of it, and then I threw it away, because today, I'm not going to stand on stage pretending I have all the answers, but I would like to take the opportunity to share with you some of the behind-the-scenes stories, some of the challenges that we faced, some of the decisions that we made along the way. And so, it's kind of a building the on-chain payment infrastructure that serves Europe, lessons from the trenches. So let's dive into it. So, it's obvious for us, as European founders, that we face one challenge. The on-chain economy is mostly and overwhelmingly denominated in dollar tokens. So I guess many of you can relate to this. We may have funded the company in euros, we hire and we pay salaries in euros, but when it actually comes to managing the corporate treasury, this means that we need to swap into dollar stablecoins, incurring fees, and then back again on the way out to actually make the salary payments. And along the way, we bear the risk of FX rates moving to our disadvantage. So it's manageable, but as founders, we should not really be wasting brain cycles on those things. So, the obvious answer seems to be, hey, let's create a euro stablecoin. But it's actually more than just a stablecoin, because if we think about all the stablecoins out there, they were not invented to solve the treasury function of a company and make payments. I mean, they were a solution for crypto traders and speculators to actually exit the market at volatile times, be able to survive crypto winter, and move between exchanges without touching bank accounts. And for that dollar denominated stablecoins were actually a perfect solution. So for a euro stablecoin to be valuable, we also have to solve what we call the last mile problem, which is actually connecting the banking system with blockchain somehow. Actually moving funds from bank accounts on-chain and hopefully be able to do it in the other way as well. So when we started Monerium many years ago, stablecoins were emerging as a category. And like then, like now, we had broadly three token designs available. These would be your fiat-backed stablecoins, where every token in existence would have the equivalent in a bank account. Boring, right? Then you'd have the crypto-backed stablecoins, which effectively tried to do the same, but instead of fiat in bank accounts, you would have over-collateralized cryptocurrency as the backstop. And then the third component, or the third design, would be your algorithmic stablecoins. Now many of these more exotic designs have, or at least some of them have succeeded, but many of them have failed quite miserably. And here on the graph, you can see the Terraluna graph, which used to be one for a very long time, and then suddenly a black-swan moment and it went to zero. And if you actually shift this time series a little bit to the left, this could have been the Icelandic banks, where I come from, a few years earlier, where they all fell overnight. So for us, we also understood that if this were to become a mainstream thing, stablecoins, money is inherently political, so it doesn't matter if money is moving on crypto rails or some other rails, they would always be regulated. So the design decision was kind of made easy for us. We wanted to build a euro stablecoin that was boring but efficient. So we started working. We hired the first employee, Jonkunar, who is our in-house lawyer, somewhere in the room, and we started to work. Six hundred pages later, the application was ready, and we had designed a company with all the right procedures, contingency plans, and a whole nine yards. So the next challenge was actually to figure out how do we get the money from the banking system on-chain. At the time, some of the more reputable exchanges were able to open up bank accounts, denominated in US dollars, because that was used for trading. So this wouldn't necessarily have helped Monerium in any significant way. And this also didn't align with the vision that we had, so what we were building was something different. It was something that should be modular and embeddable into the fintech products of the future, and none of that existed for the on-ramping through exchanges. We quickly discovered one very simple solution. So how about we take the IPAN, which is the way you used to route payments in Europe, and we associate it with a blockchain address, effectively creating a virtual bank account on top of your wallet. We thought this was brilliant. And this became a very, very, very efficient way to move money across the boundaries, and solving the last mile problem. And a little peek inside here, this became so effective that we got on the radars of scammers who knew nothing about crypto or DeFi, but would be using our infrastructure to be scanning people. So for those of you who remember when we instated invite codes, that was actually us trying to weed out the scammers. Effectively, if we found one on there, we could trace the lineage in the tree and get rid of them all at once. This was a painful lesson that we learned. Now, today, since we launched publicly three years ago, our users have transacted, really, over 4.7 billion worth of transactions, and 1.5 billion of those transactions have actually been moving across the SEPA bridge. And 80 to 90% of the volume has actually happened in the last 12 months, so it's growing like crazy. The next lesson actually came from integrating Eurostable coin into DeFi. So if you're a regular DeFi project, many of you around here have probably used the method of allocating some portion of the tokens to yourselves or to the treasury. You can use those tokens to incentivize behavior, seed the liquidity pools, you know, life is good. We had kind of imposed a constraint on ourselves with having every single token backed by a Euro somewhere, right? So we couldn't just pre-mine Euros. They had to really exist. And for a small team with a relatively small balance sheet, we couldn't just buy our way into the market. That's not the way we could solve it. So the only possible way we could think of was to reach out to like-minded people and convince them to rally the troopers. And after a few failed attempts on a few different chains, we actually found a community, a home, in this very room. And I think it's good to kind of shout out some of them, but there are many more. I mean, Gnosis, KPK, Aave, and a lot of others have really helped out on this journey. One of the key unlock was actually to get those founders of those projects to onboard for their personal account. And once they actually had tried it, you know, receiving their salaries and making payments to the landlords, there was sort of an aha moment where, you know, they would become missionaries overnight and become these robots that would just move mountains to make sure that, you know, enough liquidity existed so that they could themselves do the things that they wanted. So the next lesson was, it seems like once you have a stable coin, you have the IPAN for easy top-up, and enough liquidity in DeFi, that proved to be a great foundation to disrupt card payments. So GnosisPay was here on stage before me, so you know all about that, and now Metamask as well. And this second generation of cards, they actually work a little bit differently. So they allow you to hold your stable coins in a self-cosocial wallet, and then at the time of sale, or point of sale, they will actually make the tokens available for settlement. Just to be absolutely clear about where we are in this journey, if you think about the value chain of payments, it is effectively the issuing bank, the settlement network like Visa and Mastercard, and the merchant bank. And today, the way it works is the issuing bank is using stable coin rails, then redeeming that and settling over fiat rails. We are actively working with Visa and Mastercard to get our stable coins approved as settlement tokens, kind of unlocking the next layer in the value chain, but the real unlock will come from when stable coins will move from the card holder directly to the merchant, and none of the other thing is needed. I actually think that we are just at the beginning of what is possible with this technology. I get really excited about the ability to hold yield-bearing stable coins in Aave, and because of the atomic nature of blockchains, they will be able to unwrap the tokens at the point of sale to make them available for settlement. And conversely, for credit card kind of behavior, we can think about a future where a loan, you use your crypto collateral to take out a loan at the point of sale, which then gets used for settlement. So I think there are great things happening on this front. Our vision was always to go to market through our partners, as I mentioned earlier, and we spent many years trying to convince the crypto wallets of the time to embed our solution to unlock the functionality that I'm showing here. We failed. Most of these first generation of crypto wallets would either be crypto only, some of them were kind of integrating with DeFi, and a handful of them would be trying to onboard and on-ramp and off-ramp maybe through the card system, which would be very, very expensive, 1%, 2%, 3%, 4%, 5% in some cases. But for the use case at hand, it didn't really matter because prices of crypto swing like crazy, and it was all worth it. So it wasn't until recently that we started to see a new kind of wallet that is more tailored to normies. These wallets would effectively try to focus on simplifying the management of the private keys. They would swap out words like exchange or crypto trade, yield, for something more simple like savings accounts and payments. And it's fantastic to see some of those wallets out here, the battery wallet, rebind, seal, there's now also Greenhood's wallet that are integrating many of the components that you've heard about. You will be able to import your Gnosis Paycard into those wallets. You will have integration into the IBANs, making the payments very easy, and then savings accounts that get their yield from Aave. And there are a great many things happening here. And I was really proud yesterday when I saw a partner of ours tokenize it, who are creating a legal investment platform, kind of a legal ICO for Europe, where they showcase in real time how they could effectively have an investment happening where the investor was going to happen in just a few seconds. It was fantastic. It fills me with pride. And I'm also happy to share with you that through those partners, we are now onboarding more users every day than we are ourselves. So it seems like at least partially our go-to-market strategy is starting to work. So, did we make any mistakes along the way? Yes, you betcha. Many of them. Is our go-to-market strategy going through partners the best way to do it, as opposed to all the other stablecoins who go through central exchanges? Well, only time will tell. I can't tell you the answer to that. But what I can tell you is that the stablecoin market has been disrupted in a very significant way. And I think it's going to lift all the boats in the stablecoin market and also in some of the other DeFi protocols that will become mainstream as a subsequent matter. I now hear again the story that it's only going to be USD dollar stablecoins that will matter. It's all about being able to exchange a local fiat currency into a dollar stablecoin and then use that to transmit over the world and then back to local stablecoins. I just simply cannot subscribe to this idea for two reasons. Number one, I think there will be regulatory pushbacks. As we mentioned, money is inherently political. And number two, we are all here on the mission to bring the world's economy on chain. And for that to work, we need more currencies, not fewer, and especially not one, right? And in that world, we need to be able to efficiently exchange between those tokens. So earlier this year, we got our last registration because we were preparing for the next era of the company where we are going to facilitate users sending us USDC or crypto and be able to mint URI against it. We think this will solve some of the liquidity requirements for some of the changes where we haven't had as much success as the other asgnosis chain. And also, it's going to support DeFi in a way where now rebalancers that rebalance the pools will be able to trade against Monerium and create bots to trade against the pools doing it in a very efficient manner. The end result is a world where you can go from one currency to the other. This is what we call the on-chain FX, and we'll be able to do it at close to mid-market FX rates in a similar manner where we bring the liquidity from the FX markets like we did with the SEPA connection. So with that, after having shared some of the stories and insights, I hope I was able to inspire some of you. The only last remaining advice I have for the audience here is, I mean, we've been at it for a long time, right? In crypto years, we're probably something like 100 years old, and we definitely have the battle scars to prove it. I think it's all about finding the right people who share the vision with you and who are in it for the long haul. With the right people and the right partner, I believe anything is possible, and we eventually will change the world. So with that, thank you for your time. Thank you, Gisli. Time for questions. We have maybe just one question. Time for one question. Oh, okay. Yeah. Thanks. Thanks, Gisli. My question is, what is your mode against other fiat-backed stablecoins? That is a good question. So I think the network effects will be one of them. And again, to the point earlier, what is going to be the right way to distribute the tokens? Is it going to be through some of the centralized exchanges? We see that some of them have had very much success, but we also see that they're paying a lot for that distribution channel, right? So we already know that USDC has been paying something up to 90% of their revenue to Coinbase for that distribution, and this aligns with the conversations we've had with the exchanges. So I'm not ruling them out. I'm just saying, like, I'm not sure that it's a great business to be in. And we always have the vision of kind of creating this modular effect that I talked about, and I think having, you know, many integrations, different kinds of integrations that are more tailored towards real-world users, because let's be honest, the ones in here, it's just tip of the iceberg, right? What I'm talking about is the rest of the world. And so we are very focused on being able to service use cases like GnosisPay and others that are on that same mission. I hope that answers the question. But it's inherently a tough one. I don't know the exact answer. Cool. Thank you so much. Excuse me. Thank you. Thank you.
transcripts.summary: The speaker, Gisli, the new CEO of Monerium, discusses the challenges and lessons learned building on-chain payment infrastructure in Europe, focusing on euro stablecoins. He highlights the problem of the on-chain economy being dominated by dollar tokens and the need for a euro stablecoin to solve the last-mile problem by connecting the banking system with blockchain. Monerium chose a fiat-backed stablecoin design for regulatory reasons, associating IBANs with blockchain addresses to create virtual bank accounts. They faced challenges with scammers and had to implement invite codes. Monerium has facilitated significant transaction volume, especially in the last 12 months, and has integrated euro stablecoins into DeFi, partnering with projects like Gnosis and Aave. This has led to disruption in card payments through GnosisPay and Metamask. Gisli envisions a future where stablecoins move directly from cardholder to merchant and discusses the importance of multiple currencies on-chain, not just dollar stablecoins. Monerium is preparing to allow users to mint EUR through sending USDC or crypto, aiming to improve liquidity and support DeFi. He concludes by emphasizing the importance of finding the right people and partners to achieve their vision of changing the world, acknowledging the challenges and uncertainties along the way. In response to a question about Monerium's moat against other fiat-backed stablecoins, Gisli emphasizes network effects, a modular approach, and focusing on real-world use cases beyond just crypto trading.

transcripts.text: Hello everyone, it's a pleasure to be here. I think we are at a very exciting time, where DeFi is becoming accessible to a much wider audience. It was not very long ago. The first thing I would like to gauge is how many people here agree with the statement that DeFi is accessible. Your brother that's not on crypto, or your mom, someone like that, can use a DeFi product. Could you give me a show of hands, just so I get a sense? Okay, so like 20-ish percent. I have the very strong opinion now that we have accessible DeFi products, so you can actually on-board people that don't know anything about crypto, don't know anything about that, so you don't understand a wallet, don't understand a single concept, and I'll try to give you the sense on why I have come to believe that and what I have been seeing in the field. For context, I have been working full-time in making DeFi easier and more accessible to use for the past four years. I have been building Picnic, which is the product I'll showcase here. The very basic flow our users see when they use Picnic is you log in, and you can use a wallet, but most of the users, like 90 percent, are using email. You deposit money via Monerium or a stablecoin partner, and you have Euro stablecoins or DIN rail stablecoins, and you can swap that to any token you want. So basically, you don't need to know what is a seed phrase, on and off ramp, and getting the right exchange to support the right network. All those things are pretty abstracted, and the flow is super easy to use, and you don't need to know which chain you are on, like you don't need to know about gas. In this example, you're paying gas with EURY, and you don't need to know that you need to approve a token to swap. So basically, every little complexity of the flow is pretty much solved, I would say. The main reason that makes me believe we got there is because we have some testimonials that I think are quite insane. I would not expect those sorts of testimonials to be happening like two years ago or something like that. So, for context, most of our users are Brazilians. A lot of them are not very sophisticated, and we have been talking with a few users and getting stories like this one, which is a person that his main occupation is being a fisherman. He's not very educated, and in his own words, he can barely use a cell phone, but he can buy tokens on PICNIC. We have another one, which is some 64-year-old lady that is not very tech-savvy and can also use PICNIC, and she was really happy because she bought Bitcoin for the first time. So, the UX is not too unsimilar to what we have been seeing in terms of Web2 products. You can get normal people to use it, and that changed the game quite a bit. Given the context that UX now is pretty good, the main thing I have in my mind now is how do we build use cases that are 10x better? So, if you're just thinking about custody, you have options. If you're more sophisticated, you're probably using Safe, Ledger. There is not a whole lot of reason to use a solution that depends on the email security to custody your funds, and if you're less sophisticated, centralized exchanges might be a good option as well. They have a bunch of layers of security and things like that. So, I understand it's not 10x better than the existing solution, so that's not a super strong driver of growth. Same thing to buy Bitcoin to own an off-ramp and to get yield on DeFi products. You have tools like DeFi Llama for super advanced users that will do a better job. So, the result of this is that just good UX is not enough to grow. I think UX got to a point that you can actually use DeFi products, but why will they use it? What is the super strong benefit you're getting on using it? UX is not enough. The thing that I'm actually very excited about this moment, I think we found a very clear use case that is super appealing to a lot more people. So, I'm Brazilian. We have been super focused in the Brazilian market, and in the past three weeks, we got a recent law that increased taxes on USD purchases by 3.5%. So, now, a picnic is 4.5% or 4% cheaper than life, and that does a rag-arb, so any stable coins allow you to do that. So, for example, a thousand reais are getting you $179 on picnic, and the same amount gets you $172 on life. And the really cool thing about this, still very early, but these are notice-based transactions across all chains. Picnic is the yellow one. It has been... Oh, the orange one, sorry, and it has been growing, like, last week, it grew 50% a week. Prior to that, it grew 70%, and every time we talk with users, the market pool is super strong. So, crypto users are using this a lot, but the thing that's surprising me is friends that are coming to Europe to travel, they are telling me, man, like, how do I get this card? The card's taking too long. I'm getting a lot of inbound interest, and it has been a different thing to watch. In the experience, it is super straightforward, so in Brazil, we have something called PIX, which is a payment QR code, and once you pay that, you get Brazilian real estate coins, and you have USDC in the card that's ready to spend. So it feels a lot like Web3. You don't need to know anything about Web3, which makes me think, like, when I see this product and I look at metrics, it feels a lot like the time I worked at the B2C product, which is basically looking at conversion funnels, so you're looking at every step, what's the user's doing, how conversion is going, and, like, how do you make the card order faster? How do you make the user retain? So we have been thinking a lot about adding mobile app, diminishing flow times, and the market changes a lot. So right now, we have been really focused in getting users out of Binance, getting users out of Metamask, but with this card, which is by far the cheapest way to spend in dollars for Brazilian users, you start competing against TWICE, you start competing against local banks that have USD offerings, and you have a really compelling product for people that just want to travel. So now I think we have the tools and the setup ready. I think Web3 has the UX that is good enough to be useful for non-crypto people, and the big question for me is, like, how do we operationalize that, and how do we optimize those products to actually be useful? So any Brazilian that's traveling now, their best option, financially-wise, is to use a product like this, that is fully built on DeFi, and is saving you 4% or 4.5% of everything you spend internationally. That's it. Thank you. Thank you so much, João. Let's open it for questions. There's one, is it, no? Okay, questions, questions? No? Okay, there's one here. So why do you think it's so hard in crypto to get good UX? I think it's a hard technology to build on. We spent a lot of time just building custom things to make it work, so in fact, we were the first safe ERC-4257 integration I know of, and we needed to build a lot of custom infrastructure just to make it work, and then you get the edge cases and different chains, different things. I think it's just hard, and things are new, so you cannot reuse a lot of strong stuff that has been built, and you also don't have that many references to copy, so you need to think through a lot of things. Thank you for the question. Anyone else? Any other questions? Cool. Thank you for listening. Thank you so much, João. Thank you. Thank you.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses how DeFi is becoming more accessible and showcases Picnic, a product aimed at simplifying DeFi for non-crypto users. Picnic abstracts away complexities like seed phrases, on/off ramps, and gas fees, allowing users to deposit via email and swap tokens easily. The speaker emphasizes that good UX is now a reality, and highlights a real-world use case in Brazil, where a recent tax law makes Picnic a cheaper alternative for USD purchases. This has led to significant growth and interest, even from non-crypto users. The speaker believes that Web3 now has the UX to be useful for non-crypto users, and the focus should be on optimizing these products. The speaker states that getting good UX in crypto is hard due to the newness of the technology and the lack of reusable components.

transcripts.summary:
Lorenz from Grow2Pi hosts a workshop on application-level data deep dives, trends, and insights, focusing on EIP 7702 and account abstraction on Ethereum. The agenda includes explaining EIP 7702, the evolution of public goods funding, and a live demo on unlocking on-chain analytics for dApps through attestations. Lorenz highlights the shift to a dApp era due to reduced transaction fees and increased throughput, made possible by data sharding and Layer 2 solutions. He discusses EIP-7702's native account abstraction, enabling batch transactions, sponsored gas, and programmable account logic. He shows how to use the Open Labels Initiative to attest contracts, unlocking free analytics on Grow2Pi, emphasizing the importance of on-chain data for dApp success and funding opportunities. The live demo walks through attesting the CowSwap DEX contract. Participants discuss metrics like wash trading detection, cross-dApp user connections, user retention, and integration with proof-of-humanity protocols.
The speaker discussed proof of humanity concepts, mentioning a 'handprint' as potential proof and a testnet. They also referenced Zillow's work in this area and Gitcoin Passport, which aimed to prevent account farming by ranking users based on their social media presence, though it was later sunsetted. The speaker concluded the workshop by offering assistance with data questions and promoting RotoPi, a free analytics service for dApps that are part of the Open Labels Initiative, allowing users to track their dApp's performance across the Ethereum ecosystem.

transcripts.text: Hi everyone, I'm Julien Nesque, I'm Gnosis DeFi VD and I'm going to speak about how everything started about creating a centralized financial system and somehow in the rails, we went on to do and trade 14 coins and what are we doing at Gnosis to bring it back to where it was. So let's start in the beginning. Gnosis started in 2017, we launched the first decentralized prediction market platform and it proved to be one decade too early. It turns out that neither the UX nor the infra was ready back then to mass adoption and poly market success proved that we were too early. So we had to pivot and we pivoted, we built, we became a cornerstone of Ethereum infrastructure, we built GAO, we built the SafeMoon SIG, we acquired and kept building Gnosis chain and now I think things are finally becoming ready for achieving mass adoption. But what started as a cyberpunk dream of banking the unbanked, of exiting the system, of creating a decentralized censorship-resistant financial system, became into either an unregulated decentralized casino where people are just talking and smiling with insiders to launch an exchange coin to dump on retail or a bunch of centralized services that do provide value but do not really care about our values. So let's get back to basics, let's bank the unbanked. Stablecoins are actually providing massive value right now and they do serve two different use cases. In the global north, stablecoins are a UX improvement, they really improve, they are acting as programmable money, they really improve the UX, they are much easier to integrate, they facilitate access to a global liquidity layer and in the end they do provide access to a credibly neutral financial settlement layer. In the global south, stablecoins are actually providing another use case and they are giving access to users or people from censored countries or with very unstable economies to stable value and this is really valuable too. But the problem is that all of these users are using services that are really centralized. transcripts.summary: Julien Nesque from Gnosis discusses the evolution of decentralized finance (DeFi) and Gnosis's role in bringing it back to its original vision of banking the unbanked. Gnosis started with a decentralized prediction market platform in 2017 but pivoted to Ethereum infrastructure. Nesque highlights the value of stablecoins in both the global north (UX improvement, programmable money) and global south (access to stable value in censored/unstable economies) but notes centralization issues. He contrasts the cumbersome UX of 2021 crypto onboarding with the improved, user-friendly wallets of 2025 which abstract away complexities. Gnosis is creating 'Circles' enabling users to create their own money and receive universal basic income and cross-border payments via GnosisPay. He details use cases like Argentinian freelancers receiving USDT and Brazilians sending money from Portugal. He showcases features like accessing DeFi yields through SEAL, earning yields until the moment of spending and a decentralized lending protocol-powered crypto credit card using AAVE. He invites developers to build products facilitating real-world finance. He ends by inviting everyone to join Circle.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker, Nenad from ENSO, introduces a workshop about making it faster to get ideas on-chain. ENSO aims to simplify the process for developers by providing cross-chain intent APIs, allowing users to move tokens between chains and vaults with a single transaction. This eliminates the need for manual integrations, extensive Solidity coding, and lengthy audits. ENSO offers four main API groups: routing, tokens/positions, integrations, and wallet/TDL information. The routing API optimizes paths for token movement, including swaps, deposits, and redeems, while the bundle API allows for more control over the path with actions like harvesting, adding fees, borrowing, repaying debt, and bridging. The workshop includes hands-on challenges using tools like Happy Path, the ENSO SDK, and a token/protocol navigator.
The discussion covers dynamic values in bundles, where users can pipe results of actions into subsequent actions. The receiver of funds on the destination chain can be defined as a smart account or EOA. ENSO has smart contracts on various chains where funds land, allowing atomic execution of bundled calls. Users can inspect these contracts to ensure specified actions are followed. ENSO simulates requests twice on chain forks to ensure they pass, using an open-source simulator called Temper. The conversation also highlights ENSO's approach to attracting developers: building and open-sourcing products to demonstrate API capabilities, integrating DeFi protocols, and offering hands-on integration demonstrations. Key practices include focusing on developer experience, building actual products to showcase capabilities, and providing immediate integration demonstrations. The most popular bundles are looping and rebalancing, with examples like staking pipelines and leveraged positions available in the documentation. ENSO simulates all requests, provides call data, and offers an open-source simulator for users to verify actions independently.

transcripts.summary:
This is a live coding MiniApps workshop. The goal is to take the audience from zero to a live MiniApp. The speaker will provide background on why MiniApps are cool and how to set them up, with the main focus being live coding and implementing features. The speaker built the number one open source Firecaster client and is currently building Vibes Engineering, a factory to generate MiniApps. MiniApps make it easy for users to engage with blockchain and perform on-chain transactions with just a few clicks. Examples include buying an eSIM, donating meme coins cross-chain, sharing a social graph on a map, and playing a Wordle-like game. The speaker discussed how to create a mini-app, emphasizing using a laptop for coding along and providing resources via a QR code and vibes.engineering.com. To run a mini-app, you need a startup project, PM install, and a preview tool using Cloudflare for a tunnel. The preview tool shows the Firecaster user ID, username, and profile picture. It allows for on-chain transactions, such as signing, sending ETH, and minting NFTs, all simplified compared to traditional methods like MetaMask. The live coding demo involves building a mini-app for circus, displaying a list of Firecaster friends and checking if they're on Circles for potential trust connections. The speaker prompts Cloud Code to fetch Firecaster friends using the Naina API and integrate Circles, showing how they connect and what tools they use to debug and prompt the LLMs.
The speaker discusses Firecaster developer tools, focusing on the manifest tool for domain association. They explain how to register a domain and view its mini-app configuration, which includes icons, images, text, URLs, and categories, all stored in a JSON file located at `.well-known/firecaster.json`. Account association, connecting the domain to a Firecaster account, requires mobile signature generation, a process the speaker finds annoying. Firecaster plans to offer a feature to host this file, simplifying management. The speaker also discusses integrating the Circus SDK, detailing challenges encountered while trying to identify specific addresses of users on Circus 2. They managed to implement a solution after several attempts. The demo now shows followers and checks if they're on Circus, though it currently only checks primary Ethereum addresses. The speaker plans to share the completed integration on Firecaster.

You can actually just like build something really cool, make it available, and get access to credit and have a really good product. And I think that's really something that will power the next generation of DeFi builders. Yeah, we're very excited for that. Perfect. I think we've run out of time. Yeah. Just one last question. Do you have a date? Well, it's very soon. Okay. I can say we're working every weekend and weekday, so we're getting very close.  Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. We have questions here.  We have questions.   Okay, so. Thank you so much, Stani, Marcos, Marcelo. Let's open it up for questions. One question there on the front, please, on the front. Thank you so much. This has been excellent. I kind of wanted to ask maybe a little bit more of like a regulatory question. With now that the U.S. market looks like we're moving towards a period of time where at least the U.S. administration sort of considers that DeFi might be a core element of the sort of like United States policy going forward, how are you thinking about maybe engaging, frankly, like Wall Street and the sort of like wider market that maybe exists outside of crypto? And sort of like what ways does that reflect in the protocol itself or not? Yeah, I think that definitely there is a kind of 180 degrees turn on the kind of regulatory side, especially in the U.S., compared to going back just, you know, one year earlier. And I think that's obviously there's a couple of things. So there's a lot of interest in stable coins. So the Genius Act is in a place where it's going to pass. There's going to be a lot of stable coins from big tech, thin tech, commerce, e-commerce, and other types of use cases. And some of them we'll find into DeFi because DeFi is essentially an environment for best financial opportunities. Why? Because that's where the best algorithms exist that can be matched instantly with liquidity. So there's those kind of like perfect conditions to find these opportunities. And then I would say there's another piece besides stable coins is the institutional interest in tokenization. And one of the things that I kind of like try to, when I talk to institutions, and there's a lot of actually inbounds at the moment than ever before, is that like once you tokenize, you have to figure out like what the hell you're going to do with the asset on chain. But I think that all the roads will lead to DeFi eventually because RWAs are a way to scale the DeFi opportunity. Stable coins are the way to access and consume the DeFi liquidity and also extract the yield opportunity as well. Globally, it's the best technology to distribute it across the world. So I think now the climate is probably better than ever before. And last week I was in D.C. I was at the White House and I was in Capitol Hill. I was at the SEC. Surprisingly, they let me in there. But it's been like a really interesting, because in the past, and many of you who's been building DeFi for two years now has a little bit like anxiety about the regulation. And even if you're deep down the bottom, you're building kind of like a freedom technology, empowering technology. At the same time, you have this uncertainty. And the uncertainty is what basically creates the distance between institutions and consumers and accessing DeFi. So I think now specifically it's really good timing to build DeFi. And we probably see a lot of institutional integrations. So it's been really good at the moment in terms of like the inbound. Do we have other questions? No? No? One last question? No? Okay. Well, give it a round of applause.
transcripts.summary: The discussion revolves around integrating Balancer with Aave's new V4 architecture. Aave V4 introduces liquidity hubs and spokes to improve capital efficiency and manage risk. Liquidity hubs store assets, while spokes are configurations for borrowing and supplying liquidity. This architecture aims to solve the 'chicken and egg' problem of seeding liquidity in new markets. Go, offering predictable borrow rates, plays a special role. Balancer's integration allows for BPT (Balancer Pool Tokens) to be used as collateral on Aave, boosting capital efficiency. The panelists discuss the potential of RWAs (Real World Assets) in DeFi, with concerns about on-chain liquidity and off-chain risks. Aave V4 introduces risk premiums for different collateral compositions, making borrowing rates more personalized and accurate. The panelists also touched on regulatory trends, particularly in the US, where there's growing interest in stablecoins and tokenization, which could lead to greater institutional involvement in DeFi. The new architecture aims to provide access to credit lines for developers, fostering innovation by removing the need for bootstrapping and focusing on product development. Overall, Aave V4 aims to fragment risk while maintaining capital efficiency and promoting the growth of DeFi.

transcripts.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about probably the most impactful event that affected self-custody this year, which is the hack on Bybit. This is not a simple exploit. It was a very targeted attack by a nation-state actor on Bybit, and I think it's something where we should take the time together as an industry to reflect on what this means for us, how we approach self-custody, what takeaways we can take from that, so I want to spend all of the talk about that, about the takeaways that we took and that the industry should also have internalized. I'm sure most of you have followed this incident and are mostly aware of what happened, but for those who are not, I just want to briefly give a summary. So the North Korean-sponsored state actor, the Lazarus Group, was able to compromise the safe wallet front-end, and using that, was able to deploy code that was very tailored to Bybit, which was using the safe wallet front-end, and actually the code that they deployed there, what it did is, first, it prevented one of the signers of the Bybit multisig to sign at all, so completely blocked that for some reason, and second, all the other signers, when they would use the safe wallet front-end, they would see the transaction they want to do, but the front-end would forward a different payload to the ledger devices, and this was used then in order to trick the signers of the multisig to confirm this transaction, and this transaction, which was a malicious transaction, upgraded the account, so it did a delicate call, it upgraded the account to another singleton, which is a malicious smart contract, which then allowed the hackers to take full control of that account. So yeah, that's the rough summary, the outcome is very unfortunate, Bybit lost 500,000 ETH during that process, and yeah, it's been, in my view, the most impactful event on self-custody as mentioned. So let's go into the learnings there. First one is secure self-custody is a constant battle. Secure self-custody is not a solved problem, and I don't think it will be ever a completely solved problem, that's the thing with security, there is no perfect security, you can just maximize as much as possible, harden different systems, but perfect security is a myth, but that means that securing self-custody is an ongoing process, especially as tactics of attackers change, as the environment changes, as also the industry, the tooling that we use, the stacks that we deploy is changing, so it's something that we cannot, as an industry, stand still, we need to constantly evolve, respond to tactics, build up new defense systems, that's one thing, it's constant, but it's also an unfair battle, because when we look at custody in custodial solutions, the attackers need to compromise just one entity, that's the thing that we don't like about intermediaries, about custodians, that they become the central point of failure, but then the investments into security, to protect against these attacks, they're socialized across all users, in self-custody, the protections, the investments into security need to be tailored for each user, and that's, it's just an uphill battle, because on the other hand, you have actors, like the Lazarus Group, who are willing and able to invest millions of dollars just to hack one user, because if it's a big enough user, the investment actually is worth it, so that just means that the users themselves need to actually be fighting this battle against potentially much bigger entities, and this creates a very imbalanced battlefield, but that also means, actually, that we, as an industry, should give the tools to the users in order to fight this battle, I think that it's clear that different users, depending on their use cases, they need different defensive tooling, and especially users at the scale of Bybit, they just need much more hardened security, much more tooling in order to stand this battle. Takeaway number two, even strong on-chain security can be broken through off-chain trust assumptions. As an industry, we've invested a lot into on-chain security, into audits, simulations, formal verifications, like we've really done a lot there, but users are not interacting with Solidity, they're interacting with JavaScript, interacting with, like, off-chain components, with wallets that they download from the App Store, with a lot of things that are on top of the on-chain security, and that means that we create an extended transaction supply chain that depends on a lot of components, on libraries, on relayers, on indexes, a lot of off-chain infrastructure, we're kind of building this Web 2.0 stack that sits on top of the Web 3.0 account, and that needs to be dealt with in the same way that Web 2.0 security needs to be dealt with, and that is different approaches than the on-chain security, and the key thing is that the longer this transaction supply chain gets, the more complex it gets, the harder it is to ensure that this chain doesn't break at any point, that there's no weak link in it, and the real challenge there is that when such a chain breaks, it's quite easy to point where is the weak link, but the hard part is at any point of time before something breaks to make sure that each of the links is hardened maximally, and the more complex we get building these Web 2.0 solutions on top of the Web 3.0 stack, the harder this gets for us as an industry. So, for takeaway number three, and that's actually for me a silver lining here, is that client diversity differentiates self-custody from custodians, because after the hack, the safe order team right away took down the front end, so it investigated and remediated, hardened the security of the front end, and that required the front end to use at times of uncertainty and the work that had to be done, it wasn't possible to keep it online, and in any case in traditional finance, when the front end is down, even just for maintenance, users cannot access their assets, they're completely locked out. I think here it was good to see that during that time, there were projects on the ecosystem stepping up, offering alternatives, products that have been existing before, being able to help users do transactions during that time, there's mechanisms like CLI that we can run locally, there's like a decentralized front end on IPFS, the eternal safe, you can run the stack on your own, which also a lot of users actually do, and which also I think should be supported, and that should get easier, but that meant that during that time, in self-custody there's no need for bank run, because someone else was drawing funds from their accounts, doesn't affect anyone else, and that I think shows the power of self-custody in the end, but it also showed challenges, where even though there are a lot of solutions out there where you can interact with your safe account, some of those products, they also depended on the transaction queue, which was also taken down during that time, some projects have their own transaction queues, they have some redundancy, but that also means that we need to think client diversity for the entire stack, and we cannot just limit it to the front end, and we need to make sure that we can decentralize as many parts of the stack as possible, and I think this is relevant generally for self-custody, for different DeFi products as well, that they have access points beyond the canonical interface, it also is very relevant in the context of smart accounts and 7702, where potentially like very custom implementations may not have this redundancy, and then they become suddenly dependent on the availability of one specific front end, that's something where further investment is needed, and especially on the safe side, I think there's, yeah, certain things we took from that learning, where we need to make sure that there's redundancy across the stack. Takeaway number four, we need better tools to educate, and then education to enable users to verify transactions. Yeah, we often say, don't trust verify, and we need this ability to, as a user of self-custodial solutions, to be really the last line of defense, and be able to verify the transaction down to like the payload, the methods that are being called, like this is really a key thing of our industry, but it's also easier said than done, and I think that's something where we need also to invest further, where in this case, Bybit verified. They verified what they saw on the front end was what they intended to do, but that's not the full verification that's needed to really have this last line of defense, because the front end told a lie, the ledger devices told the truth, and they relied on the front end there, and that's something where education is needed, but also better tunings in order to make it actually feasible for people to verify the transactions that they sign. And there's already a lot of initiatives at the back of the Bybit incidents that is working towards that, both in the safe wallet front end, where there's better ways to guide users to tooling, and better ways to verify transactions, but also the ecosystem players, ledger is pushing for clear signing, also together with MetaMask, the safe utils tool from OpenZeppelin, and also from the Ethereum community member who wrote the initial script, like these things are needed, but we need to do more there, because it's still too difficult to verify transactions, even with these toolings today, and we need to make sure that people can really have human-readable instructions that they confirm on a trusted device, or trusted wallet, and that needs, yeah, we need to do more. So, takeaway number five, we don't just need stronger security, but we need layered security. And to explain that, right now, essentially we have two layers, two high-level layers of security. One is the security of the transaction supply chain, that goes from the front end that you use, the RPC, the SDKs, end-game packages, like everything, every line of code, every dependency in there, that is part of actually crafting, or turning the user intent into the actual payload. But the other layer is the transaction verification, and that's really this last line of defense I talked about, where the user can verify on a trusted hardware or software the payloads that they're signing. And while I think we need to harden both of these layers, I don't think this will be enough. I think we need additional layers of security that actually can ensure that even if those assumptions break, that the outcome is not catastrophic. I think that's, yeah, that can be achieved in different ways, like this can be on application, on a protocol level, where it could be like hooks in the context of modular AMMs, it could be assertions that are enforced by a sequencer, different ways that we could actually have execution guarantees on transactions, that even if the user signs something wrong, these fail-safes catch the bad outcome, so they can at least reduce the harm. And here just a call also to the community, especially people building on SAFe, to explore guards, because they can really enable that. Guards, they're essentially a plugin that does pre- and post-transaction checks on each transaction, and that enables things like enforceable policies, whether they're provided by an application, whether they're set as custom policies by the users, but there could be policies like, my SAFe can only transfer this amount of assets to this specific other SAFe or something like that, that then every transaction, no matter what you sign, needs to fulfill this check and otherwise reverse. Guards also can enable things like co-signers, where there's external parties, maybe a decentralized network having the right to check transactions and either give a thumbs up or thumbs down, and therefore allowing more of these fail-safes to live, whether they're on-chain, whether they're off-chain, to provide these execution guarantees. Also resource locks, that's also a topic that's becoming more popular generally that in a way allows additional escrow logic before assets leave an account, but there's different ways how it can be implemented in SAFe. There's actually projects already doing that in different ways, hyper-native blockades, they have such co-signers, Jocera has their chat system, like the Zodiac team has built this already way in the past, but we need to push on that front, because this can build up a third pillar of security, which makes sure that we have fail-safes in place in case the other assumptions break. One simple thing that the SAFe team has been building now is a delegate call guard, which essentially would just limit to what Singleton's account can be upgraded to a curated set, and this would have closed at least this specific attack vector that private experience, but the design space is much broader than that, and like it really allows to cover many different attack vectors in different ways. Now to the last one. So final takeaway for today, self-custody needs to become more cypherpunk again. I think there's always this tension in whatever we build between on the one side, simplicity, UX, mainstream adoption, and on the other side, the values of cypherpunk, which is censorship resistance, privacy, and security, and I think that's especially in recent years where we at the industry wanted to push for more mass adoption, we wanted to onboard more users, this can easily dilute the very values of what we're building, and that's something where we need to be mindful at least of trade-offs, but also actively push against and make sure that we retain these important values of our ecosystem. That's something, at least at F.A.F.E., we want to double down on that for a new initiative, which is F.A.F.E. Research, which really aims to solve the hard problems of self-custody around censorship resistance, security, and privacy. This will take a lot of work, they're not easy problems, but that's important that we continue to invest into that part as well, and like there's a lot of problems, it's just a subset of things that we need to cover there. For everyone that's part of SAFECON tomorrow, which I highly recommend, I think it's on the fifth floor here at the DAPCON venue, I would suggest you come by the talk at 2 p.m. from Richard, who's actually leading this initiative, where he can tell you more about what that actually means and how that will look like. I see time is up, but maybe to end with, there's a lot of people in this room that are fighting this exact battle, and I know that it's often very hard, because it feels very much like an uphill battle, like there's constant new threat actors that we need to consider. It feels like a never-ending thing, because we've been building for a long time, we've been hardening security across the board, and so we see a lot of hacks and exploits on a monthly basis. I just want to thank everyone that's fighting this fight together with SAFE. I think it's especially also in today's world, where we see financial censorship, we see data breaches of centralized parties, we see even intermediaries sponsoring military parades. I think it might be the most important fight that we're doing, and so I think it's crucial that we keep at it, we don't give up, and we really retain the passion for SAFE custody and also the values of our industry, and don't lose that. Yeah, that's it. Thank you very much. Do you have any practical tips for teams that want to avoid such supply chain attacks? I mean, there's the boring answer, which is there's certain standardizations, especially in Web 2.0, SOC 2.0 compliance, MDM files, the best practice is just in Web 2.0, there's a lot of literature, training that we can do, that needs to become a must-have for the industry. That's one thing. But maybe the more practical thing, just assume at any point of time that there's a target on your back, and that feels like paranoia, but it really is important, because we need to assume that it is, and we need to operate always under the assumption that someone at this very moment tries to infiltrate our systems, tries to infiltrate the team, be hired in a position, like somehow trying to get to our users, because they're actually not trying to get to us when we're working SAFE custody, but to our users, and we need to make sure we're operating with the interest to protect the users there, and that needs a little bit of paranoia, and like always, thinking twice about everything we do.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the Bybit hack, a targeted attack by a nation-state actor (Lazarus Group) that resulted in the loss of 500,000 ETH. The attacker compromised the safe wallet front-end, manipulated transactions, and upgraded the account to a malicious smart contract. The speaker outlines several key takeaways from the event including: the constant battle for secure self-custody, the vulnerability of on-chain security due to off-chain trust assumptions, the importance of client diversity to differentiate self-custody from custodians, the need for better tools and education to enable users to verify transactions, and the necessity of layered security. Finally, the speaker emphasizes the importance of reinforcing cypherpunk values (censorship resistance, privacy, and security) in the self-custody space and announces the launch of SAFE Research, an initiative focused on addressing the hard problems of self-custody. The speaker encourages paranoia to teams in order to avoid supply chain attacks.

transcripts.summary: Hannes from ZEAL introduces the smart wallet that aims to bridge traditional finance and crypto by offering a user-friendly experience built on secure smart contracts, specifically Safe. ZEAL focuses on daily earning spenders, allowing users to earn yield on idle money while keeping it accessible for spending. The wallet uses pass-keys for security, addressing seed phrase issues, and employs an on-chain validator for biometric signature verification to avoid centralized dependencies. It solves address fragmentation by deploying wallets deterministically across networks. Key features include 'Recharge,' which automates moving funds between yield-earning accounts and spending accounts, and cross-chain deposits, enabling users to deposit into their accounts from various networks in one click. ZEAL subsidizes gas fees and offers free on/off-ramping with partners like Monerium and Unblock. They are launching a special activation program where users who register with a specific link and spend 50 euros with their card receive a 40 euro reward.

transcripts.summary: Sharon and Sonny introduce their company, Nosis HQ, which aims to simplify on-chain business payments, addressing the banking challenges faced by startups and on-chain projects. They focus on reinventing business accounts for stablecoins, serving clients like Mento, Pixelmon, and Picnic. The company highlights the mainstream adoption of stablecoins, noting their growth from $1.9 billion to $200 billion in five to six years. While stablecoins are gaining traction, Nosis HQ emphasizes that business adoption is still in its early stages, with only $3 billion in business payments using stablecoins compared to a $37 trillion market. They aim to streamline fragmented payroll processes and partner to create a cohesive experience. Nosis HQ offers features like connecting wallets, various payment networks, multi-currency support, and reporting tools, all designed to be compliant and user-friendly. The presentation includes a live demo of their platform, showcasing payment options for both crypto and traditional bank transfers, along with virtual cards for business expenses. Sharon shares a real-world example of using the Nosis HQ card to fund a WeChat Pay wallet at a Chinese restaurant in Malaysia, illustrating the card's connectivity to local payment networks.

What you care is about how much risk or how much permissions you have given to it. In this example, you know that at every month, you will be able to spend $999 USDC. So whether that key is compromised or not, you know that this has as much risk as you've given this AI agent for, whether that's a pass key or a server key or a secure enclave key. Awesome. Anyone else? Fantastic. Thank you so much, everyone.
transcripts.summary: Pedro, the founder of WalletConnect, discusses improving the wallet experience in Web3 by reducing the need for constant signing of transactions. He introduces Smart Sessions, a solution developed in collaboration with wallet partners, which allows users to grant applications specific permissions for actions like time-bound access, spending policies, or smart contract interactions. This eliminates frequent wallet pop-ups and enables AI agents to automate on-chain tasks within defined policies, like swapping tokens or managing loans. Smart Sessions support recurring scenarios like dollar-cost averaging and improve the gaming experience by removing the need for transactions for every in-game action. They also enable developers to create subscription-based services and redefine the wallet experience by allowing AI agents to act as intermediaries between apps and blockchains. The goal is to empower users with choice, control, and composability across the WalletConnect network, making on-chain interactions more frictionless and automated. In a Q&A, he discusses how developers can implement Smart Sessions with different key management solutions, focusing on the importance of user-defined policies to mitigate risk.

transcripts.summary: The speaker, Francesco, discusses optimizing agentic economies and workflows for DevRel (Developer Relations), leveraging interviews with agents and builders. He introduces a universal framework for DevRel, including the DevRel pyramid and builder funnel. He highlights the importance of permissionless innovation and building a driving developer ecosystem by aligning frameworks and speaking the same language across different stakeholders. Francesco presents a Maslow Pyramid for builder needs called the Hierarchy of Builder Needs. He also introduces a developer funnel focused on value-driven onboarding and building safe spaces for developers before promoting specific products. Francesco discusses using AI to change the game, focusing on content optimization and the need for LLM-readable documentation and API playgrounds for agents. He notes that DevRel needs to cater to both human developers and AI agents. Francesco outlines what humans and agents want, highlighting the need for standardization and predictable schemas for agents. He discusses how AI can speed up access to resources and basic education. He presents six categories that can be optimized with AI. He introduces a third framework outlining human progression to agent native, showing how to optimize tasks with agency. He closes with a question: Will AI take our jobs? He hopes the audience learned something about the frameworks.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker, Denim, co-founder of Envio, discusses multi-sigs in motion, focusing on safe data and smart contract wallets. Envio aims to make public blockchain data more accessible and performant. The talk covers the dataset itself and the tooling used to create a real-time dataset, including safe chain network distribution, safe deployment activity to understand chain adoption, and operational usage of safes. He highlights that safes offer extra security, shared ownership, non-repudiation, recoverability, and flexibility. Denim uses Envio's HyperSync and HyperIndex products to analyze safe data across multiple networks, revealing insights into safe deployment patterns, network adoption, and how safes are used in practice. The data shows a concentration of safe deployments on certain networks and suggests that safes may not be primarily used for multi-signature security, but also for flexibility and programmatic benefits. The speaker also shows examples of how they queryed and visualized these data sets. Finally, he shows some case studies and tools like Snub, Log3, and Chain Density that have been built using Envio's technology.
The speaker discusses a publicly available dataset and encourages viewers to explore it. They caution that the data provides directional insights and requires further analysis. They then answer questions about analyzing signer behavior using on-chain data, acknowledging limitations in capturing pre-executed or failed signatures. The speaker suggests that analyzing signer behavior, such as identifying frequent signers and their activities, could reveal valuable insights. They explain the data structure and show how additional information can be extracted and queried from the data.

transcripts.summary:
Matt from PARA introduces PARA as a comprehensive wallet and authentication suite for crypto applications, combining Web 2.0 and Web 3.0 authentication with universal wallets secured by passkeys and MPC. He highlights the preference for single sign-on experiences and the challenges posed by the proliferation of Web3 wallets. PARA aims to solve these challenges by offering universal embedded wallets linked to users rather than apps, enabling seamless control and interoperability across different Web3 applications. Matt also discusses account abstraction, sponsored gas, and customized permissions to enhance user experience and security. PARA's solutions prioritize user control, ownership of assets, and frictionless transactions while integrating familiar Web2 authentication methods. He then explores the PARA examples hub for mobile, web and server implementations.
The discussion covers Para's functionalities, including wallet connection, guest access, integrated on and off ramps, and code generation for various chains. Examples of wallet creation, authentication, and transaction signing are provided, along with information on custom chain support. Para uses an open-source MPC protocol, and developers can access it via an API key obtained from developer.getpara.com. Security measures include API key authentication, allowed origin settings, and a secret API key for server-side verification. Para is used to sign transactions, and users can verify transaction details through optional pop-ups that display information based on a mapping between application data and user-friendly descriptions.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker discusses value accrual for tokens, emphasizing that tokens should have a purpose beyond just existing. The discussion revolves around governance tokens, their shortcomings, and how to improve them. Key points include: Historically, tokens have been used for capital formation; governance tokens initially aimed to give holders a say in project direction but often failed to provide financial interest; governance is not always a sufficient demand driver. The speaker suggests creating better incentives to hold tokens, such as linking the treasury to the token and exploring utility or speculative value. The speaker also advocates for a focus on long-term incentive alignment, the potential of vote escrow and staking mechanisms, and a gauge system where token holders make decisions over capital allocation.
The discussion covers several key points about token management and value creation within protocols. It emphasizes the importance of having a clear reason for people to buy a token, the need to create and capture value for users, and aligning stakeholder incentives. Lockers are presented as a potentially better instrument for token management compared to staking, allowing for more adaptable parameters like cool-down periods and voting power changes. The conversation explores the concept of 'bribes' as a way to incentivize stakers indirectly for legal reasons, creating value for the network. The discussion also touches on the use of gauges for capital allocation within DAOs. Gauges can be used to set minimum and maximum budgets for different categories. Examples of projects using gauges, such as Ave and Benki, are mentioned, with Sushi being highlighted as a project that allocates fees through a MasterChef contract. The Mode project is cited as an example of using a gauge system to distribute OP tokens and incentivize projects within its ecosystem, fostering inter-project collaboration and token ownership. Overall, the conversation emphasizes the need for careful consideration and experimentation when implementing token management strategies and capital allocation mechanisms.

So unlike Bitcoin, where the ideal is to hoard or hodl, as we say, Ethereum's native currency, Ether, is always in motion. It's used to pay gas fees, secure the network, and reward contributors. So Ether isn't just sitting on a mattress, right? And this is where our contribution comes in. We added a new one called the infinite garden. Now this idea sees Ethereum as a living, breathing ecosystem, which is organic and involving and full of potential. But like any garden, it needs care, and it can grow wild or grow stale. And while it invites endless experimentation, it also faces the risk of becoming fixed and less of a garden, more of a monument. So we'll dive deeper into this later, but for now, just know it's a metaphor that captures both the hope and the tension at the heart of Ethereum's future. So for this research, here's our research approach. We interviewed key figures from Ethereum's core development group, and what's interesting about Ethereum core devs is that they're part of a porous group, so anyone theoretically can be a core dev through consistent contributions, and there are no formal barriers. So our interviews weren't limited to just developers. We also spoke to researchers and coordinators, and here are some of the people we interviewed, including Vitalik, Danny, Pooja, Tim, Alex, Ben, and Trent. And our interviews were semi-structured, meaning we had a set of open-ended questions that allowed for deeper exploration of topics as they came up. Now I don't have time to fully dive into how Ethereum governance works, but here's a quick overview of the key stakeholders involved. So we have the core devs, the full nodes, the stakers, the media, the dApp builders, and the end users, and this structure forms what we call a polycentric governance system. Essentially, it means that multiple overlapping decision-making centers operate autonomously but interact with each other through cooperation, competition, and conflict resolution. No single entity holds control, but governance happens through coordination among these decentralized bodies. So now, having said all that, and doing some of the context setting for the research, I'll discuss some of the key themes that emerged. So the cyberpunk theme is one that was pretty prominent. For anyone who doesn't know, the cyberpunk movement began in the 1980s. It emerged from online hacker culture as a protest against the growing power of the state to monitor its citizens through digital networks. So they were a group of advocates who, they basically used cryptography as a route to non-violent direct action and social and political change. So we found that some of these values still permeated in the worldviews or imaginaries of Ethereum devs. We had quotes by Ben Eddington stating things like, we are for decentralization, we are against political control, and we are for credible neutrality, and making Ethereum robust against capture in all its aspects. And so while it's still surprising that Ethereum's roots are tied to cyberpunk ideals, what stood out in our findings is how many of the people we interviewed see themselves as part of a broader lineage of the cyberpunk heritage. And this traces directly back to the infrastructural mutualism social imaginary that's grounded in open source collaboration and decentralization. So there is a deep resonance in Ethereum core devs where they view their work as an extension of the cyberpunk principles and broader historical lineage. Now another key theme that emerged during our research was conflict resolution, specifically how core devs managed differing perspectives within their group and within the wider Ethereum community. So our interview took place around the time of a major Ethereum protocol upgrade known as Shapella, which went live on April 12, 2023. And this upgrade allowed for participants in Ethereum staking mechanisms to withdraw the ETH they had locked up during the transitions from mining to staking, which was a huge milestone for the ecosystem. So many of the developers we spoke with emphasized the clarity of the decision-making process, reflecting Ethereum's collaborative governance approach. Despite some setbacks and maybe back and forth discussions on the technical side, we found that the considerations were relatively straightforward, as Alex Stokes put it, and the process was pretty streamlined. And Danny Ryan also reinforced that decisions were largely based on rough consensus, meaning that complete agreement is not required, but a general alignment is reached among participants. And also Ben Eddington has highlighted how decisions are generally made through discussions where descending opinions are welcome and heard. You know, this very much aligns with how developers work, which is based on this pragmatic engineering ethos that is committed to excellency and precision. Another key theme that emerged was market pressures. So one of the key research questions we had for developers was to understand the extent to which market pressures influence the decision-making of Core Devs. And what we found was that after Ethereum's transition to staking in September 2022, developers did not initially prioritize enabling withdrawals of staked ETH. However, other participants within Ethereum's polycentric ecosystem, notably stakers, media, and end users, felt that unlocking staked ETH should be the top priority. And so in response, the Core Devs adjusted their focus, deprioritizing other upgrades, and shifting their efforts to enable withdrawals through the Shapella upgrade because they wanted to deliver on that promise, and they felt the imperative to deliver on that commitment. So we specifically found Ben Eddington's remarks important because he emphasized how developers have a degree of autonomy from market pressures, and they do not allow to sway them from their core mission, stating, mercifully, we've been free of commercial pressures. Core Devs are pretty resistant to being told what to do, and we will make our own minds up. Okay, that's pretty cyberpunk-ish, right? Okay, so now we come to the term Incident Garden, right? So this is the imaginary that we are sort of contributing to the broader literature of imaginaries. So the Incident Garden, this term was coined by Ayame Aguchi, which was the former executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, and it perfectly captures the essence of Ethereum's ethos in Aya's own words. She describes Ethereum as a protocol for human coordination. Coordination is a game, but not that one is played to win. Coordination is more like tending a garden, where one works only so that the garden continues to thrive. So this analogy reflects a temporal dimension to the thinking of Ethereum core devs. Social imaginaries provide a way for understanding our place in time and space, among others, and within history. Beginning in 2020, Ethereum's co-founder Vitalik Buterin introduced what is often referred to as the Ethereum Roadmap. However, it's important to note that this roadmap is not an official or formal document. Everyone must follow. So rather, it collates various long-term research trends of Ethereum's protocol development, and the roadmap converges towards a sort of endgame, the point where Ethereum's protocol will be so mature that it will no longer require major upgrades, and its development will stabilize. So for core devs, their primary task is tending the Incident Garden, and just like any Incident Garden, there is always maintenance to be done, but at the same time, seeds are being planted for the long term. So you might be wondering, okay, so what's Incident Garden, great, what does this all mean? Okay, well, I think this is interesting because while clear structures of processes and practices in the Ethereum exist, such as EIPs, all core dev calls, and research forums, we found this particularly social imaginary important because beyond EIP-1 and a README text, Ethereum lacks a formal constitution or governance document. And these social imaginaries, we argue, serve as the essential enabling conditions for Ethereum's governance to function seamlessly. So in the absence of formal guidelines for off-chain governance, these imaginaries play a vital role in defending the boundaries of acceptable actions and behaviors. As a result, core devs lean heavily on these implicit imaginaries to ensure cohesion and within the Ethereum community, they guide them by fostering a shared sense of foundational values, long-term alignment, and nuanced understanding of the ecosystem's collective expectations, which is important for a collective without a formal hierarchy for maintaining legitimacy. Which is to say, also, let's not overlook the role of culture in Ethereum's governance. So the Infinite Garden suggests an imaginary, it's an imaginary that suggests a dynamic ever-evolving ecosystem where growth and transformation are ongoing, but a key challenge we discovered was for core devs in maintaining cyberpunk values as the ecosystem grows. And these concerns reflect an underlying anxiety, as Ethereum grows, the original cyberpunk ethos could become diluted. For the core devs, this growth signals success, but it also invites the possibility of new visions of Ethereum that may diverge from the foundational values they aimed to embed into the protocol at the origins. So these are the findings of the paper. The paper is currently in publication, and of course we are always happy to continue the conversation and hear out your ideas. Feel free to reach out to me or Pollr on Twitter, this is my crypto Twitter. And yeah, I will now hand it off to my colleague, Dr. Paula Villas-Ennis, who will speak with you on the developments that occurred in Ethereum since this paper was written. Thank you so much.
transcripts.summary: The speaker introduces a research paper titled "Attending the Infinite Garden: Organizational Culture in the Ethereum Ecosystem," co-authored with Dr. Paul Dylan Ennis. The presentation will outline the paper's core arguments and key findings, followed by an update from Dr. Ennis on recent Ethereum developments. The research explores how culture shapes Ethereum's governance through social imaginaries, which are collectively held beliefs and norms about technology. The paper identifies several social imaginaries at play within Ethereum, including the "world computer" and the "hacker engineer," and introduces a new one: the "infinite garden," which represents Ethereum as a living, evolving ecosystem. The research approach involved interviewing key figures from Ethereum's core development group and identified key themes such as cyberpunk values, conflict resolution, and market pressures. The speaker concludes by discussing the importance of social imaginaries in maintaining cohesion and legitimacy within the Ethereum community and acknowledging the challenge of preserving cyberpunk values as the ecosystem grows.
