transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the evolution of Ethereum's social layer and governance, building on a paper called "Tending the Infinite Garden". The paper identifies the 'infinite garden' imaginary within the Ethereum ecosystem and the speaker now reflects on its limitations. Initially, academic papers focused on centralization in crypto, but have evolved to understand blockchain communities as polycentric. The speaker notes the original paper focused on cooperation and conflict resolution among core developers but missed the competition and conflict stemming from other stakeholders. They highlight the Ethereum Foundation's evolving role from a background entity to a guiding force and introduces the "stakeholder expansion dilemma," the challenge of incorporating wider stakeholder interests without compromising cypherpunk values. The speaker presents a stakeholder set list for 2025, including core devs, researchers, organizers, the Ethereum Foundation, end users, power users, stakers, builders, roll-ups, media, and investors. They also discuss the emergence of a "pragmatist imaginary" which prioritizes Ethereum's competitive position and institutional adoption, contrasting it with the original cypherpunk values. The speaker warns against a "post-ideological pragmatism" which prioritizes the ETH asset's performance over Ethereum's values and structure and suggests a need to be aware of defections to other blockchains like Solana and the potential for a populist revolt against the Ethereum Foundation, similar to what's happening in Bitcoin.

That was the very first game we deployed. It was not exactly this format. It was more like geocaching. So you had to find QR codes that were hidden in the event, at the Congress, in that case. It was a primitive version of THC. And it was very simple, but people loved geocaching, and that was the original seed idea that also guided us to create these THC games. They just had a geocaching treasure hunt in San Francisco, that they were talking about on the news. Someone won something like $10,000. People love geocaching. Yes. In our case, you don't win $10,000. People are also happy with, like, I don't know, once we gave a prize, a piece of wood. I mean, it's nothing, but even if it was part of the game, for whatever reason, they liked it. Stickers. But, I mean, if you play these guys, don't expect to win $10,000. That is not even the money we make. So it's also quite expensive on us to make this kind of game. Yes, of course. Any questions for Alberto down here? That was a great talk. Thank you, Alberto. Thank you. I remember a year or so ago that there was Crypto the Game or something like that, that became very popular. It was even acquired by Uniswap or something like this. So it seems that playing these games with on-chain mechanisms is becoming something of a trend. Would you say that? And, like, where do you see the future of social distortion going? Like, what's your idea to maybe scale this? Or maybe you don't, maybe it's, you know, what's your vision? So, first of all, we have no vision. That's also part of STP. We don't have—yeah, we just live day by day, to be fair. We have another game we deployed a time ago that I want to do again. We like this idea of, like, on-chain pop-up games. And what you mentioned before, by the way, to try to answer your question about on-chain games, I think it's a super cool trend. There are people doing a lot of really cool games, on-chain games. What we like is this kind of on-chain games that you play in a real physical space to connect with other people. So we want to focus more on these kind of experiences. And if we have, let's say, a plan for the future, we try to develop more these kind of ideas of in-person on-chain games because I think they're quite fun.
transcripts.summary: Alberto (Albi) from Social Distortion Protocol (SDP) discusses decentralized, on-chain treasure hunt challenges (THC) on Ethereum. SDP, from the year 2045, time travels to show the present what the future holds if certain issues are not addressed. THC is a game played in a physical space, built around a narrative and organized into levels with physical puzzles to solve. The game's structure includes a master plot divided into chapters with quests and puzzles, and sometimes side quests for extra points. Onboarding is crucial, using letters to invite attendees to become players. The game uses a web application where players read chapters, locate and solve puzzles, and submit solutions. Benefits include venue exploration, social connection, and learning new skills like lockpicking or smart contract creation. Puzzles vary widely, often involving hardware and physical interaction. A leaderboard tracks progress, and finishers receive on-chain NFTs. They've run the game at various events, including Congress, ETH Berlin, and DEF CON. Albi then discusses the THC framework, an open-source framework to create treasure hunt challenges on the EDM, divided into the ADAPT front-end and the smart contract back-end. ADAPT serves as a navigator, allowing players to explore the game and submit passwords, and uses Gelato to sponsor transactions. Game assets, including quests, are encrypted using AES with the solution of the puzzle chapter, so you need to solve the prior puzzle to unlock the next. The smart contract stores hashed solutions as wallet addresses. Players submit their solutions, which are verified using a zero-knowledge proof-like method where the smart contract recovers the signer and allows them to progress. The speaker then discusses Continuous Build and Deployment (CBD), a THC companion framework that simplifies the deployment process, including making edits to quests. Albi references DevCon Improvement Proposals (VIPs) related to this kind of game. He ends by answering questions regarding the past Zuckerberg hunt and the speaker states that they focus on in-person on-chain games.

They advocate for developers to focus on development and designers on design, advocating for a separation of concerns to avoid cognitive overload and design inconsistencies. They suggest that developers should avoid over-complicating designs with unnecessary UI libraries and custom styling, instead focusing on semantic HTML and global CSS. They promote minimal design, testing early, and prioritizing functionality, allowing design to emerge organically from the product's needs. The speaker also touches on accessibility, unobtrusiveness, honesty, and environmental friendliness in design, as well as thoroughness and consistency, advocating for a clear and simple approach to design that allows developers to move quickly while maintaining a high-quality user experience.

transcripts.text: Good morning, everyone. Can you all hear me? I'm waiting 10 seconds for people to catch their feet. All right. Welcome everyone to the SafeCon. This year, we're doing things a bit differently. For those who were at SafeCon in the past years, we've been at the other side of the river. Now we thought we're integrating SafeCon within DapCon to make it easier to go back and forth. Now SafeCon is a one-day event. We're expecting up to 400 people today, and it's all about self-custody. So we got people from different parts of the industry, different types of people like researchers, builders, users, such as general self-custody advocates. But what combines us, the goal that we share, is that we want to make altogether have self-custody be secure and easy. And yeah, it's never been more important that we are able to make self-custody secure and easy than today, with geopolitical conflicts across the world, with constant data breaches of intermediaries, and with custodians, for some reason, sponsoring military parades. I think it's crucial that people in the world, they have the ability to take control. They have the right to self-custody, and they have the possibility to exit a system that they find themselves in. And that needs everyone of us. That needs the entire industry in order to make this possible. But also, at the same time, self-custody itself is being attacked. And I had a talk yesterday at DAPTCON about the Bybit hack, and the learnings that we should take from that, and a little bit of the details. So I'm not going too much into the nuances there, but just the high level, what we should learn from Bybit, which happened about three months ago. Definitely, self-custody and secure self-custody is a constant battle. We haven't solved secure self-custody yet, and it's questionable whether we will ever solve it, because self-custody means that you defend yourself against malicious actors, against adversaries that would like to somehow compromise your account. And they constantly change their tactics, their tools, the environment changes, the tech stack changes, and it's something that never stops. Like, this battle is really something that's ongoing forever, and we need to make sure that we're always raising the bar in terms of this, that we're always giving users better and better tooling in order to defend themselves against attacks. It's also a very unfair battle, because in custodial solutions, you have to case, and what we also challenge, or what we don't like, is that there's one institution responsible for custodying all the assets, but that also means that the cost of security is socialized across all those users, because it's essentially the institution responsible for the security there. In self-custody, the security is very unique per user, and the investments into security have to be appropriate for each user, but that also means that the types of defense mechanisms and the types of tooling need to be different for different users. It's unfair, because on the other side, there's nation-state actors, like the Lazarus Group, which easily can spend millions of dollars of investment into trying to compromise one single user, because if they succeed, actually, it is a lucrative investment. That's something to keep in mind. Another learning is that self-custody is relying on two main pillars. On the one side, you have the infrastructure, you have the transaction supply chain, basically all the different tools that users essentially use in order to make transactions, and that's the operating system, the device that they start with, the laptop, the front-end that they use, the application that they use, and everything in between, like the RPC, the indexer, all the off-chain infrastructure. Unfortunately, we are at a point where we've built very cool web-free technology, but then we add a thick layer of web-2 technology on top, which is adding a lot of complexity from a security perspective, and just increases the attack surface for hacks to happen. So, the resilient infrastructure making this really secure is getting harder and harder as the transaction supply chain is growing. On the other side, the second pillar is the transaction verification, which is really the last line of defense of self-custody. We always say, don't trust, verify, but that is easier said than done. We see that many users don't verify transactions in a very appropriate way, and it is because it is complex. Clear signing is not something that is propagated across the ecosystem. Many people verify maybe what they see on the front-end, but they don't verify if the payload is what they intend to do on the hardware device, and then suddenly, out of these two assumptions, what can happen is that if the transaction verification is not done properly, the infrastructure and the transaction supply chain becomes a single point of failure. That is something where definitely we need to have more investments. We need to have investments into hardening the infrastructure, working on decentralized alternatives, working on client diversity, front-end diversity, increasing the bar in terms of standards, security practices, OPSEC, all of that. But on the other side also, educating users about how they can verify transactions, providing better tooling to verify transactions, educating also about secure setups and processes, all of that. There is going to be a very interesting panel on this later today about the current status quo of transaction security and transaction verification, so make sure to check that out. I also think this might not be enough. Even though we can invest more into these two pillars, we might need to think about additional layers of security, and one proposal that I have here that I would like to also discuss with you later in talks is execution guarantees. Execution guarantees essentially meaning that there is certain logic that is part of how even if the transaction supply chain and transaction verification fail, the outcome should not be catastrophic. There should be ways that there are certain guarantees given that certain invariants that cannot be broken and that can be implemented in different ways. I have talked to people here at Dapcon. They work on a way to have assertions being enforced by sequences, for example. There's possibilities to have hooks as part of a modular DeFi protocol that enforces these guarantees, and in the case of Safe, the Safe Smart Account, there is a possibility to do that via guards, which is plug-ins that essentially do checks on transactions, pre- and post-transaction checks, and that's something that's super underutilized. We've talked in the past a lot about modules and modules being able to create new recovery mechanisms and other things, but I think what we should actually focus on more are these guards because they enable to create these execution guarantees, and they can come in the form of a cosigner, so a trusted party or even a network maybe of cosigners that runs logic and enforces certain rules, for example, that your account can only be upgraded to a certain set of singletons, for example, or that your account can only transfer a certain amount to another address. The rules are pretty arbitrary there. You can implement—or cosigners can implement anything, really, like security checks, compliance checks, whatever. There can also be policies enforced via guards, which can live on-chain, which can live off-chain, which are user-defined, which are provided by the application. The range there is also broad. Or resource locks, which is a fancy way to say escrow and escrow logic, which can be enforced on transactions. I'm glad some teams, some of them are also here today, are working on this. They work on additional guarantees, execution guarantees, as guards also, like the Hibernative team, Blockade team, working on cosigners, Drosera, as their traps have a framework, and others. I would just advocate for people that are especially building on SAFe to take this seriously, look into guards, look at the possibilities, also talk to these teams and their experiences, because I think that's something we need to do more in. A few short announcements. There will be more across the day. One is that the team is finalizing the smart account version 1.5, which the big change there is that it introduces also module guards, so guards that actually run on modules. Also execution guarantees running on modules, which opens up more opportunities to create these security mechanisms, and a bunch of smaller changes. Essentially the idea is that 1.5 becomes the long-term support, the last 1.x version, and that any future version would then be most likely a bigger change, like a v2. So that's the idea there. So we packaged whatever we think makes sense in the long term to be included in the 1.x version, and have this be most likely the final one. It's also interesting that the SAFe smart account is now being pre-deployed by all major L2 stacks. So whenever a new L2 launches with any of these stacks, they actually come with the SAFe smart accounts be pre-deployed there. That just enables better multi-chain support, rolling out products to many networks more easily, and also reduces central party deploying these contracts there, which helps decentralization. Now, a bittersweet announcement. After Bybit, we temporarily paused the development of SAFeNet. For those that remember, SAFeNet was announced as a vision last December. It was the initiative for SAFe to work on interoperability, to create unified balance across networks. When the Bybit hack happened, we needed some time to think about what is actually the best focus for us in this situation. Is this really the problem that we want to solve? Is it really us needing to solve this? We realized there is a bunch of teams working on interoperability right now. Chain abstraction at some point was pretty much every team pivoted to chain abstraction. So there's a lot of development there. There's even initiatives from L1s, from the Ethereum Foundation, from L2s to create native interoperability. Finally, given our realization that now is the time to invest into security rather than convenience, all these three things together make us realize that it's not the right time to bring SAFeNet as envisioned to the market. It's sad for myself because a lot of blood and sweat went into this, and we have made quite some progress. We want to make sure that this progress isn't going to waste. So next week we are open sourcing SAFeNet, hoping to get feedback and signal there in terms of how to take this forward with the ecosystem together. There are very interesting learnings there from SAFeNet, especially on these execution guarantees that I mentioned, because that was also part of the roadmap. How can execution guarantees be enforced on cross-chain transactions as well? So there's very good learnings there inside, also text that can be built upon in the future as we focus more on the security aspect. Also, we wanted to go forward into the next phase with a better structure within SAFe. So that's why we announced SAFe Labs, which is really the product side of things. It's a fully owned subsidiary of the foundation, so it's very much ecosystem aligned, but it has a mandate to productize and also commercialize technologies around SAFe, and especially raising the bar in terms of enterprise readiness and really scaling the solutions that we already have to more audiences. This team is being led by Rahul Rumala, who's also here today, focusing particularly on SAFe Wallet and SAFe API technologies and products that we've been working on over the last years. He will be here doing a talk at 1.30, so if you want to hear about what's next for SAFe Labs, what's the newest developments, make sure to check that out. On the one side, we thought it's important to really take the next level in terms of the product, but we also want to look ahead and really work on the things that make self-custody and that is really what the ecosystem originates on, like the Cypherpunk values, which we want to push forward and really work on the hard problems of self-custody. We're also having the SAFe Research Initiative going forward, which is led by Richard Meissner, and this initiative really focuses on the core values of Ethereum, which is censorship resistance, security, and privacy. So that's always the tension when you build up products. Do you focus on simplifying things, great UX, mass adoption, or do you actually work on the less shiny, less marketable aspects, which are nevertheless the more, or at least equally important aspects to building a product, which is censorship resistance, security, and privacy. There, we want to have a team that's purely focusing on long-term challenges that we can solve. There, Richard will talk a bit more about already the initiatives that are in progress right now, but also going forward, and also the mentality that we want to apply to this research, because it should be also practical research that supports the ecosystem. Yeah, there are two. Make sure to check this talk. Yeah, so generally, we want to be focusing with different mandates on different aspects, but with one shared mission. So we will have going forward the foundation, which I'm leading with the mandate of fostering the SAFe ecosystem and generally the self-custody ecosystem, SAFe Labs, which is productizing technologies and also commercializing them, taking them to the next scale, and SAFe Research, which is pushing for cypherpunk values and solving the hard problems of self-custody, SAFe Labs by Rahul and SAFe Research by Richard. And the shared mission and what ties everything together is really to make self-custody secure and easy, and yeah, this needs these different focuses. Yeah, there's going to be a lot of other announcements throughout the day and talks and panels. Make sure to hang around here. Very interesting, also at 5 p.m., Xiaowei from the Ethereum Foundation will come here and talk about making DeFi cypherpunk again. So that's an interesting one, but also very interesting panels on security, on on-chain organizations, and many more. So glad to have everyone here today. Looking forward to also chats on the side, one-to-one, and yeah, thanks for being together with us on the battle to make self-custody real. Thank you. Thank you. Oh, I mean, question. Yeah, I mean. Sure. Sorry? I mean, you need to always anticipate it. Like, honestly, like, we should always operate with the assumption that someone at this very point tries to compromise your systems. And so, yeah, this is something we need to anticipate. Predicting is hard, at least not in this scale, in this exact format, because if we would have anticipated that attack vector, it would have been possible. More questions? Would you say the problem mainly was ledger needs a bigger screen?  Would you say the problem is mainly that ledger needs a bigger screen? I mean, there's not one single problem, especially in this case. It's probably a few links that got broken. Like, if you imagine a chain, like, sometimes the chain breaks, and then it's easy to point, like, these are the points where the chain breaks. It's hard to predict it before, where are the weak links. I think clear signing and being able for people to verify transactions is one aspect that needs to be worked on, but also the infrastructure security is another thing, and just missing fail-safes is also another thing. I don't want to weigh them against each other. That would be bad.
transcripts.summary: The SafeCon event focuses on making self-custody secure and easy, a goal made increasingly important by geopolitical conflicts and data breaches. Self-custody is a constant battle against evolving threats, requiring ongoing improvements in user tooling. Unlike custodial solutions where security costs are socialized, self-custody places the security burden on individual users, creating an unfair battle against well-funded adversaries. Self-custody relies on resilient infrastructure (transaction supply chain) and transaction verification, but the increasing complexity of web-2 technology layered on web-3 tech increases the attack surface. Better transaction verification is needed, as the infrastructure becomes a single point of failure if verification is inadequate. Execution guarantees, enforced through guards or other mechanisms, can add additional layers of security. SAFe is finalizing smart account version 1.5, introducing module guards and execution guarantees on modules. SAFeNet development is temporarily paused due to the focus on security. SAFe Labs, a product-focused subsidiary, will be led by Rahul Rumala, while the SAFe Research Initiative, led by Richard Meissner, will focus on censorship resistance, security, and privacy. The speaker also addressed a question about the Bybit hack, emphasizing that there wasn't one single point of failure, but rather a chain of broken links.

transcripts.summary:
The panel discusses the vision of 'On Chain to Bank Them All,' focusing on the growth and challenges of the crypto ecosystem in reaching a billion users and potentially banking everyone. The panelists explore the role of financial Legos, regulatory considerations, and monetization strategies. They delve into the importance of user experience (UX) and education to onboard new users. The conversation touches on the path to growth for protocols like Morpho and COW, including potential integrations with centralized interfaces and the need for a hybrid system. Circle's role in providing a regulated money layer for the internet is also examined, emphasizing the importance of liquidity and network effects. The panel concludes by discussing monetization strategies for Web3 companies and the potential for a flywheel effect, where developers, fintech players, and users reinforce each other's growth.
The discussion revolves around incentivizing distribution partners in the DeFi space, with a focus on revenue sharing models and the importance of self-custody. Kao protocol is profitable and shares fees with partners for integration. The conversation shifts to the significance of self-custody in the broader ecosystem, with Circle emphasizing its commitment to providing self-custody options and enabling financial access for those traditionally excluded from banking services. The potential risks associated with under-collateralized loans and the responsibility of integrators in protecting customers are also addressed. Morpho sees itself as a marketplace for risk, and believes that those distributing specific products should do their own risk assessment. The conversation concludes with a quick round of predictions about the future of crypto and traditional finance. Panelists believe that infrastructure is coming together and want to achieve the goal of banking a billion of people and self-custody is extremely important for that.

And the builders are building these apps, are able to innovate on their user feedback, and are therefore driving users very efficiently through go-to-market efforts to those apps and to the chains that those apps are built on. And those users are the ones that are bringing more value on-chain, new value on-chain, and more usage of the chain. So the idea here, you see here on the right side, is that incentives for builders become really smart. They're really transparent because they're fully on-chain, they're fully based on that on-chain growth that we really want to see as a community. They're permissionless, so it doesn't matter who you are as a builder. If you're driving that on-chain impact, you can get the incentives. You don't need to know anybody or be located in a specific place or be able to attend a conference in a beautiful city like Berlin. And it's outcome-based, so it's only paying when the outcome, that on-chain growth that we want to incentivize, happens. It's not for anything that happens. We're not paying for anything that is happening before the on-chain impact. There's different programs for that. The idea here is to really incentivize the actual growth. So how it works, again, in the framework of these three stakeholders, the protocols, they define the outcome, as I mentioned. We call it the on-chain KPI. They find a reward contract. This is a smart contract. We call it a reward tool. They deploy it, and they set the duration of this reward campaign. The builders, they integrate DIVI through our builder hub. It's about 10 lines of code, just a couple of snippets. And they start onboarding users to the product. They don't have to do anything else about the funding. They just start driving usage to their product. And the users, as they are onboarded to these products, they transact, they bring value on-chain, and all of that user's activity is measured by the DIVI protocol through that integration that's listed. And so DIVI is able to attribute all of the user's on-chain actions and usage to that builder, and that is what determines how much funding the builder gets. So based on that verified on-chain impact that the users have through the app, the app builders are receiving incentives for that verified impact directly from the protocol through the DIVI campaign contract. So we have a couple of campaigns live already. We've learned so much. I'll share that in a second. But first, why do these growth teams, and Layer 1 teams, Layer 2 teams, on the protocol side, why do they love it? They love it because there's no overhead. They don't need a team of 10 people to reach hundreds of builders, to incentivize them, and to even understand the type of impact that these builders are driving on-chain. It's very scalable because the DIVI campaign, because it's permissionless and it's on-chain, can serve five builders or thousands of builders. Anybody can sign up and it's really high ROI for the growth team because they're only paying when the builders are driving the on-chain growth, the on-chain impact that is defined by that KPI. Any funds that aren't used at the end of the campaign, the growth team or the protocol team can claim back. So they really keep the full control. It's very, very automated and efficient for them. On the flip side, for the builders, why do they love it? It's very transparent, same reason, but it's very clear what kind of incentives they will get for the impact that they will drive. They don't have to do the politics dance or game. They don't need to be fluent in a language that's maybe different to their native language to be able to apply to the grant. So all of that time-consuming grant application process and reporting is gone. It's very transparent attribution, so they themselves can understand, I got this much in incentives because I drove this much impact, or my users drove this much on-chain impact. It's all transparent and all that data is available through the Divi app. And that's what results in the builder's long-term commitment to a protocol. They have predictability. Because these campaigns keep going live, these protocols launch multiple campaigns, and they know that they will be able to continue receiving incentives based on the impact that they drive, so these campaigns are super transparent. So with Divi, we like to say that Divi helps grow the Web3 Pi for everyone, for protocols, for builders, and for users. So the way this campaign works is that the top-used apps, so the apps that drive most on-chain usage, they're still the ones that get the most. Like, it's proportionate to how much on-chain usage they're driving, but it's not just the top builders. Every builder that's driving on-chain usage will get a proportionate share of the campaign pool. They just have to register for the campaign. So all participants in a campaign get something that is pro-rata based on their impact. And so it's very transparent and fair. It really incentivizes post-impact rather than making guesses on who is going to have the most impact or grow the pile the most. So what's the result? There's no early advantage. There's no modes. Everybody can sign up at any point in time during the campaign. Any builder with an app that is live on mainnet can sign up. There's more funding available when the ROI goes up because it becomes even more efficient for the foundations, the ecosystem growth teams to fund this campaign and to continue to fund the builders that are driving the most impact. And the small builders will win more. Again, there's no politics. There's no overhead for them. They can really just build, ship, and earn. So here are some of the protocols that are using Divi today and some of the ways that they're using it or planning to use it. Some of these are not live yet. VANA, they're creating data dials, and so there are L1s for user-owned data. RWA Chain, who launched recently, their mainnet was literally a week or two ago. So they're going to use Divi to incentivize their testnet builder community to deploy their mainnet really fast rather than wait for, I don't know, months. It can take a long time. It's kind of like putting a carrot in front of the builder and be like, if you deploy fast, you have all those rewards, all the incentives to claim. Tether is planning a campaign to drive circulation of USDT. I'll dive into the fellow public goods, the fellow DAO campaign in a minute. We also have one with Lisk, and we're also experimenting with a builder community to grow our own builder community that is participating in multiple campaigns with Scoutgate. So this is the fellow DAO campaign, fellow public goods campaign. There's 105 builders. I think the campaign is like four weeks in now, so some of this data on the chart is a bit outdated. 50,000 unique users referred or participating or using fellow as a chain through these 105 builders and a ton of gas usage. So the KPI that fellow public goods is incentivizing is gas usage of fellow because that's the seller's revenue model as a layer two. Fellow public goods knows all the builders, so they're doing all the registration onboarding, and I have seen already the first month, if you compare the first week of the second month in purple to the first month of the campaign, gas consumption has already doubled for the top builders. So it's really like providing that flywheel. If you provide incentives to builders, they'll just drive more on chain usage in the next month. It's very easy if you're a protocol or gross team to launch a campaign. You define the KPI. You define the budget and the duration of your campaign. We, the core team behind Zevi, can help you implement what we call the impact reward function, so how much you're going to provide incentives per unit of impact. You fund things for a contract, deploy it, and then we go into builder onboarding, and it's all then automated on the Zevi dashboard from there. The builders integrate some snippets of code. Some people report that it takes like two hours, maybe half a day, depending on how Web3 native the app builders are. And then together we grow the price. So the builders build, the on-chain value grows because they bring more users, and Zevi is able to track and attribute all of those users' on-chain usage to that builder in real time, and builders can then go to the Zevi dashboard and claim rewards at the end of each reward period based on all of that traction that they address. So this is how we are rethinking Web3 funding. We're moving away from hype and from politics, from manual, like outdated process, into impact-based funding of builders, automated so they don't sync in time and paperwork. They can sync in, or not sync, that's not the right expression, but like invest time in evolving their UX and their product. And what is really nice is that it's permissionless, so builders don't need to know anyone. They can just start experimenting, or they can be really further along their builder journey and their app growth, and they can join Zevi's campaigns at any time. So the idea is to forget retro, and for builders to build, ship, and earn. So if you're a builder, you should head over to app.zevi.xyz. You can see all the live campaigns and also past campaigns there, depending on which protocols you're building on. You can even sign up for some of the campaigns now. You can join the Telegram community, that's what the QR code is here for, and get updates on new campaigns that go live, or follow us on Twitter as well, with app.zevi. So we're ready for the next evolution, which is one where we don't fund hype, we fund outcomes. Thank you. Thank you, Denise. Okay. Funding in the... Oh, before you go, we have some questions with the crowd. Oh, great. If you can spare a few minutes. I was just going to say, funding in the Ethereum ecosystem is a design space that has interesting challenges, and if we have any questions for Denise before we go to lunch, now is your opportunity. If not, we'll let you go.
transcripts.summary: Denise, co-founder of Bivi (now Zevi), discusses the problems with current Web3 builder funding models like grants and hackathons, which she argues are broken and don't effectively incentivize long-term impact and on-chain usage. She claims these models reward incumbents and lead to a 'bounty hunting' culture and political grant processes, creating an unsustainable growth loop. Denise introduces Zevi as a solution, an on-chain protocol that allows ecosystems to pay builders only when they drive measurable on-chain results, avoiding the pitfalls of traditional funding methods. Zevi aims to create a three-stakeholder ecosystem where protocols launch incentive campaigns, builders build apps that drive on-chain impact, and users bring value on-chain. She highlights the transparency, permissionless nature, and outcome-based incentives of Zevi, emphasizing that it helps grow the Web3 ecosystem for protocols, builders, and users alike by moving away from hype-based funding to impact-based funding.

transcripts.summary: Marcos Montero, a customer engineer at Google Cloud, discusses building Web 3.0 agents in Google Cloud, focusing on the agentic web, its building blocks, and a reference solution architecture for DeFi. The agentic web adds an execution layer to Web 3.0, enabling decentralized intelligence and autonomous UX. AI agents, defined as applications achieving goals through observation and action, have evolved from basic chatbots to complex systems with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and reasoning loops. The architecture of AI agents involves a runtime with orchestration, memory, agent definitions, models, and tooling, enabling end-user interaction through various prompts. Use cases include automating wallet operations, DeFi tasks like automated trading, and governance decisions. Google Cloud offers AI services like Gemini and Vertex, along with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) and GenKit frameworks. The Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A) facilitates inter-agent communication. Agent Engine, built on Cloud Run, provides a serverless runtime for agents. Google Cloud also provides Web3 services like Blockchain RPC for reading/writing blockchain data and Blockchain Analytics with indexed data. A solution architecture for DeFi includes a root crypto-based agent and sub-agents for wallet management and trading/staking, hosted on Google Cloud, using KMS for key storage and Model Armor for generative AI guardrails.

name: What would it really mean to build a world computer?
description: The original vision of Ethereum was — at least nominally — to build a ""world computer"". Before debating whether Ethereum has succeeded or failed in doing so, or even whether the attempt itself is worthy, we must ask ourselves the question: what is a world computer, and what would it really mean to build one?

transcripts.summary: The speaker, Christopher, discusses the concept of a "world computer" and its historical context, particularly in relation to Ethereum. The term was coined by Vinay Gupta, describing Ethereum as a magic computer in the cloud where anyone can run programs. The speaker argues that Ethereum, as it stands, is not a world computer but rather a replicated state machine. Taking the metaphor seriously requires a system where users can send messages, run programs, and trust that they will execute correctly. This involves abstracting away the messiness of a distributed system, making it behave like a unified cloud computer. Two fundamental things are needed for a real world computer: logical centrality, and correct abstraction of the underlying distributed system. The speaker then presents two paths for Ethereum to achieve this: one involving Anoma, a project he works on, and another involving reworking the EVM. Anoma aims to distribute application state across multiple ledgers while maintaining a single object interface for users. Alternatively, the EVM could be upgraded to control state movement, add asynchronous message calls, and provide sophisticated indexing for distributed queries. The speaker concludes by emphasizing the importance of treating the world computer concept as a meaningful promise and highlights the need for abstractions that support heterogeneous trust and peer-to-peer systems.

transcripts.summary: The speaker, a former engineer turned designer, discusses improving user experience (UX) and developer experience (DX) in decentralized products. They emphasize the importance of making these products usable and appealing, even with underlying technical complexities. The presentation advocates for a two-layered approach to design, focusing on both developer UX and end-user UX, arguing that a better developer experience leads to better end-user products. The speaker uses examples comparing centralized and decentralized storage solutions like Cloudflare and Filecoin, and R Drive built on Arweave, suggesting design improvements to the latter. They propose minimizing setup complexity and delayed decisions for developers and suggest UX primitives to mitigate protocol limitations, focusing on speed, access, security, and trust. Specific recommendations include designing for perceived performance, using hybrid architectures, improving observability with status indicators, ensuring perceived safety, and building trust by surfacing redundancy and file health. The presentation concludes by emphasizing that improving the overall experience, from developers to end-users, is crucial for the widespread adoption and success of decentralized technologies, drawing parallels to the importance of good bathroom design.

transcripts.text: Thank you. Hi everybody, thanks for showing up at this early hour. Yeah, so I was asked to talk about whatever I want and the reason was that about a year ago I held a talk at the Ethereum 10 year jubilee meetup where I was not all too positive all the time about, you know, Ethereum, from a good place obviously. And so I guess I'm invited to just share my thoughts on, you know, how I see what's happening. I hope it's interesting. So it starts with a little bit of history. Being in crypto used to be really simple, at least when you joined early. You would just go to local Bitcoin and Ethereum meetups to find other lost souls who had really no, you know, desire to have a normal job. And it was really a unique experience. I just shared two photos here. One, literally on the day the network launched, we had this big rainbow on the sky over Berlin. That was kind of cool. And then shortly thereafter, I was on an Ethereum meetup and funny enough, Meinhard, who is standing there in front of the network dashboard of Ethereum, now sits here in the first row. So that's very cool. Hi Meinhard. You were the leading miner, I think, on the Ethereum network back then, for like a few weeks. So it was simple to be in crypto because there was no moral implications, I feel, at all of doing this. It was a nerdy hobby. And I feel this has changed. And I want to just sort of linger a little bit on how it's different now to be in crypto. And I feel there are more ways than ever to do harm when you touch this technology. And, you know, to some extent, you should be able to harm yourself when you touch crypto because you're only truly free if you can hurt yourself in whatever you do. But I think what none of us really had on the radar is the fact that just by swapping tokens on base or using Coinbase to cash out, you're now paying for a military parade in the United States. That's kind of weird. I didn't expect this to happen. And obviously, there's probably a lot of context why Coinbase did it. But in the end, they still decided to sponsor a military parade. And I just remember how there was an ethos in crypto that was like universally shared, which is like we don't like physical violence and the monopoly on violence by the state. So pretty awkward. Now, I want to raise the question, how can we reclaim Ethereum's future? And I just want to say off the bat that I don't have any answers either. I don't really know, but I have some opinions like probably most of you. And so, you know, I'm going to share them. Since I think since I started this space, everything was always very technical. I tried to condense it into a formula, what I think Ethereum could use more of instead of less for the next 10 years. And I sort of condensed it into humility, openness, and plurality. And I just want to share what I think these words could mean here. Starting with humility, the reason I got, I think, one-shotted by Ethereum back in, I think, 2014 when I heard about it, was really Vitalik's epistemic framework that he developed in his blog posts. It just totally blew my mind how differently you can look at the world and understand things, understand causal connections between things, be it in finance, philosophy, how the Internet works, accounting. He was able to synthesize things in new ways that created genuinely new explanations for why the world is how it is and where we should go. And today I feel we kind of forgot a lot of that. And we're like in this, to me, low IQ range of like fighting about cypherpunk and defypunk and the current thing, punk. And I'm like, what the fuck is even cypherpunk? Like, is it even a good ideology to adopt? I mean, I don't know, I'm not a historian on cypherpunk, but when I read my Twitter feed, everybody's saying, yeah, Ethereum should be more cypherpunk again, or now it should be defypunk. It's like, what the fuck is this even? And the best, I think, epistemic framework that I found in my, I guess, 40 years of being on this planet is what's being referred to as fallibilism or a fallibilist mindset. I stumbled upon it through David Deutsch, a really great philosopher and physicist. He co-invented quantum computing in the 80s. And it's the idea that you can be infinitely optimistic in this world just by virtue of the fact that errors are discoverable and fixable over time. So just as much as problems are inevitable, so are solutions. Provided that criticism stays free and knowledge remains conjectural. Meaning, as long as we stay immune to any kind of ideology, be it socialist or fascist or cypherpunk or this punk, but we just stay epistemologically humble, we can solve every problem that comes our way in this industry. And I don't understand why we need to play this stupid game of trading one ideology for another. I just don't understand it. Next one, openness. Obviously, Ethereum is an open network. I think Ethereum is one of the most open infrastructures you can find on the web to build on. Obviously, that's its premise. At the same time, I feel over the last 10 years, we've acquired some sort of neo-institutional rot throughout the industry, which means this layer of professional careerists and middle managers who just gatekeep things, I think, in this ecosystem. So I don't want to go too deep into this because it's a complex topic and to some extent unavoidable, but I feel we have too much gatekeeping in Ethereum, and I think that might be part of the reason why other ecosystems seem to be accelerating faster at the moment, because maybe there's less gatekeeping in other places. Just putting that one out there. And lastly, plurality. This is something that sort of has been with me, lingering with me now for a while, and obviously there are books about plurality, and I'm far from an expert on this philosophical stream of plurality and so on, but I do think it's important I want to mention it here. Here's a picture of David Clark. There's this famous interview, I think, from 2012 or 2014, or I don't know. He's being interviewed on Bitcoin, and in this short segment he says, well, you know, what I learned as the designer of CCPIP is that all things that we think of as specifiable or technically constrained very quickly end up embedded in a social ecosystem, which in some sense defies the simplicity of the protocol that you've designed. And I feel in crypto and Ethereum, maybe specifically, we've always had this expectation that just by virtue of designing a simple protocol that has some incentives maybe well aligned, we now solve the real problem of rolling this out into the world, and we have not. And I feel Ethereum, if anything, should become more embedded in the world and adopt a more pluralist mindset and not be so dogmatic, which goes back to this epistemic humility, about, you know, well, is it fully decentralized? Is it not fully decentralized? Does it follow this current dogma or that current dogma? I feel this has been holding us back now for too long, and I think we should be more open to various ways of doing things. So that leads me to this Ethereum slide, which, sort of looking back, obviously it's not a correct or the only way to look at the last 10 years, but I feel that in the early years, 2013 to 17, we really rewarded the early believers in this idea of a new settlement layer, decentralized, open, permissionless, and programmable, Turing-complete, right? That was the one differentiating factor to Bitcoin. In 2018, we rewarded the early, you know, DeFi plumbers laying the financial pipes to make it possible to swap the tokens, to take out loans, all that stuff. Afterwards, we rewarded, and I think most recently, we've seen it with stablecoin issuers, the people who really believe that we should bring fiat on chain and stocks on chain and securities and all the stuff. I feel these people are being rewarded now, and the open question is, well, who will be rewarded next? What do we want to see in this ecosystem develop more of? And I feel that if we blindly follow down this, you know, cypherpunk, cypherpunk, cypherpunk stuff, I'm not sure we're making the right decisions, because at least, you know, and that's probably very debatable, but this idea of, you know, trust no one, verify everything, only trust in the numbers might lead us to build a low-trust society as opposed to a high-trust society. But I think we're all much happier as humans in high-trust societies, and there is this paradox in crypto where if you have a high-trust society, you probably don't need a decentralized ledger in the first place, right? You could do it, right? You could count stones like people did it thousands of years ago instead of, you know, having some ledger in the cloud. Paradoxically, I think the way the world is developing, we need to develop infrastructure where you don't have to trust no one, but I'm not sure it's a good north star to have culturally and, you know, philosophically in terms of what kind of society do we build. So I feel the opposite of trust no one is build bridges. And I feel Ethereum needs to build more bridges. Personally, I've been a bridge builder in this space now for 10 years, and it's been fun and frustrating. The first, you know, bridge building I've started doing was back in 2017 when I founded, I think, the first crypto lobby organization in Europe. I mean, it was in Germany at the time. And then a couple of years later, I founded with other great people in Europe the first, I think, community-focused crypto lobby organization in Europe, in Brussels, called the European Crypto Initiative, EUCI. And we've been building bridges to regulators where, you know, most people in the space think it's not worth talking to regulators. We've been educating them on DeFi and, you know, giving— like, we spend thousands of hours in calls and meetings with regulators explaining them why what we do matters and why there is some deep moral truth and justification in what we do, like some inherent goodness that this world needs to sort of move forward. And, you know, with this kind of signaling, we are able to reach people far beyond, you know, sort of what we should be able to reach and impact, which is great. And lastly, sorry for shilling my project now, I suppose, but that's, you know, an example of what I consider bridge building is a Web3 social application that I've been now developing for over three years called Common Ground. And the idea of Common Ground, again, is to bring, you know, people from all over the, not just crypto space, but kind of the Web3 space, together on, you know, in one environment in their own communities and be able to, you know, collaborate better, exchange knowledge, and retain knowledge better, and so on and so forth. I feel building bridges in Ethereum has been a pretty, you know, ungrateful job for the last decade. I don't want to complain, but I think there wasn't too much support. I think now might be the time where we want to, you know, spread our aperture, make it bigger, and bring, you know, more attention to these kinds of efforts too, not just the technical development. That's pretty much everything I wanted to share in this little talk. Thank you very much for listening. I'm happy to answer any questions if you might have them. Thanks. Thank you, Florian, for your provocative talk. Any questions? Right here, down front. Here's your microphone. Hey, Florian. Thanks for the shout-outs. Do you think you moved the needle on regulation, or did you just kind of spend a lot of time and they were like, thanks, but we'll do it the other way? Actually, yeah, we did move the needle a lot. Let me pick two examples. I think the biggest one is that we managed to exempt decentralized finance, so DAOs, decentralized protocols like Aave and so on, to exempt them from this regulatory burden of this European regulation called MICA that entered into force earlier this year. There is a paragraph in there, Recital 22. It's not even a real paragraph in the text. It's like a preemptive exclusion that says, well, if your project is not operated in a centralized way but fully decentralized, you can ignore this entire regulation and continue doing what you do in this sort of illegal space, as Gavin Wood called it. And that's kind of ridiculous that we achieved this, to me, because, I mean, crazy. Can you write those lines? Pardon me? Who wrote those lines? So, I wrote a long report on how this came into the final text. The suggestion came through the Portuguese team inside the council, but then how did the Portuguese, so there is a long chain of causality how to find that, but I would love to actually share this. I've long thought that crypto should have some sort of retro-PGF, but for public policy impact. Frankly, we were told that this would not be a good idea because that would make political outcomes sort of purchasable or sort of like monetize them. I understand that viewpoint, too, so I don't really know how to solve this. Yeah, thanks for asking that question. That's a great question. Other questions for Florian? One of my favorite aspects of Ethereum culture is its willingness to critique itself. So, thank you so much for your great talk. Please, a round of applause for Florian.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the evolution of crypto, starting from its early days as a simple, nerdy hobby to its current state with moral implications. He emphasizes the need for humility, openness, and plurality in Ethereum's future. He critiques the current low-IQ debates and suggests a fallibilist mindset, emphasizing that errors are discoverable and fixable. The speaker also addresses the issue of gatekeeping in Ethereum and advocates for a more pluralistic approach, encouraging bridge-building rather than adhering to strict dogmas. He highlights his efforts in building bridges through crypto lobby organizations and his Web3 social application, Common Ground. In a Q&A, he mentions influencing regulation, specifically exempting decentralized finance (DeFi) from certain burdens in European regulation.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker is conducting a workshop on building a DevNode package, specifically focusing on creating an OSIS (on cloud infant scale) package, which is a private cloud storage solution. The workshop covers the entire process, from setting up the development environment to publishing the package. The process involves initializing a DevNode repo using the DevNode SDK, creating a Dockerfile based on the official OSIS image, and configuring a Docker Compose file to manage environment variables and volumes. The speaker also emphasizes the iterative nature of package development, highlighting the importance of testing and debugging each iteration. Key steps include pulling the OSIS Docker image, initializing OSIS with specific commands, and handling potential issues such as password settings and HTTPS requirements. The workshop further explores using a setup wizard for a more user-friendly installation process and leveraging HTTPS for secure external access to the OSIS instance. Finally, it touches on publishing the package using the DevNode SDK, which provides a link for release and version bumping.
The process of publishing and signing releases involves connecting a MetaMask wallet to sign the release. Once the signature is verified, it appears on the UI. The signature, along with package and wallet information, is added to the IPFS package and published on the R repo manager. This manager holds the version and IPFS cache, displaying the signature when it's on the node. Support is available on Discord.

So there will be an active part to this workshop as well in a few minutes. In order to actively participate, you're going to need a Linux machine with ideally Docker installed and about four gigs of RAM. Less should work as well, but four gigs would be recommended. So let's dive a bit into the background behind Vero, why it exists, what it is, and so on. The reason why Vero exists has a lot to do with something called client diversity. It's an idea in the Ethereum space where Ethereum doesn't want to rely on a single client implementation in order to keep its blockchain going. So the idea is we should have multiple clients that all track the same blockchain. And that way, Ethereum is much safer from these client bugs, because if one client has a bug, we don't want the whole blockchain to stop going. So that's a quick intro to the idea behind client diversity. It's much more important to the whole system than many people think or are aware of. There's a good article by Dan Kratz-Feist on his blog or his website, which goes into the importance of client diversity. So yeah, that's the recommended read. So currently, thanks to this whole idea and making it a priority for Ethereum, we have six available consensus layer clients and five clients on the execution layer, which you can choose from, and you can basically choose any of those. Ideally, that would mean that each of those clients would be run by a proportionate number of the network. So in case of the consensus layer clients, we'd be looking at about 70% of the network on each consensus layer client. And in terms of the execution layer clients, we'd ideally see about 20% of the network on each execution layer client. So that's the theoretical and ideal scenario. The reality is a bit different. On the consensus layer, we see some clients are being used much more than others, especially Prism and Lighthouse, which we see on the top here, are used by a lot of people, probably a bit too many. This picture is not completely up to date, like Lodestar is shown as 0.1 to 0%, but it's higher than that, as well as Grandin. But it's like a roughly accurate picture of things. And then on the execution layer side, it's a lot more uncertain. All those orange blocks in the middle that you see, those are areas of uncertainty. So we don't know which clients some people are running. But this situation on the execution layer side has improved a lot since about a year ago. So we are currently in a much better space in terms of client diversity than we were that one year ago, especially Nethermind has made a big rise in terms of adoption. So now that we're in this state where all the clients are likely used by less than two-thirds of the network, are we out of the woods? Are we good now? Can we stop worrying about client diversity, right? That's the question. And I'm here to say that we really are not quite out of the woods yet because of multiple factors. One of them is the client usage data. Like I showed on the consensus layer side, it's not 100% accurate. There were some changes in the most recent network upgrade, which made measuring this less accurate. Then there's also the fact if a client is used by more than 33% of the network, so one-third, it can still be dangerous in some edge cases. Then there's also the possibility of two clients sharing a very similar bug like we saw recently on the testnet. So if multiple clients share the same bug, they can still get over 66%. And then one more thing is kind of under-discussed, which are failover mechanisms. Many node operators run multiple client combinations in a kind of failover mode where if one of their clients goes down, they switch to the other one. And this could do the wrong thing, actually, because if you run these two clients and one starts following a different chain, you don't necessarily always want to switch over to another client as soon as something's up with the first one, unless you know what's actually going wrong. So that's the failover mechanisms. As a node operator, especially as a professional one with like a responsibility for other people's money, you want to avoid these client bugs as much as you can. But the hard truth is we cannot completely avoid client bugs, right? These are complex pieces of software. They're going to end up containing some bugs at some time. Ethereum is constantly evolving, like clients are optimizing, so there's always some room for bugs to be introduced. But we can reduce the impact of these bugs. So in this case that we have on the slide here, we have three client combinations, and we basically split up our validators among these three combinations. The pros of this approach is that if everybody were to do this, we would be in a very good space. So it's good for a network if you do this. It's a simple approach. It's relatively easy to set up, and it still reduces the impact of client bugs. But in this case, if, say, one of these client combinations does have a bug, still like a third of your validators would go offline. So there is some kind of impact, but it's not huge. transcripts.summary: Luka, the CTO at Serenata, introduces Vero, a software developed to protect validators from client bugs. Client diversity is essential for Ethereum's safety, and while there are multiple client implementations, the reality is that some clients are used more than others. Client bugs can't be completely avoided, but their impact can be reduced by using multiple clients and sophisticated methods like Vouch and DVT. However, these advanced approaches often lock users into their ecosystems. Vero aims to avoid client bugs without complexity by being a multi-node validator client that's simple, secure, observable, and compatible with all client implementations. Vero monitors slashing events and shuts down validators to prevent slashing. The presenter then leads an active workshop where participants set up Vero, the remote signer, and the flashing protection database.

transcripts.summary: Jordi gives a presentation about Zisk, a ZK prover developed inside Polygon, which uses a high-level language like Rust for building circuits. The major announcement is that Zisk is spinning off from Polygon to become an independent, open-source project with a team of eight. This decision allows Polygon to focus on aggregation layers and choose any ZK technology, while Zisk can serve a broader audience. Zisk aims to generate proofs as fast as possible for applications like roll-ups and cross-chain communication, using parallel processing and GPUs. It maintains 128-bit security and is fully open-source, including GPU code. Zisk features a 64-bit RISC-V architecture and a full ZK prover stack based on PIL2, with a recursor for fast proof aggregation (150ms). Internally, Zisk uses sub-proofs (AERS) and specialized state machines connected by a bus using LogApp technology. The architecture supports variable-sized proofs by adding more sub-proofs. Performance numbers show the execution part is very fast (1.5 GHz), and while window computation currently takes 6 seconds, it's expected to improve. Proof building on GPUs takes 7 seconds, and aggregation takes about 150 milliseconds. The goal is to achieve real-time proving, around 12 seconds or less per block. The team is focused on optimizations, pre-compilers, auditing, and formal verification, seeking community support. Zisk divides the proving process into four stages: execution, windows computation, building the proof, and aggregation. The memory is divided by address ranges, and the state machines are adjustable based on hardware.

transcripts.summary: Sebastian from Ethnosis and Hopper discusses Nusselt VPN, focusing on bringing decentralization (the 'D') back into DApps. He highlights the importance of privacy and anonymity in peer-to-peer systems and introduces a new version of Nusselt VPN as an unrestricted proof of concept. The VPN utilizes the Hopper Mixnet to route packets through multiple nodes, making it difficult for entities to track user data. The goal is to provide anonymous access to Web3 infrastructure without user tracking or reliance on centralized RPC providers, indexers, or APIs that leak user metadata. Sebastian demonstrated a live demo of the VPN, showing how it connects to the Hopper network and routes traffic. He also discusses the VPN's surveillance resistance, multi-hop architecture, and compares it to traditional VPNs and Tor. He also touches on upcoming features, such as unblockable exits and residential IPs, and acknowledges the challenges of the current setup, including the need for a separate Hopper node. Future plans include edge nodes for direct Hopper network access and a streamlined user experience. He emphasizes the use of GnosisChain for its decentralization and resilience, as well as the separation of operational and financial concerns through the use of Safe. The project is supported by GnosisDAO and will be offered by a new entity fully owned by GnosisDAO. During a Q&A, the speaker addressed questions about balancing decentralization with the need for security, throughput for the HopperNet, and scalability.

transcripts.summary: The speaker introduces the concept of futarchy, or decision markets, which uses prediction markets to aggregate information and make better governance decisions. The idea involves creating conditional markets that trade assets based on different decision outcomes. The difference in prices between these markets informs the decision-making process. The speaker discusses challenges in implementing futarchy, including subsidizing markets, dealing with manipulators, and addressing decision selection bias. They also note the importance of political dynamics and organizational politics. Kelvin introduces futarki.fi, a project launching on GnosisDAO, where users can trade GNO tokens conditional on milestones being reached or not. The aim is to use markets to determine the best decisions, using the token price as a core metric. He explains how to trade on these conditional markets and highlights the importance of betting on the impact of milestones, not just predicting their occurrence. The project integrates with FlatOS, Sphere constructs, and CalSwap to provide liquidity and ensure accurate resolution of market outcomes. He invites viewers to join their Discord to contribute milestones and explore applications for other DAOs, emphasizing that the launch is just the beginning of their efforts to pioneer more competent governance through futarchy.

transcripts.summary: The discussion centered around the success metrics for Ethereum and the broader Web3 ecosystem, focusing on adoption, reduced exploitation, and the creation of new products. Metrics discussed included the transition from investment-heavy to customer revenue-focused, lower prices on key financial services, and the invention of lasting innovations. The conversation touched on the speculative phase of crypto, the need for end-customer revenue, and the balance between building platforms and creating useful applications. Further topics included the nature of Ethereum as a tech ecosystem startup or religion, the challenges of fragmentation in the ecosystem, and strategies for standardization, such as virtue signaling, software development by organizations like the Ethereum Foundation, and transparency. The potential of Ethereum being displaced as the world computer was considered unlikely due to its credible neutrality and decentralization. Other points included the importance of consumer demand for decentralized products, the role of prediction markets, and the future of money, particularly in relation to government regulations and the potential for digitized US dollars backed by high-powered money like Ether and Bitcoin. Self-custody was defended as a key principle.

So, if you would have some ideas for developers or builders, what should they be aware of during the coming months or years? I think first and foremost, it depends on what you're building, right? If you're building a trading application, you're building some kind of synthetic savings coin, or you're building a lending protocol, there's going to be much more regulatory implications in those types of products. So, I think you need to have a very clear idea, first and foremost, what it is you're building, and at an early stage in product development, understand where the regulatory touchpoints are, because there's a lot of evolution in the regulatory landscape today. And you might build a product which is amazing, and there's demand for it, but you might get stuck with regulatory limitations going forward when you want to distribute that product. So, my message to builders is, at a very early stage, start thinking about these questions. Start speaking to people who understand what's coming, what's already in place, so that you don't find these blockers in the future. Maybe I would say, think about the market and go-to-market strategy as well. So, if you are interested in the European market, you would need to look into the regulations, as you mentioned. Think about not only MECA, but as Kern mentioned, there are regulations that are touching upon the tech itself. There might be exemptions for, let's say, open source, et cetera, but it's not that if you don't have any crypto assets or similar, there's no regulation that applies to you when it comes to offering services or products in the European Union. So, I think that the EU is quite an attractive, interesting market. It's pretty big as well, and thinking about that in advance, in early stages, could help as well in the dissemination of the product. So, I would say I'm incredibly excited about all things payments. So, one thing that I would look into is, for example, stablecoin checkout experiences and online commerce. I think there's a lot of room for improvement there. On-chain FX markets, I think, are a key foundation for whatever cross-border payments might happen in the future. And then lastly, and this is potentially a little bit connected to regulations, added services for on-chain payments or stablecoin payments, settlement of tokenized assets, like services around chargebacks or fraud and how to handle all of that requires, I think, deep knowledge of on-chain infrastructure, but at the same time, European and international payments rules, and I think there's a lot of stuff to build there. So, and allow me one maybe shameless plug, we're obviously super excited about supporting any builders, developers in this space. We have built on Circle developer services platform, Discord, so feel free to check that out and hopefully we can support you as well as possible. Yeah, and I would just add, if you're starting off, don't let this complex regulatory environment kind of scare you off. I think if you're passionate about a problem that you want to solve, just get it started and don't let the lawyers scare you. If you have a good solution, you will figure out a way how to navigate this, if it's by partnering with somebody that has a license or if it is by going more into the infrastructure route that is less prone to falling under financial services. I think there will always be a way and yeah, don't let it stop you and keep building. So, thank you all for your thoughts. I'm sure we have taken something valuable from it and yeah, if you have questions, don't hesitate, we are around. Thank you. Thank you.
transcripts.summary: The panel discussed the current state of crypto regulation in 2025 and beyond, focusing on the implementation of MECA. MECA is currently applicable, especially for stablecoins, and stablecoin issuers in the EU must comply. The implementation for token issuance and crypto service providers (CASPs) varies by member state. Some have already implemented MECA, while others have deadlines in the future, such as France in June 2026. National competent authorities are supervising and licensing, leading to diverse interpretations and open questions. There are approximately a dozen MECA compliant stablecoins, with ongoing discussions about payment regulations and the role of EMPs. Companies are applying for licenses, and tokens not seeking regulation are being delisted. It's too early to assess the market's success, but MECA is progressing as expected. There is uncertainty about how MECA will affect decentralized infrastructure and DeFi. Differing regulatory opinions on DeFi exist, and many EU countries haven't implemented local laws for MECA. The willingness of registered VASPs to convert to CASPs is also uncertain. The European Commission is now focusing on tokenization, which could be interesting for the industry, but raises questions about infrastructure, such as the use of permissioned blockchains. The European Data Protection Board's guidance on blockchain and GDPR is strict and requires industry input. New regulations like DORA and cyber resilience regulations will also impact the industry. DeFi platforms should not have regulatory barriers and there is work to ensure a path for DeFi that aligns with blockchain values. There's optimism about European stablecoins gaining market share, driven by DeFi and real-world use cases. It's important to make the MECA framework compatible with other global jurisdictions. Developers should be aware of the regulatory touchpoints early in product development and consider market and go-to-market strategies. Payment solutions, on-chain FX markets, and added services for on-chain payments are areas for improvement. The panel encouraged developers not to be discouraged by the complex regulatory environment, but to start building and find ways to navigate the challenges, whether by partnering with licensed entities or focusing on less regulated infrastructure.

The hosting doesn't have editorial control over what you're putting on that web server. But then we went a different way on the internet. We did web 2.0. And this brought us a load of stuff that was missing in the original web 1. That we wanted social connections. We wanted the social graph so I could see what my friends were following. I wanted to see all my friends in one view. We needed identity built in. We needed data structure. And sometime in about 2018 he went to Myanmar and he made his case in a cave and he came back and he read a thing by Mike Maznik called Protocols Not Platforms. transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses BlueSky and AtProto, clarifying they aren't speaking for BlueSky or involved in AtProto's design, but rather sharing their appreciation for it. AtProto aims to decentralize social media, learning from the original internet's open publishing model and Web 2.0's social connections. The goal is to create a system where users control their data and social graph, even if BlueSky, the initial application built on AtProto, becomes adversarial. AtProto revolves around Personal Data Servers (PDS), structured, cryptographically signed data stores tied to user identities. The infrastructure includes relays for data dissemination and app views for client-specific needs. The data lives in a Merkle search tree for verification. Identity is managed through DidWeb or DidPLC standards. BlueSky unbundles curation and moderation, allowing users to create custom feeds and block lists. Blockchain bots can interact with AtProto, creating on-chain actions from user posts and even creating crypto accounts for BlueSky users. AtProto facilitates self-sovereign data stores, enabling decentralized applications without requiring consensus history, offering a new approach to user-controlled data and social media. The speaker expresses optimism about AtProto and encourages others to explore it, highlighting resources and links for further learning.
