transcripts.text: Well, hello everybody, I'm Brenda, I'm one of the co-founders of Teler, and today I'm going to be talking to you about how to bring oracles to L2s and beyond. The two takeaways from my talk should be that to scale oracles, we need to implement layer security, and also we need to find a balance between the fallbacks for those layer security aspects, the social layer, and credible neutrality. So over the last several years, we have been scaling to diversification, and we've seen a lot of ecosystems pop up, you know, we see Avalanche, we see Cosmos, we see Solana, and even Bitcoin is jumping into the game. And so as Teler, as we started seeing this trend, we wanted to make sure that we would be able to support all of this. And although we've done great strides, we still have a lot of work to do, but ultimately, we have been able to connect and do a lot of – connect a lot of chains in general. We still need to work on interoperability, but I think it's more in optimizations than actually figuring them out. And to illustrate this point, I want to talk about this example that just happened a couple weeks ago, where a trade was executed on Ethereum on a curve pool that caused a bunch of liquidations in Avalanche. And rapidly, you know, people went off to say, like, it's the Oracle's fault, which I don't agree with, because if we look very closely to this example, we see that the liquidity, the 24-hour liquidity was actually really low. Also, there's not a lot of sources for the information in general, and whenever you have a scenario where the cost to manipulate the asset or manipulate – or the cost of attack is so much lower than the actual gains, you're going to end up with something like this. So I went ahead and took away their original post, blaming the Oracle, and I just said, you know, when the cost to manipulate an asset is less than the gain, this is bound to happen. But here, we can see very clearly that the actual cross-chain communication happened very efficiently. It just led to unintended consequences. And that's where I'm going back to why we need to implement different layers of security to make sure that our Oracles work properly. Because more often than not, we're facing these two choices, right? We want really fast data, but it can be more likely to be manipulated in terms of assets. But if we wait for more robust data or aggregations or more time, then we're risking settling with sale prices. So it's this trade-off that, in the DeFi community, we know very well. And because of that, we need to continue to optimize, but also understand the implications of those optimizations and use that to also implement those layers of security. Taylor, I'm going to tell you a little bit about my story, or our story, because as the industry continues to evolve and all of these new ecosystems continue to emerge, you're going to run into very similar problems, especially if you started off as far along as we did. We initially started as smart contracts on Ethereum. It just made sense. Ethereum had the majority of DeFi, and it made sense for us to just deploy there and become an Oracle there. And at the time, we actually had a system where all of our validators, our data reporters, had to be staked. And then, because the way that we would come to the official value that was reported, it was the first five values that came in got some minted rewards, and the medium became the official value. And then anybody could dispute the validity of the data for 10% of the stake, and if they won the dispute, they would take the whole stake. Otherwise, the data provider would get the fee for their troubles, for being wrongly accused. And so, all of this was being done on-chain. And it worked, I think, just fine when we were only in one chain. The problem that we were facing was, okay, we want to support all of these ecosystems that are emerging and all of these new chains, and it seemed like every week there was another chain that popped up. And for us to be able to go and support them, one of the things that we needed to have was an actual bridge for our token so that people can go and stake and dispute and tip the data reporters so they would know that they needed the information. So we had to make sure... The only way that we could explain is making sure that there was a token bridge that we could trust. And then once we did deploy into all of these different ecosystems, we were obviously faced with fragmented liquidity because everybody had to bridge their token and we didn't have the same amount of security that we had in Ethereum. And one of the ways that we adjusted for that was basically, when you go to another chain, you assume their risk. You have to change maybe your parameters to be able to gain the same level of security as you do in other chains. For us, that meant changing some of our variables to adjust them to the speed of the chain. So for us, one of our security aspects is the whole staking thing. And so because... And that's based... That's a function of the speed of the chain, of how quickly a new value, a new price or pricing information or whatever other information can be replaced with good data. So if somebody provides bad data, how quickly it can be replaced. And so for us, that meant adjusting some of our variables, even though we were deploying the same exact system that was fine for EVM, we had to change some of those parameters to be able to have or aim for the same security that we were getting on Ethereum. And that, you know, could only take our security as close to Ethereum so much because even though we could adjust these variables, at the end of the day, if there isn't a broad enough network as it was on Ethereum, when people ramped up the demand, we wouldn't have the exact or all the network that we needed to be available. So with that in mind, we set out to build our own app chain. And one of the things that we really wanted to make sure that we had, one, we wanted to have an easier way to expand so no more reliance on bridges and also an easier way to deploy on different ecosystems with different languages. So instead of rewriting the whole system in a new language, we would just rewrite the live client bridge and then we can reach over data. And one of the main aspects that we wanted to have as well was a social layer. I don't advocate for forking all the time, obviously, or, you know, that's a last resort type of thing that you may hopefully never have to do, but we wanted to have that social thread to hackers that if we need to, we will use it. Granted, we hope we never have to, but we want to. And then we gained some efficiencies and we went ahead and we created this whole other, you know, we have our own chain, our own way of coming to consensus. But the takeaway from this is that no matter what Oracle you use and how they come to consensus, whether they're a peer-to-peer network or they have their own chain, you're not going to get away from the fact that you have all of this risk, off-chain risk. If you don't have a proper definition for the assets or the information that you're requesting, you're actually have a lot of trust boundaries that you have to address in different ways than just saying it's the Oracle's responsibility. When you have a market of something, of an asset that has really low liquidity, you're accepting that responsibility. So, you have to come up with creative ways to come up with more robust definitions for that. You're also trusting that the APIs are not going to come down and that you're going to be able to collect the data efficiently and as fast as you need it for your protocol. But with creating our own system, we came, you know, even though we gained some efficiencies, we have a social layer, we don't have to rely on the speed of Ethereum anymore to dictate how fast we can be or can't be. We do have to also take other risks. So now we have a different set of risks than before. If there is 66% malicious validators on any chain, not just on Teller or a peer-to-peer or the things that happen within it or the state that happens within the chain, 33% can probably stop, 33% plus one can stop it or can stop the chain basically. And so those risks you assume in this ecosystem where it's so diverse, anytime that you're interacting with another chain, that's something that you have to deal with. And so aside from the risks that we already know that come with Oracle's and the external part, the ones on chain and the ones off chain, now you have to deal with this extra risk. And so this is where the point comes of having to, when you want to expand into all of these different ecosystems, you actually have to think about it, security in layers. So the first layer of security for any Oracle to be implemented properly, it's going to be your data definition and you can work with the Oracle to come up with something that makes sense for your market. Even if it's something that is low liquidity, you're just going to have to have more rails and more guardrails within your infrastructure, your architecture to be able to handle that. And so that's the first layer of security that you have to address. Then the second, obviously choosing your Oracle and making sure that you implement them correctly. We all work a little bit different and there's a lot of flavors of us from very decentralized to a lot more centralized. And it is up to what you are doing that makes it the correct decision. But once you do know what you're doing and what you choose, you have to implement them properly. And don't leave it to be the last thing after you do the audit. It should be part of your audit. And then after that, the next layer of security is making sure that you have fallbacks within your system. You want to make sure that you can either freeze the system or you might want to do caps on withdrawals or limits. Just different ways of handling what happens if you don't get any data from your Oracle, what happens if you get bad data from your Oracle and what happens if you get stale data from your Oracle. And then obviously any chain that you deploy on, you're taking on the risk that come with that. From OEB, MEV and chain congestion, that is something that you should be taking into consideration. We've all thought what happened with Black Thursday. And then within your own ecosystem, when something goes really bad, you also have to have some sort of governance or some sort of rules that determine what happens if everything goes wrong. How do you make it right for your community? OK. So a couple of weeks ago, there was this hack, CEDOS is an exchange on SUI and they got hacked or they could have been hacked for about $230 or $260 million. And they basically stopped the bleeding by all the validators from SUI decided to ignore the attacker's transactions. And, you know, I'm not condemning or saying I'm not saying that this was right or wrong, but this is something that they were able to do. Hyper liquid is another example of a, you know, of hyper liquid taking over or making it right. Or I don't know, there's a lot of controversy on what happened in hyper liquid. It was also an it was an asset manipulation type of hack. And then the hyper liquid team basically overwrote the Oracle information and they ended up making money off of it. And I think that's why it was very controversial. Also, the fact that they did it for this one hack and not for another one that involved North Korea was also very controversial. And these two examples, actually, what I want to illustrate my point of you do need layer security, but you also need to have a balance between the fallbacks that you implement, your social layer and your credible neutrality, because you don't want to undermine the very premise of why decentralized systems and networks exist and why they came about. The main premise is actually censorship resistance. So if you throw out credible neutrality and you're just going to control your system, there are better ways to do that, you know, and better and more efficient ways. There's databases. We've been using those for many, many years. So that's where you have to strike a balance. And I know it's very difficult sometimes because, you know, I cannot condemn the previous teams for doing what they did because, one, I wasn't in their place and, two, it has to be such a tremendous amount of pressure to either do things one way or the other. That is just very difficult. But they both still have a user. So if their community was fine with what they did, maybe credible neutrality for them means exactly that, keeping their community safe. And that's OK. I guess it could be a little bit different. But I think with Ethereum, right, if you deploy there and you get hacked, more than likely there's not going to be a fork. And that's fine. Like that's something that you're opting into, especially if you're doing a roll up with them. But with that, I want to go back to my takeaways. Obviously, yes, we have the capability to communicate between chains. We have a lot of different ways of doing it. Some ways are continuing to be improved upon. CK proves, you know, I think once it gets faster, they're going to be part of that as well. And they already are in some cases. But we're waiting for them to be a little bit faster. And because we already have that, I think we need to focus a lot on how to also handle unintended consequences of these interoperability and composability that we're going to be gaining as we see base rollouts and native rollouts and CK proves becoming better and better and faster and actually being implemented for some of these. And then between the fallbacks, the social layer and the credible neutrality, I'm a firm believer that crypto is not just a technology, it is a movement. And we need to be able to hold or to stand for that ethos, because ultimately I know that a lot of people don't care when things are going well. But when things don't go well, this is this is technology that is absolutely necessary. And you don't want to say, you know, if you can do this for and you can be choosing winners and losers, then there's no reason why a state actor can come and ask you to do something for them. And I think that it's imperative that we give that the importance that needs to be given. And with that, I'll take any questions if you guys have any. Thank you so much. Yes. Let's go for questions. No questions. I don't know. Up here. So what was the biggest challenge from you guys moving them, deploying contracts on different chains, having your own chain and people taking on your chain, but still connected to all the others? Is there any challenge you guys are facing in this new model versus the older model? I'm thinking like it's a very big optimization for us. I guess the biggest challenge is actually the risk that every other chain is facing, especially when you're a smaller chain, the risk, the cost of attack is lower, right? So that 33 percent, it's lower than a 32 percent of like Ethereum network. So that is definitely going to be a challenge. And that's why I think it's also important that we have all of those layers of security. But most importantly, that we admit it, because I think that a lot of the industry has just gone through, we've gone through a lot of DeFi and we continue to go through DeFi hacks that involve generally a flash loan and then some asset manipulation and liquidations and then they run away with the money. And we don't have all of these things in place for people to be able to have better guardrails for their own users. So, yeah, in terms of us, I think it just made it so much easier. I don't think that's the biggest thing is the security within that 33 percent and 66 percent. And that's something that we're all facing. And I think as you see more app chains pop up, we're all going to be facing these different scenarios and assumptions in security. Maybe base rollouts and all of that fixes everything. But until they're here, we're going to have to work with what we have.
transcripts.summary: Brenda, a co-founder of Teler, discusses scaling Oracles to L2s and beyond, emphasizing layer security and balancing fallbacks with credible neutrality. She highlights the importance of supporting diverse ecosystems like Avalanche, Cosmos, and Solana, and addresses the challenges of cross-chain communication, using a recent market manipulation event as an example. Brenda shares Teler's journey from Ethereum smart contracts to building their own app chain, detailing the difficulties faced with token bridges and fragmented liquidity. She stresses the necessity of adjusting security parameters to match the risk profile of each chain, including having a social layer as a fallback. Brenda outlines key security layers: data definition, Oracle implementation, fallbacks (freezing systems, capping withdrawals), and awareness of chain-specific risks like MEV and congestion. She references the CEDOS and Hyperliquid hacks, which shows a need to balance fallbacks, social layers, and credible neutrality to maintain the core principles of decentralized systems. Ultimately, interoperability requires managing unintended consequences, and the crypto ethos of censorship resistance must be upheld.

transcripts.text: Thank you so much. Hi everyone, thank you for staying for the second part of the day. I hope you are enjoying DAFKON and Berlin Blockchain Week so far. With this presentation, we are continuing the conversation that Brenda started on oracles. We'll be talking about the oracle renaissance, decentralized data for a trustless future. So what exactly do I mean by that? In this presentation, I would love to cover how we are basically going to the next iteration of oracles, from simple data feeds to real world interoperability layers. Before that, I have a personal story I would love to share with you today. Two weeks ago, I found this in my building. Apparently, a water pipe broke, and because of that, the whole building had no water. I tried to have a shower, but well, you need water for that. Brush teeth, also not gonna happen. Make coffee, you need water too. This got me thinking. Suddenly, all the things that I took for granted were unavailable. Data in decentralized applications is a lot like water. It flows quietly in the background, and most of the time, we take it for granted. But you really notice when it's gone. My name is Bianca Buzza. I'm head of DevRel at Chronicle. The team at Chronicle is the team behind the first oracle on Ethereum back in 2017 at MakerDAO. In 2023, it spun out of MakerDAO. It continues today to power Maker, as well as other protocols in the web free space. So back to our oracle renaissance. So we're moving away from simple data aggregators. What we're building now in terms of oracles is infrastructure for real world interoperability. So basically, we are connecting real world with on-chain. And oracles nowadays help us answer questions which are a bit more complex, such as is a tokenized asset actually backed? Is it appropriate for a financial contract to execute? Can users trust what they're interacting with? In terms of data feeds, or the main categories of data, we have three main categories. It's true that technically you can put any sort of data and get that delivered by an oracle, but I would argue that these are the top three most popular use cases for oracles and data. So number one, we have crypto price data. Here we're talking about real time pricing for cryptocurrencies. Then we also have non-crypto price data, such as prices for fiat, stocks, or commodities. And finally, what I believe is the most interesting use case nowadays, is attestable data. And I'm saying that because we are seeing a rise in terms of real world asset tokenization. When it comes to attestable data, here we're talking about any verifiable piece of information. Some very popular examples are proof of funds and proof of ownership. And now to kind of back my statement earlier about the growth of real world asset tokenization, this is a screenshot I took in December last year. And the total RWA value was at $14.9 billion. I recommend this data is from rwa.xyz. It's a very good website if you're looking for insights about the real world asset market. You can see it broke down by chains, by where the data is coming from, and some other insights. I did a few days ago the same exercise. I went to check this source again, and guess what? The value now is at 23.14 billion. If you do the math, that's a 66.5 increase in a bit less than six months. That's a lot, I would say. However, we're just scratching the surface. If you look at the total market for gold, currencies, real estate, and commodities, that's over $40 trillion. What does it mean? This means that there is a great opportunity when it comes to tokenization, but also this comes with great responsibility. So why tokenize, you would ask? What are the benefits? Shared system of records. Using tokenization, you can get an unambiguous view of asset ownership. At any given point in time, you know where the asset resides and who owns it, and also it reduces information asymmetry. Then we have customizable asset custody. With tokenization, we can have various custody models ranging from self-custody all the way to institutional custody. Programmability is another benefit, and here we can achieve great operational efficiency via automation using smart contracts. Asset fractionalization is another one. We can now have micro-units of ownership. This basically reduces the barrier to entry. So if you think about a tokenized real estate, for example, you can have units of a share of that, and this enables to have what we used to have as traditional illiquid markets become more dynamic and bring additional liquidity. Lastly, composability. Now we can package and repackage different pieces of collateral, making a more efficient use of it and increasing liquidity. However, as you can imagine, there are not only benefits. We have some challenges as well. In fact, I recommend this report by the World Economic Forum. It gives a great overview on the benefits, challenges, and how all this is evolving currently. And here I noted some of the current challenges when it comes to tokenization. The first one is legacy infrastructure integration. Another important one is the fact that we have inconsistent global standards. And probably, in my opinion, the trickiest one is that we need to ensure that we have compliance across different jurisdictions. However, while these challenges are definitely significant, and we need to tackle those, I think as Web-free builders and people who are interested about the ethos of Web-free and decentralization, there is even a greater challenge we need to address, and that's about transparency. So the problem with tokenized assets is that unlike crypto-native assets, they're not inherently transparent. And also, they lack liquidity verifiability. So why is that happening? Well, the underlying assets reside in traditional financial systems. And as we know, those are off-chain, or packed, and siloed. So basically now, blockchains have the problem that they can't verify that these assets are fully backed, and neither the protocols that are built on top of those blockchains around them. Therefore, users are forced to rely on the promises and the reputation of the protocols, the apps, and exchanges they use. So we're kind of back to square one. So what's needed? How do we solve this? Real-world assets will only reach their potential if the data behind them is verifiable. As builders and users in the Web-free space, we need to demand transparency by design and verifiability. It's also very important that we're not reintroducing the same systemic risk that currently we have in traditional finance. However, there are some good news. We have Oracles, and as we know, Oracles enable trust and transparency. They enable to verify off-chain credit worthiness, and they provide key data, such as purchase dates, yields, and maturity dates. Also another very important property is that they allow the syncing of the lifecycle to the on-chain. So basically, you can clearly track how an asset goes through the different stages, such as issuance, transfer, and settlement. That's why at Chronicle, we're building the Verified Asset Oracle. This is our Oracle for the real-world assets. And the way it works is that it connects directly to the custodian, so there is no middleman, and it provides real-time, independent, tamper-proof attestation of the data with what it puts on-chain. This means that basically, we empower DeFi protocols to handle tokenized assets in a risk-appropriate way. And I'm sure now you're gonna ask me, okay, what's a risk-appropriate way? What I mean by that, imagine, for example, a DeFi protocol that wants to check the underlying assets it's actually there. And if the asset is not there, or if the volume of the asset is less than what it expects, then they can take certain measures. It can do a circuit breaker, or it can do a liquidation, or some other measure. What is important here is that builders have verifiable data that they can trust and make decisions based on that data. That's it on my end. I hope you found something interesting today. I would like to invite you to check the documentation portal if you want to learn more about the Verified Asset Oracle. Also, in about two weeks, we're launching the dashboard for the Verified Asset Oracle. It's gonna be a good visualization of all the data the Verified Asset Oracle puts on-chain. So, definitely something to check out when the time comes. Thank you so much. I hope you enjoy DEBCON and Berlin Blockchain Week. Thank you. Let's open it up for questions. One there. Thank you. I have a question about custodians. What are those and what happens if they go bust, basically? Yeah. That's a good question. So, the custodian is the one, basically, that has the assets. So, the idea is that you don't have the middleman, so you connect directly where the assets are, such that you can have an independent third-party assessment that, okay, the assets are actually there. When it comes to what happens if they're not there, you verify you have this sync, so you verify all the time that the assets are there. But, yeah, this is the promise, basically. You have this continuous syncing of the off-chain and on-chain, and you say, okay, at this point in time, the asset is here, and so on. More questions? No? We're good? Okay. Thank you so much. Thank you.
transcripts.summary: Bianca Buzza, Head of DevRel at Chronicle, discusses the evolution of oracles from simple data feeds to infrastructure for real-world interoperability, emphasizing the importance of verifiable data for tokenized assets. She highlights the growth of real-world asset (RWA) tokenization, citing a significant increase in market value and the benefits of tokenization, such as shared systems of records, customizable asset custody, programmability, asset fractionalization, and composability. However, she also addresses the challenges, including legacy infrastructure integration, inconsistent global standards, and ensuring compliance across jurisdictions. The main issue is the lack of transparency with tokenized assets, as the underlying assets reside in traditional financial systems that are off-chain and siloed. She introduces Chronicle's Verified Asset Oracle, which connects directly to custodians to provide real-time, tamper-proof attestation of data, empowering DeFi protocols to handle tokenized assets in a risk-appropriate way. She encourages the audience to explore the Verified Asset Oracle's documentation and upcoming dashboard for data visualization.

transcripts.text: Thank you. You're welcome. Thank you. So, nice. So, I'm Julie. I use she pronounced and to quickly introduce myself, I am currently a smart contract auditor with ChainSecurity. This is going to be a little bit relevant and also, if I don't say it, the tax authority is going to yell at me in Swiss German, so we don't want that. I'm also a developer at Randomoo, and it's a bit relevant, and a maintainer, one of the maintainers of ethereum.nix, which is also a little bit relevant. So, to get into this presentation, what does this title mean? Well, I decided to do a little experiment in my free time around how we build and distribute software. And the questions this presentation will answer are what do we mean with software supply chain? How do we currently protect our supply chain? What I think we could do differently, and what I learned during this experiment. Is this a Nix talk masquerading as a blockchain talk? Yes. Are the exits locked? Also, yes. Now, let me ask you, how do you obtain your software today in the world? Maybe it comes pre-installed with your hardware. Maybe you go to an app store or software, open source software distribution. Maybe you get it on CD-ROMs, it's a bit old. Maybe you get it through IPFS and torrents. Maybe you get it from books, you get it from t-shirts or QR codes. There are many ways to get software onto the end user's device, and all of these means are what constitutes the software supply chain. Now, what can go wrong in the software supply chain? Well, if it's unavailable, you will eventually not have the software you need. If there are bugs, you could get buggy software. And worst of all, if the supply chain is compromised by a malicious actor, you might receive compromised software from it. So it's important, it's a part of our infrastructure, and we should make sure that it is robust. Now, I divide the supply chain in two big pieces. One is the source code, and the other is the compiler pipeline. So the source code is the way we write software. It's mostly humans responsible for this, and they write software that should follow the requirements of the user. And to secure this, you need to decide who you trust, you need to audit the software or read it yourself. It really depends on your threat model. The other part is the compiler pipeline. It's almost entirely automatic. It's all the processes you use to take the source code and transform it into something that can run. So I'm going to refer to this mostly as a compiler, even though there are so interpreted methods to run software. Now, how do we make sure that the compiler pipeline has been run correctly on the software that we are about to use? There are currently in the world two methods, I think, to achieve this. One is re-execution, and the other is attestation. Now, the first one, re-execution, is very similar to how most blockchains work today. Basically, it is you re-execute every computation yourself, or you recompile everything from source yourself to make sure that everything was done correctly. It's great because you don't trust anyone, you just verify yourself, but how many of us actually compile our software from source? It's not very practical, and it's also not very scalable for the purposes of a blockchain, and I will come back to that later. The other method is attestation. It's what a lot of software does. You have a big build server somewhere that will run the computation to compile the software, and then it will cryptographically sign the software in some way, and then it will distribute the software with the signature. This is very simple and very efficient to verify, but you get this big central point of failure that you need to protect very well so it doesn't get compromised. Now, concretely, compromises do happen, and I will show you three case studies, one of which is the SolarWinds hack, which happened in 2019. It happens that state-sponsored hackers were able to hack SolarWinds, and through that, because a lot of people used their software product, they were able to distribute malware and even managed to compromise the US government. The second case study is the XZUtil attack on the open source, in the open source world. So at some point, a malicious maintainer was trusted with operating this critical library that was used in particular by the SSH daemon on Linux, which is how you can connect remotely to your machine to administer it, so it has the ability to become administrator on the to package releases, which are almost source code, but not really. It's a bit of a strange thing in the Linux pipeline, and many Linux distributions were affected, and we don't know that anyone actually got hacked from this. I think they were discovered just too early to be able to exploit the malware, but this happened and caused a lot of noise and concern in the affected parties for very good reasons, and the third case study, which we might be more familiar with here, is the Bybit attack. In 2025, the web frontend for safe wallets was compromised, and this was enough to trick Bybit signers, which were responsible for their assets, into signing a malicious transaction that compromised their wallets, and just like that, $1.5 billion were gone, and in the pocket, I think it's North Korea, yeah, it's North Korea that did it. And so this was a supply chain attack, right? The frontend was a malicious version of the frontend was distributed through the safe wallets website. Now, there's also a theoretical paper that I like by Ken Thompson. It is a special version of the C compiler that has the ability to, when it itself compiles a C compiler, injects the battery into the new C compiler, and so through the generations of compilers, it can propagate malware, and this was never actually exploited, but it highlights how the trust assumptions are transitive throughout the supply chain, and you have to trust the compiler of the compiler, a bit like living beings are not purely the results of their DNA, but they also need to be gestated in order to exist. Now, let's look a bit at threat model. I'm not here saying that if you are coding web games, you should be worrying about Ken Thompson or doing complex stuff. This is fine, this is a very contained piece of software, it's not going to do a lot of damage, and you also don't need an audit on that, but a lot of infrastructure, especially blockchain infrastructure, has already been targeted in supply chain attack, so I think there's value in trying to understand how our supply chain works and how to make it more secure. Now, to introduce the part of my title, which was verifiable computation applied to the software supply chain, verifiable computation are all of these methods that we have to outsource a piece of computation to an untrusted party and be able to verify that the untrusted party actually computed the thing correctly without re-executing ourselves. For example, you have CK-proofs, you have certain crypto-economic schemes that I will go back to later, and I noticed that a lot of people work on this, but they never talk to the people who are on the software supply chain, so there's kind of a siloing of research, and I think there's value in trying to connect those two areas to try to bring value from one side to the other, and that should bring us to my experiment. So, in one phase, I put a compiler inside of ZKVM and made it work that way. In ZKVM, if you may notice, it is a system that can run computation and produce zero knowledge proof that they were executed correctly. So, it is a form of verifiable computation with no trust assumption and just cryptographic assumptions. Now, what I would like to see one day is that people can verify the cryptographic proofs and look at the source code without having to compile everything themselves. And this means that you can still have a build server, but it can be untrusted, which is an upgrade from the current situation. I use the RISC-V ZKVM. It's a RISC-V ZKVM that I found off the shelf. I didn't choose it for any specific reason, but it worked for me, so that was good. And the compiler I started with is called HEX0. It's a project that is trying to make the smallest compiler possible, and it can just read hexadecimal with comments and output a program. The goal is to be able to bootstrap from this very small compiler all the way to much bigger compilers by compiling less minimalistic compilers as you go along. And there already existed a RISC-V Linux version, so this made my work easier. I could just port it and port those components to RISC-V inside of the R0 VM. So, I made a little demo. There's no live demo, but I can explain it, which is almost better. So, I had a tool that can verify bundles that contain source code, executable, and a proof that the executable came from the source code. And I made a Hello World for Linux x86-64. So, if you want to go see the demo, you can build the proof yourself. You can verify the proof that I give you, and if you're satisfied with the proof, you can also run the Hello World. Now, the caveat of this approach is that currently it takes 10 to 20 seconds to generate a bundle with the proof, which is not great, of course, especially for such a simple program and compiler. And ZKVM teams are making new versions a lot. So, I did this on RISC-V version 1, and they already announced version 3. And it's also not compatible with any other ZKVM that I'm aware of. So, we have this standardization problem, which makes this approach a bit complicated at the current stage. Now, there are also alternative approaches that we could look into, because this idea of I'm just going to use zero-knowledge proof is a way to make something that is maximally paranoid. But we can find more pragmatic and incremental approaches to still improve security compared to the status quo. For example, we could compile inside of a trusted execution environment like Intel SGX or something like that. There's still going to be a central build server, but it's going to be harder to compromise it because you have to compromise the TE. So, strictly speaking, this is an improvement. And this also has very little performance impact, most likely, and probably less complexity also than doing this inside of a ZKVM. Something a bit more further along in the spectrum are those crypto-economic models, where you can assume that the majority of the build servers, you have multiple build servers or multiple blockchain validators, and you assume that the majority of them are honest, and so you can accept builds that were signed by the majority. You can also use these systems like ELLs, which is used in Polkadot, that can select a subset of validators and then check their work with another subset of validators and achieve some more scaling with that technique. And you can select your build servers either based on token stake, which is what we usually do with the blockchain, but you can also imagine a system where a bunch of individual human developers come together and say, okay, we are all going to each run a build server and we're going to make a supply chain that way. This was an idea that was suggested to me by Jeff Burgos, by the way. Very, very interesting idea. Now, another last thing I want to point out is that we don't have to use one of those approaches. We can have models where you combine multiple approaches. This example is the proposed finality gadget for the Ethereum R1 roll-up, and what it does is it combines ZK, CEs, and optimistic challenges in such a way that two of those systems have to fail in a very specific way for the roll-up to accept an invalid state transition. So you could imagine doing something similar for a supply chain with, for example, a combination of TLE and majority honest model. Now, let's do a little bit of science fiction. If you like trains, you might have seen one of these track playing machines that is able to lay down its own tracks and then roll all the way onto them. I think this is fascinating, and this is also something we could do in the blockchain space, where the blockchain itself, after it has scaled its ability to do verifiable computation a lot, can start compiling its own infrastructure, its nodes or its front ends, and hosting them that way and progressing forward while proving that its software is correct. Of course, this is a long shot, but there's a way you can start from hex zero and compile yourself all the way to some of the Ethereum client software already. So maybe this is something we can do at some point. Now, how do I conclude a talk like this with a lot of experiments? What I came up with is, you know, you can just do things. You can just go grab an off-the-shelf ZKVM and do things like that without asking anyone's permission, and I think it's fun. I think open source and the Infinite Garden are a nice place to do this. So what is the computation you do on chain is taking the source code, which anyone can more easily than the binary read and verify, and then you run the compiler itself on chain and you get an output. Now you have this output is a client for the blockchain, so you can download it and replace your clients with an upgraded version that can continue verifying the blockchain as you go. So you put the track and then you roll on top of the track. Okay, yeah, it's interesting. All right, more questions? Do you think that this could be an interesting use case for verifying smart contracts? I think smart contracts, I think, yeah, I think it's even more doable because smart contracts are much smaller in terms of software than a lot of clients, and that's something I'm open to looking into in the future. Okay, do you have, do we have more questions?
transcripts.summary: Julie, a smart contract auditor and developer, discusses software supply chain security and her experiment applying verifiable computation to it. She defines the software supply chain as all means of getting software to end-users and highlights potential vulnerabilities like unavailability, bugs, and malicious compromises. She divides the supply chain into source code and the compiler pipeline, emphasizing the importance of securing both. Two methods to secure the compiler pipeline are re-execution and attestation, but both have drawbacks. She cites real-world examples like the SolarWinds hack, XZUtil attack, and the Bybit hack to illustrate supply chain vulnerabilities. She then introduces verifiable computation, such as zero-knowledge proofs, as a way to outsource computation to an untrusted party and verify its correctness. Julie's experiment involved putting a compiler inside a ZKVM to generate zero-knowledge proofs for software builds, allowing verification without recompilation. While currently slow and not standardized, she suggests alternative approaches like trusted execution environments or crypto-economic models. She concludes by encouraging experimentation and proposes a future vision where blockchains can compile and host their own infrastructure, ensuring software correctness.

transcripts.text: Hey DappCon, today I'll be talking about a new class of dApps that I've been looking into as part of the Ethereum Foundation's App Layer Fellowship, where we try to anticipate and unblock use cases that can drive new waves of adoption. So I think as we all know, crypto's adoption story kind of starts in the dark web, where Bitcoin was used through the Tor network to help people purchase usually illicit substances, but eventually people kind of realized you'd be better off holding your Bitcoin rather than spending it, and then it just turns into a speculation asset, right, where people want to hold it. And I think that Ethereum has experienced a similar arc, where it started off with a vision of a world computer to enable e-commerce and the Internet of Things, but then very quickly people realized that the highest ROI way to use the chain was to launch and trade tokens and create an ecosystem of tools around that. But it's starting to feel like 15 years later, we've kind of come back around to the origin of crypto, of commerce. Maybe not as we expected it, but we have the major fintechs and governments paving the way for stablecoin adoption, with PayPal, Stripe, Shopify, and many more companies on the way to offer stablecoins to the masses. And pretty soon probably the key onboarding path for new users will be through stablecoins, buying or selling regular goods and services. But stablecoins are really just the first step, and it's definitely not the end state that was originally envisioned for Ethereum, enabling a whole world of commerce, Internet of Things, and basically disintermediated trade, disintermediated exchange of goods, services, assets for individuals, communities, businesses, through smart contracts. And so we need to get into the harder stuff that a lot of people here have been working on. And the kind of adoption path that I'm arguing for here is to work on the increasingly difficult primitives beyond just payments that are going to unlock this future vision that I think a lot of us share. For example, identity, peer-to-peer reviews and ratings, verification, dispute resolution for when things go wrong and you need refunds, reimbursements, insurance, which today is a common component kind of baked into peer-to-peer marketplaces, and embedded credit lines. And then once we do all of that, we can unlock the kind of holy grail of these more crypto-native, fully on-chain and smart contract-mediated transactions that are not purely financial and self-referential. And so this is basically the process where we need to perfect and then embed these primitives into the mainstream system, the same way we've seen stablecoins succeed, and then more and more of those legacy systems go on-chain, and eventually they themselves are part of the smart contract economy, and it then opens the door to the more ambitious visions that smart contracts enable once more of the legacy system is on-chain. And this is just a small snapshot of what people have tried over the last 10 or so years in terms of decentralized commerce, but of course these were all far ahead of their time because we didn't have these underlying primitives in the way. So Socket has this sharing economy vision, universal IoT devices that are self-owned and enable access rights through smart contracts, District OX, and Swarm City, which envisioned like a sharing economy and an interoperable backbone for marketplaces that would all tap into the same reputation system and inventories, OpenBazaar with a similar vision that more so levers Bitcoin and IPFS, D-Travel is an example of the idea of decentralizing Airbnb, Trip Protocol, and many other attempts at decentralized ride-sharing ecosystems. But basically all of these projects didn't really get anywhere. And here's why. So one, the most common thing I heard when talking to marketplace founders, people who attempted this, it was just the basics that we all know that have plagued Ethereum and blockchains over the years of complex onboarding, high gas fees, and then the fact of everything being transparent, just limiting the extent of real world commerce that can happen there. The primitives that we spoke about, basically every one of these projects was needing to build the full stack of commerce in-house because they couldn't rely on existing systems of arbitration or reputation. And so they really missed a big opportunity to get shared network effects from different kinds of marketplaces, tapping into the same underlying inventories, liquidity, and so on. Also, there was clear strategic missteps from the way people thought about on-chain businesses early on, often focusing entirely on pure decentralization, having everything on-chain or everything in decentralized tech, which was not ready, right, so it really degraded the user experience and didn't actually provide a superior alternative to the legacy marketplaces. And then tokens being another kind of part of this, at first, every marketplace basically was using tokens as a means of payment, so instead of using stablecoins, they were using their own token, and tokens as a means of governance, which has led to many messy situations. And even if all the kind of technical problems are resolved, I think the hardest part for any marketplace, on-chain or off-chain, is obviously network effects, and so there needs to be creative solutions that actually help these new kinds of platforms compete with incumbents and create new marketplaces that the incumbents in Web2 just can't serve. So where are we today? Well, one, Ethereum has scaled. The UX is far better with account abstraction, and soon all the L2s are going to feel like one unified Ethereum with cross-chain messaging and a variety of other initiatives to make chain interops more easy. This is just a small snapshot of the experiences that we've all had and how dApps can actually work for us today. And then privacy. I think privacy is something that we often overlook because we feel like regular consumers don't care about privacy, but when it comes to everyday commerce, privacy is more of a practical security issue. People aren't going to use the on-chain Airbnb where everyone knows where they're staying who they're paying, how much they're paying at all times, where they're riding to, what they're buying, what they're selling. So obviously privacy is like a... having no privacy is a non-starter for actual marketplaces for real-world goods and services. And then I think one interesting approach here is fluid keys, self-addresses, where you don't necessarily need to have the whole transaction be private, but you have obfuscation and who the funds are going to, so you can have an address generated on the fly for every new transaction without them being linked to one another. And then we have different approaches at selective disclosure, where you can actually validate identity with several solutions, having a lot of traction there, and credentials, information about someone that you only prove a selective attribute of, rather than the underlying credential itself and who issued it and other details. And ZKTLS has been one of the biggest explosive changes of the last year, where a lot of these solutions are actually usable to import credentials from Web2. So instead of needing to create our own crypto-native ecosystems of attestations to build trust, you can just import them from the Web2 world. So you can take your Upwork history or your Airbnb history or whatever credentials, your host, and just import them, and smart contracts can validate that you have those in order to unlock rewards or just access to more users who want to consume your services. One interesting experiment recently was Cursive's private set intersection, which uses MPC to blind match people who have the same needs and wants. Next, open social protocols, I think, unlock a whole new wave of potential marketplaces that can tap into these. And so I think for the most part, people have thought of open social as social networks and entertainment, but I think the potential is way bigger, because once you have a social graph like that, you can then bootstrap, actually, marketplaces on top of it. So you can use the social graph as a reputation layer through algorithms like Eigentrust or PageRank or just social proximity to understand the trustworthiness of an actor and the chances that they'll deliver on the service the quality of good that you want from them. And the social protocols also serve as a discovery service. So with CarCaster, for example, you have hubs, and so you can broadcast your offers or your requests as tasks, as posts. And then the mini-app kind of angle is another interesting, even more recent development that we've seen from CarCaster, World, where people can build an app and it can inherit all of the kind of integrated wallet, notification system, while also tapping into that social graph. And in World ID's case, you have authentication as well. Here are just some simple examples. Slice, doing e-commerce through a CarCaster mini-app. And then Icebreaker, which lets you post for a job or look for a job, again, through the CarCaster social graph. They actually also use ZKTLS to import your LinkedIn connections, creating a better network effect bootstrapping externally. And these are just some examples of simple CarCaster-based apps that are market-focused. So we have a kind of CarCaster marketplace, which basically looks like a Facebook marketplace. You just post in a channel what you're selling, and then the UI automatically turns that into like a familiar format of an e-commerce store. And then Bounty Caster takes a slightly different approach. Instead of a CarCaster channel, you can just make the post, but you tag the Bounty bot, and then it indexes you in their UI, which is a Bounty marketplace. Then AI agents. So I think AI agents solve a more fundamental problem in marketplaces that actually gives us a higher chance to decentralize them. Because smart contracts are obviously deterministic, and therefore we can only verify objective information that's inside of the ecosystem itself. But with AI, we can kind of get subjective data analysis embedded into transactions. And so one example of this is just listings. So today we rely on the platform marketplaces, obviously their databases are hosting all of the different offers, but then also they do the recommendations and the filtering and the matchmaking to help us find what we're looking for, because we don't want to look through millions of listings. But with AI agents, we basically supercharge the ability of people to do search client-side. Also, the process of pricing and closing a deal is also very subjective, right? I'm sure people have all used these marketplaces where there's a price, and you go back and forth to get the price to something that both parties agree on. And AI agents, this is just one example from virtuals, can do this back and forth through basic human text messaging, through text. And then they can resolve it on-chain through smart contracts. And then on the actual payment part, we have a lot of new standards lately that are tailored towards AI agents so that they can use simple HTTP requests to make a payment. Coinbase has X.402, and then we have Skyfire and Payman. And what these let you do is define these kind of conditions, limitations on who you can buy from, who you can send money to, how much you can send. And then beyond these primitives, we have some new experiments that I think kind of show the way of what's coming when it comes to on-chain commerce. So Slice, like I mentioned earlier, is basically trying to bring commerce on-chain. So it's an on-chain Shopify where your goods are on-chain, the representation of them, the inventory, the pricing strategy. You can implement custom smart contracts to price your hats that you're selling on a bonding curve or whatever you want, as well as referrals and all the other things that we can do with tokens. Keep, you can think of it like a Web3 Stripe Connect. And really what it does is behind the scenes uses account abstraction and stablecoins to handle payment orchestration in the marketplace without requiring anyone to have a license like you would in Stripe because it's non-custodial. Then local is more focused on local services. So building a transaction graph and then deriving a reputation system from that, that they can then price insurance for transactions through an AMM so that the actual services that are rendered there, like food delivery, can happen reliably. And they actually already have pilot live in northern Colorado with a food delivery app called NOSH. And then this is super recent. This is just last week. Coinbase and Shopify announced the Commerce Payments Protocol, which also uses Stripe, to really not just do stablecoin payments, but bring the authorization flow of payments that is typical in a Web2 commerce environment on chain. And so they actually developed new smart contracts that handle this kind of authorization flow of you pay an escrow and then the merchant's API or the merchant itself approves the inventory is available, let's say. And then the payment goes through to the receiver. And then it reverts if that isn't done in a sufficient time frame. And this is super programmable. You can add all these different kind of hooks to make it work however a particular merchant needs. And so what I found is kind of some high potential low-hanging fruit is to really make DCOM take off. One is to have a standard or some sort of way of abstracting over the different identity and reputation solutions out there. So we have loads of credentials, anonymous credentials that people can assign to particular addresses and accounts, but really these don't talk well with one another. And if you're building a marketplace today, it's really not clear which one to go with since none have a sufficient network effect. I also think there is a really big opportunity for the listings to be shared, the inventory. And this is what could really create a 10x better experience than traditional commercial marketplaces where the inventory of Upwork or Fiverr is separate and even different kinds of services could interoperate their inventory if there's standards around what is a listing. And this can basically create a way better liquidity between marketplaces and programmatic combinatorial options where you buy things from multiple places at once. And when it comes to reputation, I also haven't really seen reviews, which is a really critical primitive in all Web2 marketplaces. You leave a rating score, you write a text review sometimes, and this really creates that web of trust that's relied upon. And I think you could simply do this on top of something like the Ethereum attestation standard. And risk management is definitely the most complex area, and that's why Web2 commerce has exploded. It's because you know that you can rely on the platform in many cases to help you if you have some sort of problem. If you need your money back, they have insurance baked into everything. And if you have an issue, you can talk to customer support and they can help you resolve your issue. And like I said, with AI agents, I think there's a big opportunity to do this, but there's also simpler ways, like even just having a centralized company that's just like, hey, we do arbitration for all these different marketplaces and they're just the third party that checks if something goes wrong and hits the switch of whether to reverse the payment or not. And so a big question I get is what kind of marketplaces are going to take off first? So given that a lot of the pieces are falling into place, where should we focus? Because it feels like Web2 has already dominated and monopolized everything, and we should just focus on finance and let Web2 handle commerce. But I would disagree. I think that there's plenty of markets that are not served by the incumbents because they're either too fragmented or they're in a regulatory gray area, or they just haven't been made legible because the transaction costs aren't worth getting them represented in these marketplaces that rely on spin-techs that charge decent-sized percentages. Also, I think that there's a near-return potential to focus on markets that are higher margin with differentiated inventory. So basically, this is because when you have low margin and commoditized markets, like let's say Uber, where it's really just driver time is the key metric, like how long is it going to take to get you a driver and what's the cost, these are really better served by vertical integration, where you have some company that has a ton of data and they can really optimize the algorithm around squeezing that extra margin. And eventually, maybe protocols will be able to compete there, but I think there's a way greener space to start in. Just some examples, I think many more exist. But areas that you can't just off the top of your head think of, oh, I use this all the time for that, I know we have a great experience, maybe these are a little more illegible by the current system. And so I hope I've made a compelling case for DECOM, for having interconnected marketplaces that are built on open building blocks and open standards, and if you want to read more about this, feel free to scan the QR code, and thank you. Thank you so much. Let's open for questions. Raise your hands for questions. No, raise your hands. Okay, I guess we're... So I was looking at the features that you mentioned. About for identity, what we can use, and do you think Circles can also be used? I saw the mention of World, so I wanted to ask. Definitely, definitely. So I think Web of Trust is a powerful tool, as we saw kind of in Forecaster implicitly, but in Circles it's very explicit in the data model. And as we see network effect and traction there, not only I think you could use Circles for identity, but also for payments, because it's basically a decentralized credit issuance system. And so based on how much you trust someone, you can accept their Circles token. Yeah. There's a question there. Thanks for your talk. It's very interesting to finally build like the parallel economic world we wanted, like in the mean. Like, you know, with Morpheus saying you don't need any money, where are you going? But I'm looking at it from the supplier side. Like, if I am a supplier at some point, I need to buy more stock, then I'm going to need like, probably need like traditional fiat money, right? So I need to rent also? And I have a feeling like if governments are feeling threatened, they might ring fence this. So what can we do about this? I have a feeling that they are going to cut off the supply. Yeah, so I think in peer-to-peer marketplaces, it's not as clear because you have, you know, supply is one side of the market and the demand is also there. So the suppliers can just be, you know, regular individuals, not necessarily big companies. And maybe what they're providing is, you know, a service that has low CapEx, right? It's just your time. But when it comes to, yeah, anyone that would have costs, sure. But yeah, I don't think it's a problem if they're off-boarding. If, you know, Bitcoin miners are selling their Bitcoin for fiat all the time to pay for electricity and, you know, Bitcoin still works. And that's really what I was trying to make the case for with the progressive substitution is that even if we're only substituting a small part of the stack at a time, the aggregate effect, I think, could get us to that future. Thanks.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the potential for a new class of decentralized applications (dApps) focused on enabling commerce beyond simple payments. They trace the evolution of crypto adoption, from dark web transactions to speculation and stablecoins, arguing that the future lies in building primitives like identity, reputation, and dispute resolution to unlock on-chain transactions for goods, services, and assets. The speaker analyzes past failed attempts at decentralized commerce, highlighting issues like complex onboarding, high gas fees, lack of privacy, and strategic missteps in decentralization and token use. They suggest that advancements in Ethereum scaling, UX improvements, privacy solutions like fluid keys and ZK-TLS, open social protocols, and AI agents are paving the way for on-chain commerce. The speaker then showcases examples like Slice, Keep, Local, and the Coinbase/Shopify Commerce Payments Protocol. The speech concludes with a call for standardization in identity/reputation, shared listings, and better risk management, suggesting that initial focus should be on underserved markets with higher margins and differentiated inventory. A question-and-answer section follows, addressing the use of Circles for identity and the need for fiat off-ramps for suppliers, emphasizing the importance of progressive substitution even if only parts of the stack are replaced at a time.

There are 73 Layer 2s that are currently being operational, and there's 82 more in the development. And this is all like all people and funding being applied to create even more box space that frankly nobody needs. And it's a misallocation of capital in the industry. And it's kind of a bit sad to see this, to be honest, because ultimately, what we do is we're building a lot of infrastructure, but we do not serve enough users to actually justify this investment. And that's also one of the reasons why we try to kind of still focus on many things that are really where the user stance is in the focus, and where we hope we can actually create a more vibrant ecosystem for people to actually do stuff that are not necessarily speculative. As mentioned, two Gnosis projects, GnosisPay and Circles, have been created with this intention in mind. But there are also others that are quite exciting, like FireWords. They're also here. They're building basically a kind of Google Docs, but in a decentralized way, integrating a lot of the crypto primitives, which make it a unique experience. So that's kind of where we are right now. Now, that's also not the full truth, because there are successful parties that are benefiting from all of this, and that is companies like Coinbase. There's also, again, from the same time stamp from yesterday, how many people are actually operating on Layer 2 that are the most successful. In this case, Base is right now the most successful Layer 2, and we have about 20 times more users on Base compared to Ethereum today. And, well, it is problematic, because obviously those are basically networks driven by centralized exchanges that are not necessarily value aligned with what we had in mind. And I think that was just something that has happened recently. Coinbase started sponsoring basically the parade of the US Army, and that's how this photo came about. And I think it cannot be more obvious that this is not a credibly neutral platform, like Ethereum intends to be. At the same time, there's an American company that hugely benefits from the research and development, literally billions of dollars spent on basically creating the underlying infrastructure that now they can benefit from. And to have another graph that kind of underlines this here is from the wallet report by dune.com, they are tracking, in this case, their self-custodial wallets. And there are two charts here that I picked out. One is just the pure transfers that were done via this wallet. Again, they are all like self-custody wallets. And, well, one big spike at the end is basically Binance. Binance changing their strategy to be doing things more on-chain again. And, of course, they own distribution, they own the users, they can decide how infrastructure is being centralized, and that's why we have this insane spike at the very end. But also, if you would remove Binance from this, basically the market is mostly divided by centralized exchanges, which are directing the users to now use more self-custody solutions, which are obviously also mostly operational on their own networks. The second chart also underlines this, which is basically the volume that's being traded. You see here MetaMask by ConsenSys. That was a really dominating wallet over the years. It's now declining comparatively compared to basically the wallets promoted by centralized exchanges. So here we are, centralized exchanges are eating our lunch, and we have to do something, because otherwise we end up in a world where basically entire retail is basically owned by a few parties, which are not really aligned with our own values. And just to explain kind of an overview of what are the centralized exchanges currently doing, we have Coinbase, obviously a building base, based on optimism. Same like Binance, Binance Smart Chain has a fork of initially Guess and Eragon. And yeah, basically all of the bigger centralized exchanges that have enough resources, they are able to piggyback on the technology that we built and basically have the value capture because they own the distribution. So now, I think Vitalik wrote a year ago or two years ago this post in terms of what do we need to do in order to get ready for mass adoption. And yeah, he lists scalability at this point. As we saw, we have basically unlimited block base available, so we can consider this being solved. User experience has drastically improved through account abstraction, also fine. Security, I think we made major improvements. If North Korea is coming after you, it should be pretty fine. Privacy is still something that we are working on, but there are also many solutions which are being worked on, which will become viable. One thing that we kind of completely neglected is distribution, and that is obviously ultimately what matters if you want to be successful and actually also define, frankly, like how the future will be. And that's why I encourage every one of us to really think about how do we do distribution. There's not a silver bullet of how we do this. And honestly, it's also different, obviously, to compete with someone like Coinbase or Binance. And that's why you have to basically pick your battles, and you have to understand how can you be different from the competition, how can you do something that is better and fundamentally adds more value to your users than what Binance and Coinbase are trying to do, which is not easy because they're actually pretty good at building products, but it is possible, and that's what we're trying to do with Nosis Pay and Circus as well. We try to understand, okay, what are the pain points of our users, where can we go, and of course, like if you compete with someone who can operate globally, you basically have to go locally. You have to understand what can you do on a smaller scale, better than everyone else, and kind of go bottom-up in order to be relevant. Yeah, that is concluding my presentation today. I hope it is, again, like it's something where I hope we can be, let's say, optimistic about the future, but we also have to realize what the problems are, we have to realize what we have to tackle on, because otherwise we give it to Binance and Coinbase, and that's really not what I would like to do. So I encourage everyone thinking about distribution. There are a lot of people that are pitching ideas to me, and my first question is usually like, okay, this sounds all great, but it will be commoditized, and how do you distribute it? And I think that has to be almost the first question that we have to ask ourselves, how do we distribute what we build, because otherwise someone else is going to benefit from it. Thank you.
transcripts.summary: The speaker at DEPCON 2025 reflects on the initial vision of dAppCon in 2018, which aimed to foster application building on the Ethereum infrastructure. While infrastructure has seen massive growth, the application layer is still dominated by centralized exchanges like Coinbase and Binance, who are leveraging the technology developed by the Ethereum community for their own benefit. The speaker emphasizes the need to focus on distribution strategies to compete with these centralized entities and create a more user-centric and value-aligned ecosystem. He highlights the importance of understanding user pain points, focusing on local solutions, and fundamentally adding more value to users than centralized exchanges can offer. The core message is a call to action for the community to prioritize distribution in order to prevent the centralization of retail and ensure a future aligned with the original decentralized values.

name: Building Testnet Infrastructure (from the ground up)
description: When building scalable testnets which reflect real-world environments, there are many factors to take into account: ease of use for developers, performance, observability, maintenance, and cost. This workshop is meant to be an interactive session with a presentation for people to better understand how to build such systems starting "from scratch".
