transcripts.text: Yeah, so this is quite a short talk, so I'm going to give a pretty fast crash course on a lot of these things. So I've been working on testnet infrastructure for a really long time, probably like six years or something like that. I have a background in traditional system administration, so before testnets, I was doing distributed systems. And I work on a lot of things that aren't infrastructure as well. So the reason that I bring this up is because a lot of infrastructure people are just infrastructure people, but I also work on things like developer experience, and I would like to take a lot of those learnings from developer experience into the infrastructure world, because I feel like that's an area that's lacking quite a bit. So before building a testnet, what questions do we want to answer? Is it for performance testing, is it for users, is it just for developers, does it even need to be on the internet, what can we simulate on a testnet, what can't we simulate, who is going to take care of it, who's going to maintain this testnet, right? So answering these questions informs the way that you're going to build the system itself. So if you want, for example, for all of your nodes to be on the internet, maybe you don't want to build a data center, right? If you want it completely offline, maybe you want to build a data center. It's how you construct all this stuff, right? So what are your options? The cloud is an option, everybody builds stuff in the cloud, that's great, but we don't really There's been a movement, I would say, more recently in the past few years, about bringing hardware back a little bit, because first of all, the cloud is really expensive, and also you don't own it, right? It's hard to work in these areas, like decentralized protocols and things like that, where you don't have ownership, because ownership is a part of what we do. So we don't really want to use Google, we don't want to give Google money, and ownership is a huge part of this. So owning hardware actually makes a lot of sense in a lot of ways, and it can actually save you a lot of money as well. So colos are another way to do this, so instead of building an entire data center just for a testnet, you might want to just put some servers in a colo, that can also be cheap. But my main thing that I want to say about testnets, and building infrastructure like this, is you should keep it simple. You should keep it as simple as you possibly can. A lot of people, if you're looking at a project like this, it may seem like an insurmountable task, if you're building a testnet from absolutely the ground up, from zero, but it's actually not that bad if you can keep it simple. So even if you don't know anything about hardware, you can work with vendors, vendors are happy to walk you through processes, you can get multiple offers from multiple vendors, and a lot of the time they also let you benchmark the hardware that you want to get. So if you are talking to multiple vendors, have multiple options for different hardware, you can just benchmark your stuff on it, you can run your own, your nodes on them and see how they do. For software, you also want to stay minimal. And this is hard to do, because there's so much stuff that you do need in order to actually make a testnet work, obviously you need the nodes themselves, you need monitoring, you are not monitoring for your monitoring, but you really want to keep it as minimal as possible, and stay flexible. So you want to be able to add stuff after you bring all of this stuff up, because if it's an inflexible system, then it's difficult to adapt with the development process. And really, really, really keep it simple. So what you should try to do is not let people over-engineer the stuff. If you're a developer, or a founder, and you have a DevOps person, keep a close eye on them. They might, they do have a tendency to over-engineer things, so you can ask them questions, like, okay, why are you doing this, why are you doing that? And try different things, make sure you don't incur overhead in the engineering process of the stuff, and don't create structural dependencies. So this is something that I've seen before, where you make one software choice, which then incurs more technical debt later when you decide to change that choice. So things that rely on other things that rely on other things, if you take a piece out of that stack, then the whole thing comes crashing down, and that is not what you want to happen if you wanted to replace that piece. So in all of this stuff, we built one, and we kind of used this process, right? We came from the bottom, and we were like, what is the most cost-effective? What can we get for our money? What is the best option? And that ended up being hardware for us. I mean, that's the thing. One of the things that you also have to take into account is the size of the team, the amount of time you can spend to build the thing in the first place. If you are five people, you might not be able to build a data center, but you can maybe talk to your local guy at a colo and be like, okay, do you have any spare rack space? I'll just buy a server, put it in there, and then they can take care of it for you. So there's many options, and there's many options that are cheaper than people think, because this infrastructure can be very, very expensive. To give you some figures, I have seen testnets run for upwards of a million dollars a year just in costs, like infrastructure costs purely. And that is a lot. And a lot of the time, you are paying a lot for bandwidth with peer-to-peer systems, right? So this is something that you also have to take into account and also something that can be saved money on if you go for the colo or data center approach. The other thing is it's difficult to work maybe with a development process if you have a strict schedule, because hardware procurement can take a while, depending on what you want. If you need some custom stuff, like this stuff, it's a little fancy, it can take a while to get, and it can take a while to work with the vendors. If you're buying something off the shelf, this is less of an issue. And developers may have changing requirements. So you might start building a testnet data center or something, and then you get some benchmark results, or the developers are doing optimizations or something while you're doing this process, and then they're like, oh, actually, we need something a little faster. Or we need an extra 32 gig of RAM, actually. And that's something that's hard to change later. So you kind of want to buy the stuff that you actually need to use. So keep that in mind. This one is something that I've been working on, which is 87 servers with thread rippers in them. And the reason that we went with thread rippers for this testnet is because they have very high single-threaded performance. And this is important for a lot of blockchain applications, because there are some things that do not run in a multi-threaded manner. I think it obviously depends on what you're working on. But the single-threaded performance on consumer hardware is actually better than that of server hardware, generally. So this is good in two ways, because people can just buy nodes with consumer hardware and run them at home, which is what we like. But it's more difficult when you're going for server hardware, because generally, you don't put consumer-grade hardware in a server rack, which is what we've done here. And in terms of software that we've chosen for this, we went with Nomad. Sorry to all the Kubernetes fans in the room. But we decided that, or I decided actually, that Kubernetes might be a little bit too much for this if there's only me taking care of it, or some other poor guy taking care of it. And Nomad seems to be a very simple option that just allows us to run everything. Developers have a UI, they can submit jobs, and it's done. And obviously, we have the normal Grafana Prometheus stuff, and some custom telemetry that I'm also working on, which isn't ready yet. But that's basically it. If anybody wants to find out more, find me. I'm easy to find. Come and talk to me. So, thank you.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses best practices for building testnet infrastructure, emphasizing simplicity and cost-effectiveness. They highlight the importance of defining the testnet's purpose (performance testing, user access, etc.) before construction, which informs choices about infrastructure (cloud vs. on-premise). The speaker notes the rising trend of using on-premise hardware due to cloud costs and ownership concerns, suggesting colocation as a cheaper alternative to building a full data center. The speaker advises keeping both hardware and software minimal and flexible, cautioning against over-engineering and structural dependencies. They share an example of building a testnet with 87 servers using thread rippers for high single-threaded performance and choosing Nomad over Kubernetes for its simplicity. The speaker also mentions the importance of considering team size and hardware procurement timelines, as well as potential changes in developer requirements.

transcripts.summary:
This panel discussion features experts from various crypto security companies discussing methods to prevent hacks and secure transactions. Valery from 1KX moderates, with panelists Tomaso (Blockade), Andrei (HyperNative), Charles Guillemet (Ledger), and Alex (Gnosis Guild). The discussion covers recent hacks like Radian Capital and Bybit, emphasizing the need for better tools to verify transaction data and prevent malicious activities. Key points include using co-signers to simplify verification, implementing granular policies tailored to different customer types (asset managers vs. protocols), and utilizing enterprise-grade security solutions like Ledger Vault for financial institutions. The importance of clear signing and transaction checks on hardware wallets is highlighted, along with the use of machine learning and behavioral analytics for comprehensive security. Panelists agree blind signing should be eliminated, advocating for preventative measures and role-based permissions to minimize risk. They advise that user security should not rely solely on the security of their devices and caution of sophisticated attacks from malicious PDFs to compromised IT infrastructure. Ultimately, the discussion stresses the need for solutions that provide visibility, control, and continuous monitoring throughout the entire transaction lifecycle.
The discussion covers transaction blocking for users with clear explanations, the possibility of bypassing blocks, and the acceptance of signing environment risks. Diversity of signing devices is recommended for security, although the limited number of highly secure devices is a concern. Ledger's 7.7.30 requirement for contract metadata contributions and decentralizing the registry are discussed, emphasizing the benefits over using ABIs. The panel also explores the level of abstraction in representing wallets, the challenges of intent-based transactions, and the role of AI. The conversation ends with a discussion on how to mitigate risks in Web3 and increase user adoption by building trust.

transcripts.summary: The Ethereum Foundation launched the 1 Trillion Security Initiative with the goal of either having $1 trillion of value secured by a single smart contract or a billion users with $1,000 each on-chain, to increase trust in blockchain and reduce skepticism. Frederik Svantes from the Ethereum Foundation discusses the initiative, explaining it aims to show blockchain is more than just scams and hacks, but something that can enrich lives through privacy and censorship resistance. The initiative is taking a three-phased approach: mapping, execution, and communication, focusing on addressing concerns above the protocol layer by coordinating with the ecosystem. A key insight from their report is the need to improve wallet UX, address concerns about malicious websites, and make transaction signing more transparent. They are seeking feedback on solutions and plan to facilitate discussions among wallet providers and other stakeholders to onboard non-technical users, drawing parallels to moving from an Arch Linux to an iOS-like experience. While improvements have been made, they are focused on blind-signing issues, and hope to see less users losing funds in the future. Frederik's personal security model for interacting with blockchain includes practices outlined on 'howtomultisec.com', such as verifying website authenticity, contract deployment history, and using tools to decode transactions, while being mindful of the value at risk.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses Safe Labs' mission to power a trillion-dollar on-chain economy through secure self-custody solutions. They address the challenge of balancing cypherpunk values (privacy, censorship resistance) with enterprise-grade rigor (compliance, auditability), coining the term 'Cypherprice' to describe their approach. This involves re-architecting their products, like the transaction flow, to include both a trust layer (Safe platform, simulations) and a verification layer (third-party tools). Safe Labs is focusing on making self-custody secure, easy, verifiable, extendable, and enterprise-grade. They highlight new features like a secure signing companion mobile app and Spaces for managing multiple safes. The goal is to forge cypherpunk ideals with enterprise-grade rigor to unlock the potential of the on-chain economy. The speaker also answers questions about making resources accessible to a global audience, enterprise pragmatism in product architecture, double signature verification and the importance of providing users with choice.

And I think sometimes we overthink, right, like let's start with, let's assume I want to use it for myself, I know who I want to whitelist. The next step would be we have address books, maybe we start out with you somehow can link your address book to it and say only your address book, right, and then we can somehow go into the network effect, but I think we often try to jump like the canyon and don't try to do smaller steps, and this is really, yes, we have to figure this out, I think the end goal, if I want to onboard my family, if I want to onboard people on the street, they should not have to manually whitelist stuff, whether they need a good default that works, but especially also if we think about enterprise models, for enterprise teams or even for OG crypto teams, we can assume that they have at least one person that can come up with a whitelist.
transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the importance of self-custody in Web3, emphasizing that owning one's account is owning one's identity. While the speaker is passionate about self-custody, they acknowledge that it's currently broken due to security, UX, and accessibility challenges. They express a commitment to identifying fundamental issues and building innovative solutions, prioritizing security, censorship resistance, and privacy. The talk further touches on the balance between cypherpunk values and the need for accessibility and convenience. Several initiatives are highlighted, including trustless safe account deployment, restricting delegate calls, on-chain queues for transaction information, and building a co-signer network to enhance security. The speaker states that Safe Research's approach is applied research, aiming to create usable prototypes, not just academic papers. They also emphasize open research and collaboration.

transcripts.summary:
The panel discussion revolves around self-custody and how to make it accessible and appealing to a broader audience, particularly those unfamiliar with crypto, represented by the persona 'Bob the Boomer.' The discussion covers various aspects, including the reasons for choosing self-custody, addressing the challenges in transferring funds from traditional banking to crypto wallets, privacy concerns, and highlighting the unique selling points of self-custody. Panelists discuss how the value proposition differs depending on the user's geographical location, financial stability, and access to traditional financial services. They discuss the potential for regulatory arbitrage and the ability to access financial tools not available in traditional banking. A key point made is that achieving feature parity with traditional banking is not enough. Crypto must offer unique value propositions like cashback, higher yields, or easy access to real-world assets to incentivize adoption. Privacy concerns were addressed with solutions like stealth addresses. Panelists agreed that a crucial element for Bob the Boomer and other crypto-skeptics is a tangible benefit like higher yield on stablecoins.
The panel discusses user account recovery in the context of self-custody wallets, focusing on solutions for users who lose their phones and access to their accounts. Solutions include passkeys synced with cloud services like Google or Apple, multi-device setups, and social recovery with guardians. The conversation shifts to upcoming features in their respective products aimed at driving the next wave of adoption. These include credit cards focused on specific use cases for cost savings, referral programs, embedded wallets with streamlined onboarding, programmable DeFi for wealth growth, and user-friendly privacy features. The panel also explores the potential impact of AI on user interfaces and financial management, debating the level of trust users would place in AI agents for handling their finances and expressing a preference for self-management.

But I think the big thing will be showing that these actually can be more effective and more efficient as compared to traditional things. And so I think by then we will, but yeah. I think sort of like echoing like what has already been said that, you know, I think the regulatory part of it is the important unlock going forward. So, you know, while we can speculate a little bit right now, I think in the next, you know, what it's going to look like going forward. Thank you very much for the panel. We have time for one quick question or two from the audience. There we go, there's the question. You just have to wait for a minute. Yeah, I mean, like you were discussing how basically we'll see like last entities launched several tokens and the token being more related to a specific product or protocol. But I guess in the early stages of startups, there have been many organizations that are still in their early stages. You should expect them to pivot. And so like if you're an early investor that's invested in the last entity, great, you're participating in all the pivots. But like it's kind of like a bad story to tell for all the public token investors. Like one of the issues, like people saying, okay, actually tokens should trade at a discount to equity because of that. So do you see also like having more rights being given to token holders to participate in pivots for the tokens that are being launched and actually kind of, right? Maybe that's just onto insecurities after all then. No, no. So I think what's going to happen is that the token holders definitely are not going to have any rights in the last entity. And I think when you go to right now, you sort of expect the lab density to launch a token and the two things to be the same thing forever and always. And that's probably not going to be the case, right? If you hold UNI token, you don't have any piece of UNI wallet. That's probably going to be okay, right? Like, you know, I'm a UNI token holder. So, you know, the token represents probably the protocol specifically. And does that protocol survive and work on its own? That's going to be, you know, a big question. Token holders themselves will certainly have some rights and like capabilities around that network in and of itself. But I don't think that we should expect going forward that by default, the token represents the equity and the equity represents the token. Because really in the sort of like new regulatory future that, you know, we're probably going to get, that's going to be very strictly separate. So you just won't have any like labs sort of relationship to the token. The token will be specifically for the network. And then, you know, your purchase decision or your investment decision or your participation decision is going to be on the success of that network versus the success of the labs activity. Thanks so much. We'll be back in a minute with the next panel.
transcripts.summary: The panel discusses the future of on-chain organizations, including DAOs and how organizations are evolving on-chain. Topics covered include the balance between efficiency and inclusivity in DAOs, the impact of regulations on decentralization, the convergence of traditional finance (TradFi) and decentralized finance (DeFi), and the potential for tokenized stocks. Panelists discuss how institutions are exploring blockchain opportunities, regulatory challenges, and the need for clarity in defining decentralization. The conversation also touches on the potential for DAOs to be acquired by traditional companies and the possibility of organizations issuing both tokens and equity. Ultimately, the discussion covered whether or not crypto needs the institutional angle to grow, and whether the institutional angle needs now the crypto rails to grow. The biggest blocker for on-chain organizations is that they need to move more on-chain and regulation.

transcripts.summary:
This panel discussion focuses on the importance, challenges, and future of account abstraction (AA) and EIP-7702 in the Ethereum ecosystem. Panelists discussed how EIP-7702 is seen as a way to bring the benefits of smart accounts to existing EOA users. The discussion covers usability features, security concerns like denial-of-service attacks, and the need for better tooling and standardization. There's debate on whether to force users to upgrade to smart accounts or provide options while ensuring transparency and control. The conversation also touches on the synergy between EIP-4337 and EIP-7702, the potential for native account abstraction with EIP-7701, and the role of wallets like MetaMask in supporting these features. The panelists explore the next steps for protocol-level changes and adoption, while also being mindful of the potential security risks associated with delegation and account upgrades. The panel also addressed the current adoption rates of 7702, the chains it is supported on, and strategies to encourage broader adoption. The panel ends with speakers sharing whether or not they use 7702, and why.
The panelists discuss account abstraction and related technologies like ERC-7702 and native account abstraction. They explore whether users are upgrading their EOAs (Externally Owned Accounts) to ERC-7702 and generally conclude that ERC-7702 is more of an internal feature for wallets to use for batching transactions. The conversation also covers the status of native account abstraction on Rollups, emphasizing that while it offers benefits like gas savings and security features, it doesn't provide significant additional features compared to ERC-4377. They are focusing efforts on ERC-7701 to have a unified account type across networks. Finally, they address the potential for native account abstraction to support post-quantum cryptography, emphasizing that while it's not inherently post-quantum secure, it provides the flexibility to introduce post-quantum secure signature types and eliminate the vulnerable ECDSA-based private key.

transcripts.summary: Xiaowei from the Ethereum Foundation discusses their commitment to 'DeFi Punk,' which champions privacy, decentralization, open-source collaboration, and user sovereignty in decentralized finance. The Ethereum Foundation's Treasury Policy aligns financial strategies with these core values, prioritizing security, safety, and financial responsibility while investing in projects that advance Ethereum's deeper goals. They aim to bridge the gap between the current DeFi ecosystem and cyberpunk ideals by supporting trust-minimized, composable, and privacy-friendly protocols. The Foundation advocates for these values through internal operations and tertiary strategies, iterating this process over years. Key DeFi properties include security, open-source licensing, self-custody of assets, technical solutions over trust-based ones, and privacy by default. The speaker shares a framework with eight criteria to evaluate DeFi projects, emphasizing permissionless access, self-custody, open-source software, privacy, open development, trustless core logic, general security, and distributed UIs. The Ethereum Foundation encourages the community to adopt these criteria when building or evaluating protocols. Ethereum's destiny is to be a stronghold of cyberpunk values in finance, particularly for users in politically or economically oppressed regions and dreamers of an open, borderless financial system. The Foundation welcomes builders, researchers, and those aligned with these values. In a Q&A, the speaker addresses questions about inspiring other institutions, DeFi punk as a meme, supporting controversial projects within legal boundaries, and balancing transparency with privacy when deploying funds.

transcripts.text: Hi everybody, very happy to be talking to you guys today. My name is Paul, I'm with the Circles team, and I want to talk to you about the Circles Web of Trust. This is not an introductory level talk, Martin yesterday gave a presentation on this, there's been several workshops, in fact, as I guess you all know, it's been hard to kind of evade us in this conference and over the last couple of weeks. Instead this talk builds on the understanding, the basic understanding that we hopefully all have about this protocol. So let's just recall what Circles is about, here are the core three rules of Circles, everybody can come and create an account, there's no gatekeeping, and then as soon as you have an account, you're going to be enabled to create your own personal CSC token at a fixed rate of one circle an hour, and all the circle tokens that are being created by everybody suffer from a sort of constant evaporation, which is called the Demirage, at a rate of 7% per year. And on top of that, we have the notion of trusting, users trusting each other, that's just a relation that is sort of registered on chain, and by Alice trusting Bob, Alice is kind of communicating to the rest of the network that she is willing to accept Bob's circles at face value. And so if we think about it, we have one rule relating to money creation, one rule relating to money destruction, and then one rule relating to money flow, by which I mean, if you sort of took a snapshot of all the balances, the third rule would kind of govern the dynamics of how these circles can then move about. And in this talk, I'm not going to be caring at all about the first two rules, I'm only going to be interested in the third rule. And all these trust connections, they produce a trust graph, and people get really excited about the trust graph. We talk to them, we ask people, you know, what do you like about circles, and we often hear that the trust graph is what they find most exciting. And I think there's several reasons for that. One of them is that people just love graphs, full stop. One of them is that people really dig the idea of kind of curating and engineering their personal currency, and so projects like Trustlines or Ripple Pay have always excited lots of people in the community. There's also this social and local nature of trusting, so circles are fully sort of breathing decentralization and sort of giving sovereignty to the user, so not just at the tech stack level, but also clearly at how the protocol works. And people get really excited to think about secondary use cases, things they can do with this trust graph that go beyond just the circle currency. But the trust graph also brings up questions, it brings up some questions or kind of confusion. There's questions like, why do we need the trust graph to begin with? And whom should I trust? Just in practice, like, somebody comes up with a QR code, should I scan it, should I not scan it, what should be the criteria based on which I decide? Is the graph providing a proof of personhood? If so, how strong is that guarantee? And if not, what is it providing a proof of? And I think we, as a team or the communities, we're also not yet quite decided, so there's conflicting advice floating around, such as, trust all accounts you think aren't bots, or trust those who you think will provide the most value to the community, trust the people you trust in real life, or don't trust accounts by people that you believe might run a second account. So they all kind of pull in the same direction, but they target different underlying criteria. So this talk tries to sort of help answer these questions, it's just sort of my two cents on these questions. They don't represent necessarily the views of the Circle team or kind of what we're going to be rolling out or whatever, it's just me thinking about them. But why I think it matters to have this discussion and think about it is because A, lack of alignment on these questions among the Circle's user base undermines trust in the protocol and hinder adoption. So if it seems like an arbitrary thing, everybody's just trusting based on different criteria, how can this become sort of the next big on-chain money? And B, if we're really committed to thinking about secondary use cases, things that we can do with this trust graph, I think we need to be sort of confident in the properties of the graph and the value proposition, right, so that if everybody's doing things based on different criteria, what is it that the trust graph is encoding? So the main points I kind of want to drive home over the next 15 minutes or so is that A, what we prove depends on our collective trusting strategy. And that's kind of a truism, I mean of course that is true, but what I mean is that if what we're after is a proof of personhood, then depending on the collective accuracy of our beliefs and the personhood of others, we might achieve that. If our criterion is something other, another property that is sort of hidden that we want to provide proof of, then again depending on the accuracy of our collective beliefs, we might do that. If all of us are doing different things, then probably we're not really proving anything. The second point I want to drive home is that there are some good reasons, in my view, to kind of move beyond thinking of what we're doing with the web of trust approach in circles as providing this proof of personhood. And the third point is I want to quickly talk about how groups, which are a new construct in Circles v2, allow us to go beyond the web of trust approach. So let me start by addressing my view of the question why we have the web of trust and the trust graph in circles in the first place. So I think that within circles, the web of trust is primarily a technical solution to a technical problem. Circles is an ambitious project, and we kind of want to have the cake and eat it. We want to have a currency that is universally accessible in the sense that everybody can create an account. It should be democratized. The issuance should be democratized in the sense that all of these accounts can start participating in the money creation, but we also want what I would call sound tokenomics. And I know this is a loaded term, sound tokenomics, I hear means something very modest by it. I mean the rate at which a person should be able to produce circles should be one an hour. Not more, but not less. And so if you're willing to just take any two of these, it's relatively easy to see how you can do it, but getting all three of them under one hood is kind of difficult because of this obvious civil attack that you kind of open up for. And the web of trust is meant to address this issue. So when Martin, for example, gives this kind of advice, what he's getting at is that he has obviously an account that has, on the media, is anonymous. We don't know who they are. They have no form of verification. And they evidently have at least two accounts on Metri that they're sort of mixing up, right? I mean, so there's several red flags right there for why we think they are not using the protocol as intended. Right, so now how does the web of trust approach help us address this problem in detail? It helps me to construct a kind of a toy model, a mental model that I use to think about how we as a collective use our beliefs about the personhood or the properties of other people to kind of produce a currency that is universally accessible, issued democratizedly, if that is the thing, and also has sound tokenomics. So let's take the example of an online community that wants to set up a currency with democratized issuance and universal access. And the community knows that it's somehow infiltrated by accounts that have some hidden property which, for lack of creativity, we're just going to call bad. They're just so bad accounts. But bad could also be a person. It could also be people with, I don't know, things that you can't see, like certain chromosome structures or something. And we're going to define the tokenomics of the currency that they're going to come up with as sound if these accounts are somehow successfully occluded from the economy of this online community. So in thinking about what they should do, they come up with the toy rules of circles, which look as follows. First of all, give everybody some circles. And they're all non-fungible tokens, right? Everybody gets circles. And the second step, each of the participants in the community gets to decide whom to trust based on some strategy. So they have articulated a strategy and they decide, well, this is how I'm going to trust. And then third, they're going to sample a random good exchange partner. So this is this red arrow here. And so this is how this sort of day looks, or this round looks, from the point of view of this one player. But now they all participate in this game. And the task is for the good accounts to come up with a collective strategy such that the economy among them is liquid, but bad accounts are isolated. So we can now kind of formally evaluate the quality of a given strategy by liquidity, which I'm going to take here as the average fraction of their circles that good users can spend, right, spend with the transaction partner that was chosen, and adversarial exposure, which is how many circles can bad accounts pay good accounts. So we now have a mapping from every possible strategy to the quality of their strategy. And there's a simple optimal strategy, which is, well, all accounts just trust each other and none of them trust any of the bad accounts. That's the perfect strategy. Liquidity is 100%, adversarial exposure is 0%, so far so good. The only catch is that to come up with that strategy, you need to have known who's who in the first place. So that kind of begs the question, right? But people might not have full knowledge of this hidden property, but they have informed beliefs. They might have interacted with them in the past, so they might have applied some Bayes rule or whatever, and they might run around with some indication of whether a given account has that property or doesn't. And one possible strategy that they could kind of agree on is that each of them samples their trust as a function of their current beliefs, and they update them accordingly. Right? So here we have these accounts kind of having some roughly correct beliefs. You can then show in this toy model that if there are islands of knowledge for every account, this strategy will work well. So what do I mean by islands of knowledge? I'm not going to tell you, so I'm hiding some technical lingo here. But so quite clearly, the web of trust approach in this sense, in this toy model, builds on the wisdom of the crowd. And it can only work if the crowd is wise in that sense, right? If they have no clue who's who, then that approach is not going to work. Now a couple of interesting properties of this approach are that A, beliefs don't need to be optimal for a strategy to work well. Now, this approach is also naturally resilient, because you can have subsets of the economy, like the two accounts here at the bottom, that if they have accurate beliefs, and they can kind of shield themselves from other parts of the honest side of the network that have fallen prey to bad accounts, they can get sound tokenomics going among them, and they are not sort of exposed to the bad decisions of others. So to summarize, the web of trust approach works as follows. If a collective agrees on some property X of people that people should have that they want to include, and they hold collectively accurate beliefs about the actions of others, and they also choose their trust relationships according to their beliefs, then we can achieve, so then we can have the cake and eat it, right? We shouldn't consider any other information. But we might of course decide to go beyond that. transcripts.summary: Paul from the Circles team discusses the Circles Web of Trust, building upon previous presentations and workshops. He highlights the core rules of Circles: open account creation, personal CSC token creation, and constant token evaporation. The focus is on the trust connections between users, which form a trust graph. This graph is exciting due to people's love for graphs, the idea of curating personal currency, and the social aspect of trust. However, it raises questions about the graph's purpose, whom to trust, and whether it provides proof of personhood. Conflicting advice on trusting criteria exists. The talk aims to clarify these questions, emphasizing that what the graph proves depends on the collective trusting strategy and suggesting moving beyond proof of personhood towards "proof of economically trustworthy personhood." He introduces groups in Circles v2 as a way to go beyond the web of trust. The web of trust is primarily a technical solution to achieve democratized issuance and universal access while maintaining sound tokenomics, addressing civil attacks. A toy model illustrates how collective beliefs about personhood can create a currency with these properties. The speaker evaluates the concept looking at the actual circle's user base and data showing numbers for the adversarial exposure.

transcripts.summary: Sebastian from Yodel discusses the evolution of their platform from a simple payment solution to a "super app." Yodel aims to be a cardless Apple Pay, allowing users to spend their cryptocurrency in real-life scenarios. A super app, inspired by Alipay and WeChat Pay, is an application with a large user base and specific features available to third-party developers. Yodel's focus is on enabling payments in real life, in shops, supermarkets, and online. Users can pay with any token through a QR code scanning system, which integrates with existing payment networks. The process involves the user pushing money from their wallet, signing the transaction, and the YodelPay smart contract handling the swap and payment. Merchants receive fiat through established payment networks. Yodel also plans to enable tapping for payments, similar to Apple Pay. The platform has evolved from payment links to utilizing ENS (Ethereum Name Service) for storing payment preferences and configurations in a decentralized manner. This includes storing avatar images and URLs within ENS text records, which are then used to pre-configure payment pages. Webhooks are added to provide payment notifications, enabling integrations with Telegram and Slack bots. The Ethereum Follow Protocol (EFP) is used for a shared address book and trust score. The presentation also highlights mini-apps that can be opened within Yodel's super app, allowing for various functionalities like beer tabs, loyalty programs, and more. Yodel collaborates with network cities and events to build and reuse these mini-apps. In response to questions, Sebastian addresses the cost of ENS addresses, noting the availability of free subnames and tools that make ENS more accessible. He clarifies that senders don't need an ENS, but receivers benefit from having one to control how money flows.

transcripts.summary: David from BAC discusses their work in issuing real-world assets, particularly tokenized U.S. equities, in collaboration with Kraken. He draws an analogy between tokenized equities and stablecoins, predicting tokenized stocks will be the next big thing in crypto. He envisions a future where tokenized stocks are accessible to both crypto natives and traditional investors, improving access to financial products globally. BAC focuses on permissionless trading within regulation, one-to-one asset backing, and integrating with existing DeFi infrastructure. The goal is to bring trading volume from traditional finance to crypto, offering benefits like 24/7 availability and worldwide distribution. He highlights the potential for decentralized lending markets using tokenized stocks, allowing secured loans against assets. BAC aims to tokenize liquid stocks and encourages others to build on top of their work, forming the Xstocks Alliance to ensure neutrality and widespread acceptance. They are launching global distribution through Kraken and Solana, with EVM integration coming soon. In the Q&A, David clarifies that moving existing S&P 500 ETFs on-chain may involve tax implications and is working with institutions to enable share transfers to custody accounts. He also addresses smart contract risk in decentralized lending, noting legal mechanisms to recover assets lost due to smart contract issues.

transcripts.text: Wonderful, perfect. Hello, everyone. My name is Tony. I am with the Affirm Foundation. And today, I want to use the opportunity to talk a little bit about scaling year one. Scaling year one has been a big topic in the recent months and I want to look particularly into the midterm future and especially into like a future, some future hard forks and introduce two scaling EAPs, namely the late execution and block live access lists, both giving us some more scale on the L1. Before we get into the topic, let's first set a stage for what this talk is going to be about. Today, we can scale Ethereum using two levers. We have the gas limit and we have blocks. But today, I want to only focus on the gas limit. So, focusing on blocks will be done in the next hard fork. We will shift PeerDos and I want to focus more on the hard fork after PeerDos, namely on Glamstadam and what we could do in Glamstadam to then significantly increase the gas limit on Ethereum from 36 million to something like maybe 5x, 10x. In general, how to scale Ethereum, there are different things we can do. First, of course, some short-term things and this is basically involving client optimizations. Client teams are constantly working on their clients, optimizing things and we already saw a gas increase from 30 million to 36 million and this was done without even shipping some core protocol feature. So, clients are constantly improving their software and this then allows us to scale the R1. Midterm, it's protocol changes. So, do we actually need to change the protocol in order to allow the gas limit to be raised even higher? And long-term, I just put CKBMs there. This is often like the holy grail solution for scaling Ethereum and more on the long-term. But again, my talk will now focus on the midterm solutions. What can we do in the next hard fork and beyond in order to allow validators to increase the gas limit? Just to put that into a timeline, we ship Fusaka by the end of the year and there will be the Glamstadam hard fork next year and then the hard fork after that doesn't have a name yet. It will be something with Bogota, but the age is not decided yet. So, I want to focus particularly on what we can do by next year. Perfect. So, this is enough high-level context to now get into the topic. I split it up in two parts. We have slot restructuring and we have parallelization. At the slot restructuring, there are many different ideas what we can do in order to allow for more scale in the end. For example, we can do six-second slots and then keep the gas limit as it is. There is this idea of enshrined payload block separation that also kind of moves things around in the slot to allow for more time and to relieve the critical path. And then the late execution, which I'm going to talk about. And also on the right-hand side, we can see parallelization. And the main idea behind parallelization is the introduction of block-level access lifts. Perfect. So, let's get into the first part, which is the late execution. If you look it up today, there is an EAP for it. It's 7886. I would say it's still a very early stage, but it feels like client teams have some consensus that we might want to do some restructuring of what we use the slot for. And the late execution is one of those proposals besides EPVS. And the late execution, the concept is actually quite simple. So, this is how the slot looks like today. We have the proposer proposing the block at the very early of the slot, so basically at second zero. Because of timing games, we might see them proposing a little later. But in general, they have to propose the block until second four. Because at second four, here at T4, validators attest to the block. So, if you propose your block after the second four, you might not receive enough attestations and the next proposal will just reorder your block out. And the late execution now basically just extends this red line here. What we want to do is we want to allow validators to attest to a block without this block kind of risking of turning invalid. Because why do we need execution before the attestation deadline today? The reason is very simple, because blocks could turn invalid because of transactions they contain. So, for example, if I include a transaction that cannot pay the gas fee or if I include a transaction that has a wrong nonce, then the transaction is invalid and as a consequence the whole block would turn invalid. And this brings me to the challenging part here. So, how can we make sure that if validators attest to a block, that the block will never become invalid anymore? The rationale behind this change is not only scaling the gas limit, but also giving CKProvers more time to generate the proofs. Today, CKEVM Prover would need to generate the proof very early. So, there is only time between the block propagation and the attestation deadline to generate the proof. Now, by delaying execution so that we still attest, but we can use the full slot for execution, CKProvers just have more time. And today, CKProvers get quite close to real-time proving. So, I think 90% of the blocks are already below the 12-second mark, but they are far away from proving within like one to three seconds. And this is kind of the challenging thing here. And the idea behind the late execution is to give Provers more time to generate the proof. Right. So, we essentially go from like one second, two seconds that we have today for the whole execution to something around eight seconds. So, this allows you to not only kind of squeeze all the execution into the critical path right before the attestation deadline, but instead, you can use the full block to execute the transactions. And as already said, we just make more time for CKProvers to create the proof. Right. Because what we want to avoid is that validators attest to a block, and suddenly the block becomes invalid, which would mean the attestation is now facing or voting for an invalid block, and we would have to throw it away. There is a BAL hash in the header, and in the block body, we would put the block-level access list in there, which is essentially an indicator what storage is going to be touched in your block, and also the values you need to parallelize the transactions. If we have to include them in a block or not, maybe it's better to do it in a sidecar. This is still to be figured out, but this picture already gives you a sense of how this could look like. Right. In short, the block builder needs to include those BALs and reinforce that simply through consensus. So, the block builder has to, while building the block, build also the block-level access list into the block. So, for the block builder, this is not that much work, actually, but for the validators, it's very, very helpful. transcripts.summary:
Tony from the Affirm Foundation discusses scaling Ethereum, focusing on the midterm future and potential hard forks like Glamstadam. He introduces two scaling EAPs: late execution (EAP-7886) and block-level access lists (BALs, EAP-27928). Currently, Ethereum scaling relies on the gas limit and blocks, but the talk concentrates on increasing the gas limit significantly in Glamstadam. Short-term scaling involves client optimizations, while long-term solutions include CKVMs. 

Late execution aims to allow validators to attest to blocks without the risk of invalidation due to transactions, giving CKProvers more time and extending the execution window. This involves deferring execution output fields and reverting the entire block's execution if an invalid transaction occurs to disincentivize proposers from creating such blocks. 

Block-level access lists (BALs) tackle scaling through parallelization, aiming to make block validation faster. They address the challenge of worst-case blocks with dependent transactions by enabling fully parallelizable transactions. BALs involve adding a BAL hash to the header and a block-level access list to the block body, indicating which storage will be touched. This offloads work to block builders, easing the validator's task. The discussion includes design choices such as post-transaction values versus all values on disk, with a preference for the former to reduce worst-case block sizes.

transcripts.text: Yeah, so a couple of years back I was experimenting with bringing Geth on the Gnosis Chain and this is a summary of this experience and also I wanted to share some learning from that. Yeah, so differences between the Gnosis Chain and Mainnet, there's a 5 second block time which is inherited, so the Gnosis Chain used to be a chain called XDAI which has a token that is a stablecoin and yeah, the block time was 5 seconds and the idea behind this whole thing, I think, that was even before I was part of Ethereum, I think, was to get some traffic, to offload some traffic into some kind of side chain, do the transactions without going to, you know, without competing for the main pool on Mainnet, that was the time of CryptoKitty and yeah, they went for a shorter block time and this was, this has been inherited since and so we find ourselves with this block time. It's quite interesting for me because as Tony was saying just before, we want to reduce the slot time, so 5 seconds, 6 seconds, it's not too different, so that's quite an interesting experiment as far as I'm concerned. When you look, and I will go into this later, but when you look at the size of the state, you find it to be a lot smaller, which makes sense, it's a side chain that is meant to offload some of the traffic, so it's not going to have the exact same size. What's the consequence of the block time, however, is that the history is, in terms of block, is about twice as large as what it is on Mainnet. It was using this consensus called Aura, I'm not going to get too much, too deep into this, but it came from Parity and it's effectively a proof of authority consensus algorithm, but they tried to make it a bit more decentralized by using some kind of voting DAO thing, so yeah, that's the status, eventually they got rid of it. One of the interesting parts, or maybe infuriating, depending on how you look at it, it relies a lot on system contracts, so the consensus will call a contract, an on-chain contract, so you can tweak the way the consensus is working this way. In terms of history, the forks were a bit different, some people just decided not to use some EIPs during the forks, so they were activated later because they wanted to look more like Mainnet, but the original designers seemed to have decided there were some EIPs they didn't want on their chain, so it's a bit of a patchwork of history, and the work has been done by the Gnosis people to try to bring the chain closer to what Mainnet is, but yeah, historically, it's not quite true. You've got the concept of service transactions, which are transactions, for example, for the bridge that brings some tokens from Mainnet into the Gnosis chain, so you need to be able to mint and you don't pay for this, so that's another interesting difference. And then the other difference is that, for example, the other major difference is that the EL uses a stablecoin, which is XDAI, and the CL uses the GNO token. And then, yeah, I added a rant about incompatibility of the block format, but that's a detail. So if you dump the two states, like the Gnosis state and the Mainnet state, you see some interesting information, like, for example, if you look at the code, there's about 10% as much code on the Gnosis chain as the Mainnet, but if you look at the accounts, there's about 40 times more accounts on Mainnet as there is on Gnosis, that makes sense, right? Once again, it was meant to offload some traffic from the Mainnet, so not move everything. But the interesting part is that the storage nodes, however, are about half of Mainnet. That means there's a lot more content per account on the Gnosis chain as there is on Mainnet. And honestly, I don't have a definitive answer of why that is. It could be that it's mostly designed to do ERC trading or other things, so that would explain why there's a lot more contracts. But it seems that there are actually relatively fewer simple, able-to-die accounts on the Gnosis chain. And then you have the account and storage snapshot, which is pretty much the same information. The other interesting part is that the bodies, the total size of bodies is about one-third of what it is on Mainnet, but there are way more blocks, and that makes sense because the block time is much smaller, so you have less time to execute. If I'm not mistaken, the gas limit, the target gas limit currently on Gnosis chain is 17 million, so about half of what we want on Mainnet. And yeah, so you can see there are more headers, but the blocks themselves are smaller, and yeah, that makes sense. The last interesting thing is the receipt. The size of the receipt on Gnosis chain and Mainnet is about the same. And I'm actually quite curious as to find out why that is. I don't know for sure. Nevermind was just started, but they didn't have SnapSync. They were not serving SnapSync. They were using a protocol that was about to get discontinued in Geth. And, like I said, the Gnosis team has tried to bring the chain, like to modernize the chain, to bring it closer. So they replicated parity. They removed Aura by doing a merge. And yeah, like, nevermind implemented SnapSync. So things started to look a lot more like Mainnet. Yeah, so the first attempt was to try to create something, the first attempt at bringing Geth on this chain was trying to get something like history expiry. And the idea is that you would have nevermind following the chain and nevermind had implemented Aura. I didn't want to. And so the idea is that we'd get some kind of bootstrap version of Geth that would just import a dumped state from nevermind and try to pretend that this was the proper sync. And so the merge would be skipped, the whole Aura history would be skipped. And then this instance would only exist, like, would be unique. And we would spin up other Geth nodes that would SnapSync from it. For many reasons, that didn't really work out. One of them is, yeah, I had to do a lot of guesswork. It wasn't really clear that some forks were activated. And when they were, at least it wasn't clear to me. And yeah, I came also to the realization that a lot of the Aura stuff still remains behind. So I think at this point, it made sense to just re-implement Aura. And Aragon had done it in the meantime. They were brave enough to read the Rust code from Parity. So good on them. And I took it and I adapted it to Geth. So as it turns out, that was the other discovery, like the code of Aragon has drifted, especially in this part, has drifted significantly from Geth. So there was some adaptation work to do, but it was manageable in the end. And yeah, like this implementation of Aura didn't have to be good enough to run a future Aura network, if anybody wants that. It was just meant to be good enough that Geth could full sync up to the merge block and move on and ignore Aura for the end times. So full sync, when I did that full sync, it took about a month. I ran into all the peculiarities. So this is when I went from guesswork into actually figuring out what the problem, like block per block. So yeah, like for example, the most famous example is that there's a code limit that was activated at a given fork, like 24 kilobytes. People want to change that to, I think 48 is the last number. But for GnosisChain, it was not activated at the same time. As mainnet, so they activated it in Shanghai. So this is one of those examples. But now we have Geth on Gnosis mainnet chugging along and so far it's working fine. I'd say the biggest lesson of this whole story for me is that system contracts are a bad idea. They're all the rage right now. And I think it's a mistake. So that's some controversial take right here. I mean, I could list all the reasons, but the biggest one is that most clients, I accept Geth at this point, do not trace system contracts. And so if you are trying to develop a client for a chain that uses, whose consensus relies heavily on that, it's really hard to figure out what's going wrong. And it's also harder to debug, like the system contracts are harder to debug because you can't put a breakpoint in the system contract. You have to put a breakpoint at the client level and somehow you have like a lot of overhead to figure out what the contract is doing. Your behavior is pretty opaque and you probably heard of the Petra testnet fork debacle. I put, so this is actually the fixed version of this, of the code that caused the debacle to begin with. But they were expecting, like the code was expecting a, I'm looking for the word, a message to come from the contract. And because Sepolia is a peculiar chain, they deployed their own, like when I say they, I mean, ETH kind of ops, they deployed their own contract. They didn't really tell anyone how it was working. So no one was expecting this. This is not a dunk on the ETH kind of ops at all. I'm just saying this is bound to happen because to people doing DevOps, it looks like it's just delegated to the execution layer, like the consensus part is delegated to the execution. And as long as the execution works, you should expect it to work. Yeah, but then the message didn't travel. And therefore, like client devs had no idea that this was coming. Some, if I remember, it's Aragon who did it right. But most other clients were just expecting this pattern. They were not expecting a different pattern. And this is how Sepolia got in trouble during the fork. So I think it's pretty clear to me, my opinion that we should have, we should have, we should not have system contracts. Everything should be deployed as actual native client code. Yeah, that's my conclusion from this at least. Now I'm going to go over the list of changes that could be interested to Forgnosis chain. There's a protocol level and there's what VF could do. At the protocol level, I think the biggest gain Forgnosis chain would be EIP-44, namely history expiry. There's a lot of blocks. And all those blocks are almost empty, but together they take a lot of space. They take a lot of space, especially for the sink, because the full sink, you have to go over every one of them and yes, recompute the state route at every block. So that's why it takes a long time. You could do something like, for example, Aragon and REST, they do something where you just execute the transactions and they compute the route at the end. We could do something a bit similar in GIS, maybe compute the route every 10 blocks, every 128 blocks. That would be interesting to check, to do. So that could be my next experiment on Forgnosis chain, because once again, that's where the benefit is going to be the greatest. Okay, Tony talked about delayed execution. I also forgot to mention about EPVS. So sorry for this. But the idea is because the block time is so short, it might be interesting for offering some extra capacity to the chain to implement that on Forgnosis chain as well. So that would be my two favorite topics to implement if I was the one deciding what goes into Forgnosis chain. I mentioned the bloatnet. This is an effort that I work on for the EF. The goal is to really create, like make a fork of any network and try to really increase the size of the state. I think that would be also interesting to probe two things. The first one is for EtherMainnet, because we are close to a five second, of a six second slot with a five second slot. But it's also interesting, once again, to study what capacity is really available to a network with a five second block time. Otherwise, yeah, I think EF, it's pretty clear that EF needs to be able to enable, to have a better granularity in its capacity to enable or to turn on and off EIP. So that would be something great if GES could do this. Yeah, so not really a lot to say, except GC-GES could also bring something back into GES. Honestly, yeah, I guess I'll just skip this one. transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses their experience bringing Geth to the Gnosis Chain, highlighting key differences between Gnosis Chain and Mainnet, such as the 5-second block time, smaller state size, and the use of Aura consensus (later replaced). They delve into historical differences, like the delayed activation of certain EIPs and the presence of service transactions. A state dump comparison reveals interesting insights: Gnosis Chain has less code and fewer accounts than Mainnet but more content per account. The speaker shares their attempts to integrate Geth, including overcoming challenges related to Aura implementation and fork activation. They criticize the use of system contracts due to debugging difficulties and potential for unexpected behavior, referencing the Sepolia testnet fork issue. The speaker suggests potential improvements for Gnosis Chain, such as EIP-44 (history expiry) and EPVS, and notes Gnosis Chain's role as a canary chain for Ethereum. They conclude by noting that Geth is currently a minority client on Gnosis Chain and that they hope it will be more widely adopted, especially by validators.

transcripts.summary: Luis from BrainBot introduces Shutter, a threshold encryption, DKG, encryption as a service. Shutter ensures baseline neutrality, providing encryption/decryption keys for applications like encrypted mempools (live on GnosisChain) and integration with PVF transaction supply chains. They're working towards making it a protocol part for decentralized encryption/decryption, ensuring neutrality and resistance to front-running. Shutter API offers encryption as a service for governance, voting, RFPs, and gaming. It addresses information asymmetry issues, like in trading or games, by encrypting transactions, batching them, and signing them while encrypted, decrypting only post-commitment. Special encryption uses K-out-of-N parties to de-trust the encryptor/decryptor. Shutter is implemented in Snapshot governance for shielded voting (Arbitrum, Shapeshift). The Shutter API simplifies encryption implementation, showcasing use cases like sealed bid auctions, bounty platforms, on-chain games, and negotiation tools. Examples include Shutter Hongbao (timelock crypto gifting), a prediction commit/reveal app (with a Twitter bot), juror voting for Clarus, and sealed RFPs. They're developing Petal Battle (impact-focused auction platform) with Shutter sealed bid auctions, and Shutterized Voting POC for OZ Governor and Safe Azorius frameworks. They're launching an Ethereum Time Capsule for the 10th anniversary, encouraging users to share stories. Shutter API apps are easily built, envisioning agentic MCP interaction, wrapping Shutter API for cloud/chat-GPT access. They are working on event-based encryption triggers and homomorphic vote counting for perpetually hidden votes. They invite dApp developers and chains to integrate Shutter API, offering specialized encryption gadgets. The time-based decryption synchronizes with the block via keepers, who need to sync with the blockchain.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker, Nixel, discusses MaxEV, a feature in the Pectra upgrade for Ethereum. MaxEV stands for Maximum Effective Balance of a Validator, which was previously 32 ETH and is now 2,048 ETH, allowing validators to earn yield on a larger stake. The goal is to consolidate validators, reducing network overhead and paving the way for research requiring smaller validator sets, such as single slot finality. Raising the Max EB also protects against a surge of 32 ETH validators, which could overwhelm the network. For individual node operators, MaxEV enables auto-compounding of stake, improving capital productivity. The process is opt-in and doesn't change yield or proposal chances. 

Consolidation requests convert existing type 1 validators (32 ETH) to type 2 validators (up to 2,048 ETH). While targeting institutional stakers, it benefits solo stakers too. Post-upgrade, the number of validators initially decreased due to consolidations but has since rebounded. Large operators haven't consolidated due to the Lindy effect, adjusted slashing risks, customer choice, and protocol compatibility issues. The speaker discusses the reasons for the slow adoption, including the need for educational campaigns and protocol changes. Despite slow adoption among larger stakers so far, the change lays groundwork for future research directions on the Ethereum network. 

The speaker emphasizes the importance of clear communication and understanding of protocol specifications, highlighting a misunderstanding among staking protocols regarding the upgrade's compatibility. The speaker then talks about their team's approach to protocol upgrades, focusing on clarifying the process for proposing and implementing EIPs and ensuring app developers can integrate new features effectively. Finally, the speaker addresses questions about anti-correlation penalties, hardware requirements for smaller staking sizes, and the reasons behind choosing 2,048 ETH as the MaxEV. She also clarified that Type 1 validators do not get compounding interest and you need to upgrade to type 2 to take advantage of that. In closing, the speaker recommends going straight to signing up for type 2, especially if you're a casual solo staker.

transcripts.summary: Joseph discusses mistakes and lessons learned building Pawn, a universal lending protocol. He shares his background and the motivation for creating Pawn after being rejected for a mortgage due to his crypto-native status. He highlights the concept of optionality, optimizing for various use cases, and how Ethereum benefited from this approach. Pawn aims to be a peer-to-peer lending protocol for the tokenized economy, tapping into existing liquidity pools. Joseph details mistakes such as insufficient user testing, focusing on irrelevant metrics, and premature multi-chain support. He emphasizes the importance of understanding user needs, simplifying interfaces, and avoiding unnecessary features, referencing the Occam's Razor principle for UX design. While protocol-level optionality is beneficial, product-level optionality should be minimized for clarity. Prioritizing user value over perceived values, avoiding over-optimization, and allowing developers time for refactoring are also key lessons. PawnDAO manages the protocol as a credit collective, aiming to recreate a credit union-like system.

transcripts.summary:
The presentation discusses Balancer V3 hooks, focusing on how they can be used to build and customize AMMs. Balancer V3 aims to be a platform for AMMs, leveraging experience from V1 and V2. It emphasizes ease of building and customization, is fully audited, and supports 100% boosted pools. Hooks are modular plugins to extend existing pool behavior, allowing partners and Balancer to build various types of pools (wave, stable, gyroscope, quant AMM, reclam). Three hooks are currently in use: StableSearch, MEV Capture, and Akron hook. The main reason to build on Balancer V3 is the fast development cycle, allowing focus on the core idea and leveraging audited code. There's comprehensive documentation, example hooks, periphery contracts, active dev support, and grants available. Support extends beyond development to post-launch via the Balancer front end, aggregator relationships, and operations/marketing teams. The architecture includes the router, vault, pools, and hooks. Pools define the core math for custom pricing models (new AMMs), while hooks extend these pools, working with any pool type to add extra behavior. Hooks are registered with a pool upon creation and are immutable. Hooks can be integrated into various lifecycle points like registration, initialization, add/remove liquidity, and dynamic swap fees. The StableSearch hook, a directional fee mechanism protecting stablecoin pegs during volatility, is described in detail. It uses the vault guard and base hook periphery contracts. The MEV Capture hook is also presented, it internalizes value leaked from the pool to liquidity providers by using priority fees to identify MEV bots and applying a dynamic fee mechanism. It works on off-stack chains with priority fees and a centralized sequencer. The hook calculates priority fees from transaction and block metadata and has parameters like a threshold, multiplier, max swap fee, and exempted senders. The MEV Capture hook is deployed on Base and expands MEV protection to kits. Grants are available for developing Balancer V3 hooks, including size-based fees, limit orders, and cross-chain swaps.
The speaker discusses three ideas for improving the platform via hooks: volume-based fees (possibly involving oracle integration), permissioned pools (allowing specific swappers or liquidity providers), and directional fees (allowing LPs to adjust spreads based on price and market volatility). They encourage builders to reach out with proposals, which don't necessarily need to go to a forum, but should outline the builder's background, the proposal's details, deadlines, and budget. Builders can use other tech stacks in addition to the platform's, especially if it solves one of their problems. The speaker is starting with these three ideas to scope smaller projects and gradually expand.

transcripts.summary:
The discussion revolves around the current state and future of privacy in Ethereum. Panelists agree that Ethereum privacy is still in its early stages, despite various roadmap proposals. The complexity arises from attempting to integrate privacy into a public, decentralized ledger. While there is broad support for privacy, it often takes a backseat to scaling and UX improvements. Several topics were discussed, including Railgun integration, the role of cypherpunk culture, and potential use cases for privacy-focused applications. Panelists shared their visions for the future, emphasizing the need for experimentation, community support, and a long-term perspective on adoption. They also touched on challenges like fees, cultural perceptions, and the balance between individual and enterprise privacy.
The speaker discusses the cultural factions within Ethereum: OG cypherpunks, pragmatists, and post-ideological pragmatists. A hybrid culture, balancing strategic pragmatism with core values, is seen as ideal. The speaker emphasizes the importance of positivity within the community, noting that communal events thrive on it. The atmosphere at events is currently positive with privacy and cyberpunk more integrated than before. The speaker raises the idea that perhaps "everything is okay" at the social layer. The speaker concludes with a thank you and an announcement of upcoming speakers after the break, highlighting their expertise in privacy, cryptography, and hacktivism.

name: Blockchain Ethics: Pure Reason or Pure Madness?
description: This a work in progress attempting to answer seemingly simple and not very contradictory question.  "Why can we not have ethics of blockchain applications?" We seem to have a burgeoning field of AI ethics, and even with a reasonable criticism against it, AI ethics does flourish both in industry and as research in academia. Contrast it with blockchain ethics which is hardly a mature subfield, but more of a painful (and emotional) topic. Are there good reasons to care about it? This is an empirical, philosophical, and normative question.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the feasibility of blockchain ethics. They argue that while the field is significantly smaller compared to AI ethics, it is a worthwhile pursuit. The speaker presents three arguments against blockchain ethics: complexity, incentives, and the perception of crypto as a casino. They counter these arguments by emphasizing the importance of addressing complexity systematically, acknowledging the crowding out of morals by economic incentives, and highlighting the morally significant use cases of crypto. The speaker defines blockchain ethics as designing possible worlds and making value judgments about which world to choose. They suggest methodologies like value-sensitive design and ethical risk analysis. The speaker concludes by emphasizing the need for agreement on core principles, mitigating information asymmetry, and addressing regulatory challenges. A Q&A session covers topics such as the origins of institutions, community values, selective activism, and EU's ethical guidelines for blockchain systems.

name: The Holy Trinity of Censorship Resistance in Ethereum
description: Censorship resistance and decentralization have long been core principles of public blockchains, yet Ethereum faces increasing threats from real-time transaction censorship, particularly impacting DeFi users. The current Proposer-Builder Separation (PBS) supply chain has led to severe centralization, with two builders controlling over 80% of blocks and half of all relays censoring transactions. A promising approach to address this is the ""Holy Trinity of Censorship Resistance"", a combination of enshrined PBS (ePBS), FOCIL (Fork-Choice enforced Inclusion Lists), and encrypted mempools.

transcripts.summary: The talk discusses censorship resistance in Ethereum and proposes a solution using a combination of three techniques: Enshrined Proposal Builder Separation (ePBS), FOSSIL (a mechanism for inclusion lists), and encrypted mempools. The current Ethereum transaction supply chain involves users, builders, relays, and proposers, all of whom have the potential to censor transactions. The speaker suggests that in an ideal world, Ethereum should have timely inclusion of transactions, no trusted intermediaries, and hidden transaction content until inclusion is guaranteed. ePBS aims to remove the trusted relay by using a committee of attestors, while FOSSIL forces proposers to include transactions from an inclusion list. Encrypted mempools ensure that transaction content is hidden until inclusion is guaranteed, preventing malicious extraction. The speaker then described how these three techniques can work together. The talk also covers the practical steps being taken to implement this vision, including conceptual work, a roadmap towards an encrypted mempool, and a demo of an MCP server using an encrypted mempool route on notice chain.

transcripts.summary: Antonio, the co-founder of Fluidkey, discusses the journey of building a privacy solution on the blockchain. He highlights the problem of public data on blockchains and the challenges in creating user-friendly privacy tools. He explains how FluidKey leverages ENS and smart accounts to provide privacy by hiding addresses and amounts. He emphasizes the importance of hackathons for developing features, community feedback, and the need for revenue generation in privacy-focused products. He encourages users to test, provide feedback, and vote for projects they support. He also acknowledges the trade-offs between decentralization and UX, and the skills he gained like questioning and building relations to understand the needs of users.

name: Delegation and Participation in  Decentralized Governance: An Epistemic View
description: We develop and apply epistemic tests to various decentralized governance methods as well as to study the impact of participation. These tests probe the ability to reach a correct outcome when there is one. We find that partial abstention is a strong governance method from an epistemic standpoint compared to alternatives such as various forms of “transfer delegation” in which voters explicitly transfer some or all of their voting rights to others.
