00:01:45.360 --> 00:01:47.400
properties that are important for end users

37
00:01:47.400 --> 00:01:49.559
in particular such as how much extra

38
00:01:49.559 --> 00:01:51.540
storage overhead do you need to buy

39
00:01:51.540 --> 00:01:53.800
if you are trying to take advantage

40
00:01:53.800 --> 00:01:58.180
of this All right so what's wrong

41
00:01:58.180 --> 00:02:02.400
with good old data duplication By that

42
00:02:02.400 --> 00:02:05.400
I mean it's very easy to ensure

43
00:02:05.400 --> 00:02:08.160
data redundancy in a system Let's say

44
00:02:08.160 --> 00:02:12.160
we have three little chunks of data

45
00:02:12.699 --> 00:02:15.119
These three little chunks represent one single

46
00:02:15.119 --> 00:02:17.279
file for example that's chopped up into

47
00:02:17.279 --> 00:02:22.520
three bits scattered around the network and

48
00:02:22.520 --> 00:02:25.300
then we could simply duplicate them and

49
00:02:25.300 --> 00:02:27.059
have it at that What's wrong with

50
00:02:27.059 --> 00:02:29.179
this Well the problem is first of

51
00:02:29.179 --> 00:02:30.979
all this is very wasteful because you

52
00:02:30.979 --> 00:02:33.740
have to duplicate all the data and

53
00:02:33.740 --> 00:02:35.559
second of all it's actually not very

54
00:02:35.559 --> 00:02:38.600
secure The reason being is that if

55
00:02:38.600 --> 00:02:41.860
you think about it let's imagine that

56
00:02:41.860 --> 00:02:45.720
the computers storing these data are churned

57
00:02:45.860 --> 00:02:47.960
or for some reason are not available

58
00:02:48.160 --> 00:02:51.860
and by unlucky chance the computers are

59
00:02:51.860 --> 00:02:53.800
down such that both of these chunks

60
00:02:53.800 --> 00:02:55.380
three are missing and you only have

61
00:02:55.899 --> 00:02:58.179
available chunks one and two In that

62
00:02:58.179 --> 00:02:59.820
case you still cannot recover your data

63
00:02:59.899 --> 00:03:02.380
so not only is this system of

64
00:03:02.380 --> 00:03:05.479
simple minded duplication very wasteful in terms

65
00:03:05.479 --> 00:03:07.240
of storage it's also not as secure

66
00:03:07.240 --> 00:03:10.360
as it could be Enter the idea

67
00:03:10.360 --> 00:03:12.020
of erasure codes which is actually an

68
00:03:12.020 --> 00:03:14.800
old idea dating back to a famous

69
00:03:14.800 --> 00:03:16.460
paper by Reed and Solomon in the

70
00:03:16.460 --> 00:03:19.380
1960s The idea is the following Let's

71
00:03:19.380 --> 00:03:21.619
have the exact same file that we

72
00:03:21.619 --> 00:03:24.600
had before chopped up into three little

73
00:03:24.600 --> 00:03:26.820
chunks and we will pad it out

74
00:03:26.820 --> 00:03:29.259
with a number of extra chunks For

75
00:03:29.259 --> 00:03:31.960
illustration's sake on this slide two extra

76
00:03:31.960 --> 00:03:34.880
little chunks You notice that I've denoted

77
00:03:34.880 --> 00:03:37.119
them with blue and the idea is

78
00:03:37.119 --> 00:03:39.199
that these two blue chunks are so

79
00:03:39.199 --> 00:03:44.240
called parity chunks and now the big

80
00:03:44.240 --> 00:03:46.419
idea is that any three out of

81
00:03:46.419 --> 00:03:48.520
these five are sufficient to recover the

82
00:03:48.520 --> 00:03:52.399
original data so this erasure coding employs

83
00:03:52.399 --> 00:03:55.119
some form of encoding which allows you

84
00:03:55.119 --> 00:03:58.160
to reconstruct the data no matter which

85
00:03:58.160 --> 00:04:00.059
three out of these five you have

86
00:04:00.059 --> 00:04:02.300
So again to repeat erasure coding is

87
00:04:02.300 --> 00:04:04.720
about having a number of original data

88
00:04:04.720 --> 00:04:07.699
chunks padding it out with another number

89
00:04:07.699 --> 00:04:11.880
of parity chunks such that any of

90
00:04:11.880 --> 00:04:13.679
the original number of chunks is enough

91
00:04:13.679 --> 00:04:15.279
to recover the data so it doesn't

92
00:04:15.279 --> 00:04:17.660
matter whether I have access to two

93
00:04:18.140 --> 00:04:19.799
four and three or one four and

94
00:04:19.799 --> 00:04:21.579
five any three of them will be

95
00:04:21.579 --> 00:04:24.200
able to recover the data I don't

96
00:04:24.200 --> 00:04:25.399
have time to go into the details

97
00:04:25.399 --> 00:04:26.779
of how this does its magic but

98
00:04:26.779 --> 00:04:28.339
I'm happy to talk about that afterwards

99
00:04:28.339 --> 00:04:31.559
if people are interested Okay so this

100
00:04:31.559 --> 00:04:33.440
was what erasure codes are The next

101
00:04:33.440 --> 00:04:35.200
question is how we can implement them

102
00:04:35.200 --> 00:04:36.760
in Swarm and in order to understand

103
00:04:36.760 --> 00:04:39.260
that let's first understand how the file

104
00:04:39.260 --> 00:04:42.260
system works in Swarm So as I

105
00:04:42.260 --> 00:04:44.260
mentioned earlier all files are chopped up

106
00:04:44.260 --> 00:04:47.399
into small four kilobyte little chunks and

107
00:04:47.399 --> 00:04:49.320
those are randomly scattered across the network

108
00:04:49.320 --> 00:04:51.720
and the way the files are represented

109
00:04:51.720 --> 00:04:53.600
is through what is called the Swarm

110
00:04:53.600 --> 00:04:55.779
hash tree and I'm going to illustrate

111
00:04:55.779 --> 00:04:57.720
that for you There we go This

112
00:04:57.720 --> 00:05:00.179
is a Merkle tree not a binary

113
00:05:00.179 --> 00:05:04.000
one but a 128 ary one so

114
00:05:04.000 --> 00:05:06.040
it's a tree with a balancing factor

115
00:05:06.040 --> 00:05:11.160
of 128 It all starts from—not that—it

116
00:05:11.160 --> 00:05:14.899
all starts—there we go—from a root hash

117
00:05:15.140 --> 00:05:18.339
and then it points to various references

118
00:05:18.799 --> 00:05:21.880
and the references point to other references

119
00:05:21.880 --> 00:05:23.720
and so on until we reach the

120
00:05:23.720 --> 00:05:26.440
actual data that's in the bottom row

121
00:05:26.440 --> 00:05:28.359
that we have there the actual data

122
00:05:28.359 --> 00:05:30.559
chunks that we have I always use

123
00:05:30.559 --> 00:05:33.160
the convention that these rounded corner rectangles

124
00:05:33.160 --> 00:05:35.700
are the actual chunks of data so

125
00:05:35.700 --> 00:05:37.700
you see that we have slightly larger

126
00:05:37.700 --> 00:05:41.339
but still rounded rectangles here those items

127
00:05:41.339 --> 00:05:44.540
there Those are so called packed address

128
00:05:44.540 --> 00:05:47.839
chunks also known as intermediate chunks so

129
00:05:47.839 --> 00:05:49.220
those are the chunks that are sort

130
00:05:49.220 --> 00:05:51.920
of in the network and their role

131
00:05:51.920 --> 00:05:55.200
is to give the references to the

132
00:05:55.200 --> 00:05:57.459
levels—to the other levels and then at

133
00:05:57.459 --> 00:05:58.859
the end we reach of course the

134
00:05:58.859 --> 00:06:01.339
actual data that we want to retrieve

135
00:06:02.480 --> 00:06:04.040
So this is the structure of files

136
00:06:04.059 --> 00:06:05.380
so this is again a Merkle tree

137
00:06:05.380 --> 00:06:09.399
that we have Each of these so

138
00:06:09.399 --> 00:06:11.019
called packed address chunks that are pointed

139
00:06:11.019 --> 00:06:14.299
out by the arrows contain 128 references

140
00:06:15.440 --> 00:06:18.859
Why 128 references The symbol is very

141
00:06:18.859 --> 00:06:22.380
prosaic Every reference takes up 32 bytes

142
00:06:22.380 --> 00:06:25.859
of memory and then because every chunk

143
00:06:25.859 --> 00:06:27.820
has to be 4 kilobytes in size

144
00:06:27.839 --> 00:06:31.500
as mentioned that means that 128 references

145
00:06:31.500 --> 00:06:33.459
then fit into a single chunk to

146
00:06:33.459 --> 00:06:35.640
make up for the 4 kilobytes Parenthetical

147
00:06:35.640 --> 00:06:38.200
little comment There's also an option to

148
00:06:38.200 --> 00:06:41.339
get encrypted information where it's not just

149
00:06:41.339 --> 00:06:43.640
the address but also an encryption key

150
00:06:43.640 --> 00:06:45.579
that one needs to store in every

151
00:06:45.579 --> 00:06:47.839
reference In that case the size of

152
00:06:47.839 --> 00:06:50.079
every reference instead of being 32 bytes

153
00:06:50.380 --> 00:06:54.720
is increased to 64 bytes Quick calculation

154
00:06:54.720 --> 00:06:57.779
will reveal that then instead of 128

155
00:06:57.779 --> 00:07:00.140
references you can pack in 64 references

156
00:07:00.140 --> 00:07:03.179
for each of these intermediate packed address

157
00:07:03.179 --> 00:07:07.299
chunks Parentheses closed I'm sometimes going to

158
00:07:07.299 --> 00:07:10.320
mention encrypted data but mostly for the

159
00:07:10.320 --> 00:07:12.579
simplicity of the examples I will just

160
00:07:12.579 --> 00:07:15.540
stick to normal unencrypted information All right

161
00:07:16.540 --> 00:07:19.420
moving on Here is the key idea

162
00:07:19.420 --> 00:07:22.140
for how we can implement erasure coding

163
00:07:22.140 --> 00:07:25.040
in a decentralized storage system such as

164
00:07:25.040 --> 00:07:27.579
Swarm which works with these Merkle trees

165
00:07:27.579 --> 00:07:29.880
to store data The idea is as

166
00:07:29.880 --> 00:07:32.359
follows We take each of these intermediate

167
00:07:32.359 --> 00:07:36.100
packed address chunks that we've seen before

168
00:07:36.380 --> 00:07:41.940
those ones They have 128 references and

169
00:07:41.940 --> 00:07:44.119
the idea is very simple Instead of

170
00:07:44.119 --> 00:07:46.359
using all the 128 of them to

171
00:07:46.359 --> 00:07:48.200
be references we only use a couple

172
00:07:48.200 --> 00:07:51.079
of them and the rest we reserve

173
00:07:51.079 --> 00:07:54.679
for parities such that then any combination

174
00:07:54.679 --> 00:07:58.420
of M references will be able to

175
00:07:58.420 --> 00:08:00.579
recover the original data So just to

176
00:08:00.579 --> 00:08:02.279
give you a very simple example let's

177
00:08:02.279 --> 00:08:05.420
assume that this is our packed address

178
00:08:05.420 --> 00:08:07.720
chunk here with all the 128 references

179
00:08:07.899 --> 00:08:10.700
and let's assume that this number M

180
00:08:10.700 --> 00:08:14.739
is 100 That means 100 references will

181
00:08:14.739 --> 00:08:17.619
be quote real references and the other

182
00:08:17.619 --> 00:08:19.940
28 will be parities such that any

183
00:08:19.940 --> 00:08:22.920
100 out of the 128 will be

184
00:08:22.920 --> 00:08:26.459
able to recover the references There you

185
00:08:26.459 --> 00:08:28.040
go This is what it means that

186
00:08:28.040 --> 00:08:32.080
you have 100 original and 28 parity

187
00:08:32.080 --> 00:08:35.539
chunks or well references to chunks in

188
00:08:35.539 --> 00:08:38.580
this case This is the key idea

189
00:08:38.799 --> 00:08:40.859
This is how we implement erasure coding

190
00:08:40.859 --> 00:08:43.500
in Swarm and then what that actually

191
00:08:43.500 --> 00:08:45.960
means is that the real structure in

192
00:08:45.960 --> 00:08:49.200
the presence of erasure coding of the

193
00:08:49.200 --> 00:08:52.359
Swarm hash tree is like this We

194
00:08:52.359 --> 00:08:54.260
have the root hash and then we

195
00:08:54.260 --> 00:08:56.780
still have these intermediate packed address chunks

196
00:08:57.059 --> 00:08:58.919
but in each of them some of

197
00:08:58.919 --> 00:09:02.239
the references are parity references This also

198
00:09:02.239 --> 00:09:04.460
means that these lines that I used

199
00:09:04.460 --> 00:09:07.179
to connect various references with one another

200
00:09:07.179 --> 00:09:10.320
are slightly metaphorical because of course in

201
00:09:10.320 --> 00:09:12.380
the presence of erasure coding it's no

202
00:09:12.380 --> 00:09:15.640
longer true that this reference strictly refers

203
00:09:15.640 --> 00:09:18.119
to that Instead the references are sort

204
00:09:18.119 --> 00:09:20.780
of encoded in all of the data

205
00:09:20.780 --> 00:09:23.599
out there such that even if for

206
00:09:23.599 --> 00:09:25.739
some reason we're missing some of the

207
00:09:25.739 --> 00:09:28.359
information we can always reconstruct the required

208
00:09:28.359 --> 00:09:31.159
information from just 100 of those references

209
00:09:31.159 --> 00:09:35.539
out of the 128 All right There

210
00:09:35.539 --> 00:09:36.919
is one other one out that I

211
00:09:36.919 --> 00:09:39.719
will mention just very quickly the root

212
00:09:39.719 --> 00:09:43.119
hash The root is one single chunk

213
00:09:44.400 --> 00:09:47.460
but it's not structured like the other

214
00:09:47.460 --> 00:09:49.820
ones It doesn't have those references Therefore

215
00:09:49.840 --> 00:09:51.539
it has to be treated in its

216
00:09:51.539 --> 00:09:53.859
own way How can we do that

217
00:09:54.520 --> 00:09:56.679
A very simple first idea might be

218
00:09:56.679 --> 00:09:58.799
that you have is that we can

219
00:09:58.799 --> 00:10:01.619
simply duplicate the root hash have many

220
00:10:01.619 --> 00:10:04.039
copies of the same thing except unfortunately

221
00:10:04.039 --> 00:10:06.000
in the context of the swarm system

222
00:10:06.219 --> 00:10:08.919
that doesn't work The reason is that

223
00:10:08.919 --> 00:10:10.640
chunks with the same hash are automatically

224
00:10:10.640 --> 00:10:14.599
deduplicated by the system How can we

225
00:10:14.599 --> 00:10:16.080
solve this problem I'm not going to

226
00:10:16.080 --> 00:10:17.739
go into the gory details of how

227
00:10:17.739 --> 00:10:19.239
it is done but to give you

228
00:10:19.239 --> 00:10:22.099
an idea of what's done the sort

229
00:10:22.099 --> 00:10:23.559
of outline of the idea is quite

230
00:10:23.559 --> 00:10:25.359
simple which is that we have to

231
00:10:25.359 --> 00:10:28.919
tag on a hash onto the actual

232
00:10:28.919 --> 00:10:32.080
payload the actual information contained in those

233
00:10:31.820 --> 00:10:35.760
chunks such that A the owner is

234
00:10:35.760 --> 00:10:39.479
clearly identifiable and B it is such

235
00:10:39.479 --> 00:10:44.299
that these quasi duplicate chunks are uniformly

236
00:10:44.299 --> 00:10:46.200
scattered around the network such that you

237
00:10:46.200 --> 00:10:48.179
have an equal probability for any node

238
00:10:48.179 --> 00:10:50.000
to receive them We really don't want

239
00:10:50.000 --> 00:10:51.559
a situation where all of them go

240
00:10:51.559 --> 00:10:53.280
to one computer so that if one

241
00:10:53.280 --> 00:10:54.700
computer is down then we lose the

242
00:10:54.700 --> 00:10:57.200
data We want it to be nicely

243
00:10:57.200 --> 00:11:00.280
and uniformly distributed This kind of solution

244
00:11:00.280 --> 00:11:03.640
is what we call dispersed replicas These

245
00:11:03.640 --> 00:11:06.799
quasi copies of the same chunk with

246
00:11:06.799 --> 00:11:09.960
the added on tag are what we

247
00:11:09.960 --> 00:11:11.659
call dispersed replicas in the system That

248
00:11:11.659 --> 00:11:14.799
is how we solve the problem of

249
00:11:14.799 --> 00:11:17.260
replicating the root hash In the case

250
00:11:17.260 --> 00:11:18.979
of the root hash really these quasi

251
00:11:18.979 --> 00:11:21.260
duplicates are good enough because it's a

252
00:11:21.260 --> 00:11:24.280
single chunk so there's not much meaning

253
00:11:24.280 --> 00:11:26.700
to erasure coding beyond that because erasure

254
00:11:26.700 --> 00:11:28.820
coding is of course a situation that's

255
00:11:28.820 --> 00:11:30.640
useful when you have multiple chunks and

256
00:11:30.640 --> 00:11:32.380
you want to create redundancy There here

257
00:11:32.380 --> 00:11:33.859
we just have one the root hash

258
00:11:34.059 --> 00:11:36.919
and we can create these quasi duplicates

259
00:11:36.919 --> 00:11:41.419
of them All right How many parities

260
00:11:41.419 --> 00:11:43.460
should there be in the system to

261
00:11:43.460 --> 00:11:46.900
provide adequate security Well in order to

262
00:11:46.900 --> 00:11:48.539
answer that question we have to first

263
00:11:48.539 --> 00:11:50.440
agree on what we mean by adequate

264
00:11:50.440 --> 00:11:55.539
security Somewhat arbitrarily we agree that adequate

265
00:11:55.539 --> 00:11:58.940
security will be 99 9999 so six

266
00:11:58.940 --> 00:12:00.619
nines you can keep that in mind

267
00:12:01.140 --> 00:12:03.900
percent chance that we can correctly recover

268
00:12:03.900 --> 00:12:06.799
the data In other words probabilistically I

269
00:12:06.799 --> 00:12:07.960
could also say that there's a 10

270
00:12:07.960 --> 00:12:11.820
to the minus six probability of a

271
00:12:11.820 --> 00:12:15.080
fault going on somewhere All right So

272
00:12:15.080 --> 00:12:19.099
that is our target In order to

273
00:12:19.099 --> 00:12:20.679
keep this target we have to make

274
00:12:20.679 --> 00:12:22.599
some assumptions about how likely it is

275
00:12:22.599 --> 00:12:24.960
that any single chunk cannot be correctly

276
00:12:24.960 --> 00:12:29.280
recovered We assume that these probabilities are

277
00:12:29.280 --> 00:12:31.479
equal and independent from one another That's

278
00:12:31.760 --> 00:12:32.719
of course a bit of an abstraction

279
00:12:34.080 --> 00:12:36.760
but with those assumptions we are able

280
00:12:36.760 --> 00:12:40.200
to work out how many parities out

281
00:12:40.200 --> 00:12:42.179
of 128 there should be in each

282
00:12:42.179 --> 00:12:47.039
content address chunk Let me give you

283
00:12:47.039 --> 00:12:48.940
a little example to illustrate how this

284
00:12:48.940 --> 00:12:50.919
is supposed to work So example number

285
00:12:50.919 --> 00:12:53.599
one we have a per chunk probability

286
00:12:53.599 --> 00:12:56.080
of failure of one percent Again that's

287
00:12:56.080 --> 00:12:57.640
an assumption or it might be just

288
00:12:57.640 --> 00:13:00.219
a measured piece of data on the

289
00:13:00.219 --> 00:13:02.260
network It doesn't really matter We assume

290
00:13:02.260 --> 00:13:04.039
that any one chunk when you recover

291
00:13:04.039 --> 00:13:05.739
data has a one percent chance of

292
00:13:05.739 --> 00:13:09.000
going awry In that case one can

293
00:13:09.000 --> 00:13:10.440
calculate and you don't even need to

294
00:13:10.440 --> 00:13:12.219
work very hard for it that you

295
00:13:12.219 --> 00:13:15.239
need nine parities in order to ensure

296
00:13:15.239 --> 00:13:19.080
99 9999 percent probability of correct data

297
00:13:19.080 --> 00:13:22.940
retrieval On the other hand if the

298
00:13:22.940 --> 00:13:25.520
per chunk probability of failure is 50

299
00:13:25.520 --> 00:13:27.640
percent because say there's a giant schism

300
00:13:27.640 --> 00:13:29.080
that happens in the network and half

301
00:13:29.080 --> 00:13:31.500
of the network is churned and there's

302
00:13:31.919 --> 00:13:34.179
an apocalypse going on then one can

303
00:13:34.179 --> 00:13:36.859
compute that you need actually 90 parities

304
00:13:37.140 --> 00:13:40.919
So you'll have 38 original references padded

305
00:13:40.919 --> 00:13:44.080
by 90 parities and that will actually

306
00:13:44.080 --> 00:13:45.960
protect you even against such a very

307
00:13:45.960 --> 00:13:51.380
harsh failure of the system I know

308
00:13:51.380 --> 00:13:52.760
I have not gone into any details

309
00:13:52.760 --> 00:13:54.799

transcripts.summary: Yuri presents on data redundancy in the Swarm peer-to-peer network, focusing on non-local redundancy, erasure coding, and dispersed replicas for robust retrieval. Swarm aims to be a world hard drive, where data is chopped into chunks and scattered for decentralized storage. Yuri covers three main topics: erasure codes, their implementation in Swarm, and their properties related to storage overhead. He explains that simple data duplication is wasteful and not very secure. Erasure codes involve padding data chunks with parity chunks, so any subset of chunks can recover the original data. In Swarm, files are split into 4KB chunks and represented by a Swarm hash tree (a Merkle tree). Erasure coding is implemented by reserving some references in the intermediate packed address chunks for parities. He also discusses dispersed replicas to handle root hash duplication. Yuri defines adequate security as a 99.9999% chance of correct data recovery and shows how the number of parities needed depends on the per-chunk probability of failure, illustrating this with a graph and a table showing error rates, parities, and non-parity chunks. Finally, he shows the storage overhead of various erasure coding levels, from none to paranoid.

The team emphasizes the importance of their integration within the EF and their commitment to the Ethereum protocol. They value REF's unique approach and its close connection with Foundry and developer tooling. They discuss the challenges of technical debt in Geth, particularly concerning the API surface and state management. The team addresses Peter's frustrations with EF processes and management, acknowledging some shared frustrations but disagreeing with his methods and recent claims. They affirm their commitment to Geth and Ethereum, even in the face of potential pay cuts, driven by their mission and passion for the project.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses the need to 'fork' crypto, both technologically and ontologically, to recapture its original activist and emancipatory spirit. They argue that crypto has become too much like Wall Street and has lost its way, advocating for a return to core principles like permissionlessness, privacy, and decentralized crowdfunding. The speaker proposes a thought experiment of splitting crypto to retain the positive aspects like Bitcoin's hard permissionlessness, while discarding negative elements like KYC, VCs, and extractive meme coin schemes. They highlight the importance of community-driven meaning, semantic governance, and building systems that prioritize freedom and coordination. The speaker also touches on the values and trade-offs within different blockchain ecosystems like Ethereum and Solana and emphasizes the need for better decision-making systems and open communication to reshape crypto's future.

name: How to Decentralize Any Front-End
description:
This workshop is about decentralized storage, one of the key components to realize the World Computer. We'll use the time to run a storage node (Swarm), upload a website to the decentralized network, and set up ENS to make the site accessible also on web2 via eth.limo.

As we go through this demonstration, we'll also discuss challenges and solutions in decentralized storage, such as data availability, DDoS and censorship resistance, erasure coding, incentive systems, mutable vs. immutable data, and more.

transcripts.summary: This workshop explains how to decentralize any frontend, covering decentralized storage, proximity order, chunks, nodes, and network depth. The network stores chunks on nodes closest to the chunk's address, forming neighborhoods for redundancy. The network depth dynamically adjusts based on node availability. There are altruistic and incentivized networks. Incentivized networks use postage batches created on-chain with tokens. Postage batches have buckets with slots, and chunks use slots from buckets closest to their address, providing spam protection. Chunk types include content-addressed chunks (immutable) and single-owner chunks (mutable pointers). Single-owner chunks are used for conventions like feeds, which version content. The workshop includes a demo setting up a website on Swarm with DNS. The presenter uses swarm-cli to create a feed, uploads the website content, and updates the ENS record. The video also addresses questions about costs, UI tools, limitations, and the differences of Swarm to other storage options.

name: How to Build Rollups on Bitcoin
description: Ethereum has a bunch of rollups as part of the scaling roadmap. What about... Bitcoin? This talk will focus on the extreme challenges of using Bitcoin as the data availability layer, the properties of BitVM-based bridges, and various trade-offs. You will be surprised to see what is possible (and what is not).

name: How client diversity saved Holesky: Lessons for the future
description: Holesky, the largest Ethereum public testnet experienced one of the best, unplanned events for chaos testing as it hard-forked to Pectra. With an invalid block, consistent forking and a non-finality period spanning a duration of three weeks, client and infrastructure teams were pushed to Ethereum's limitations to discover edge cases that led to many fixes and lessons learned for the future. Join Nico and Phil of the Lodestar team as they detail their experiences and how the minority TypeScript consensus client Lodestar contributed to the recovery of the testnet.

name: Can we do better than git's Merkle DAG?
description:
Git is 20 years old and git's Merkle DAG model is an established standard for decentralized systems. BitCoin and blockchains more or less follow in the footsteps. Same applies to the most of decentralized technology. The Replicated Data eXchange format aimed to overcome a number of pain points in that model, such as: accumulation of cryptographic sediment, coarse-grained-ness of data units, various inherent impedance mismatches and so on.
So, how is the progress?

transcripts.summary: Viktor Grishenko, a researcher with extensive experience in crypto and other fields, discusses the architecture of Merkle-Zach and its use in blockchains and Git. He highlights the advantages of this architecture, such as bit-precise fidelity and incremental syncing, but also points out its drawbacks, including the accumulation of irrelevant history and cryptographic sediments. He introduces a project based on CRDT using the RDX data format, which is like JSON but always merges. The project aims to improve LSM databases by making compaction deterministic, ensuring identical database states across nodes without relying on a trusted code base. He discusses the benefits of this approach, such as efficient syncing and optional log downloads, and mentions a real-world application in a crypto company that counts money. He shares links to a low-level C library and an experimental Go database related to the project and answers questions from the audience about existing blockchain applications, data structure provability, CRDT conflict resolution, and use cases for CRDTs in collaborative applications and banking.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses "veiled oracles," a method for preserving liveness and ensuring protocol honesty by representing the information the protocol actually possesses, even if ambiguous. The core idea involves using encryption and commitment to ensure that anyone interacting with the protocol is no smarter than the protocol itself. The problem being solved is on-chain lending protocols, where margin positions are enforced based on oracle prices. Errors in oracle updates can lead to bad liquidations or missed liquidations, making both borrowers and lenders unhappy. This is due to convex problems, where one piece of information is stale while the other is fresh, or when one is the truth and the other is a lie. The presented solution combats commitment in a game that has second-mover advantage. By using a Cauchy oscillator, the system generates pathological random number generation (RNG) that has no pattern and stays within bounds, making it impossible to learn anything other than the possible outcomes. In positive-sum games, this ambiguous device improves welfare by creating a Pareto-dominated Nash equilibrium. This method can be applied to Automated Market Makers (AMMs) to make impermanent loss impermanent again. The speaker acknowledges that while the concept seems weird, it might not be weirder than other previously strange ideas that turned out to be successful. The speaker encourages experimentation and offers to discuss the topic further.

name: Long-term L1 Proposal: Replacing the EVM with RISC-V
description:
This proposal presents a radical idea for the future of the Ethereum execution layer, one that is equally as ambitious as the beam chain effort is for the consensus layer. It aims to greatly improve the **efficiency** of the Ethereum execution layer, resolving one of the primary scaling bottlenecks, and can also greatly improve the execution layer's **simplicity** - in fact, it is perhaps the only way to do so.

The idea: **replace the EVM with RISC-V** as the virtual machine language that smart contracts are written in.

transcripts.summary:
Vitalik discusses replacing the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) with a more efficient architecture for long-term scaling and developer-friendliness. He argues that the EVM's limitations, particularly the cost of ZK Provers, necessitate a shift. After known optimizations, the EVM will be the biggest cost. The ideal replacement would expose the instruction set architecture of leading ZK-EVMs, like RISC-V, directly to developers, potentially yielding a 100x increase in execution. While RISC-V offers benefits such as compatibility with languages like Rust and increasing standardization, it might not be the most optimal solution for proof-friendliness. Alternatives like Cairo, designed for ZK Provers, could be considered, along with future-proof options like F2 binary fields, FHE, or obfuscated smart contracts. The transition would involve a phased approach: using the new VM for precompiles, making it directly available to users for contracts, and eventually reimplementing the EVM within the new VM. This transition should strike a balance between backwards compatibility and simplicity, drawing inspiration from language transitions like Python 2 to 3 and Apple's Rosetta. The goal is to enable developers to write code in Solidity, Viper, or Rust that is significantly more gas-efficient. He believes this is a medium-term goal. He discusses other options such as eWASM but RISC-V is currently the best. He also discusses Poseidon state trees and SIMD precompiles. He ends by answering community questions.
The speaker discusses avoiding past mistakes in protocol development, particularly those made by Polkadot. They highlight the issues of ballooning protocol complexity and lack of short-term developer benefits. RISC-V is proposed as a potential EVM replacement due to its backward compatibility and efficiency, allowing for recompilation of Solidity and potential mixing of EVM and RISC-V functions. The speaker defends the Solidity language and favors a five-year timeline for ossifying Ethereum after implementing scaling solutions and replacing the EVM. They call for analysis of VM choices (Cairo, RISC-V, MIPS) and POC implementations. The speaker stresses the importance of flexibility in EVM extensions to accommodate various use cases, including layer-2 solutions and account abstraction. They are optimistic that other EVM-compatible ecosystems will adopt RISC-V if it proves beneficial and has good tooling. The speaker addresses concerns about the complexity of adding contract calls and gas metering to RISC-V, arguing that these are manageable with existing Ethereum implementations. Current ERC standards are expected to remain compatible. Standardizing the interface design of VMs is proposed for future flexibility, emphasizing a syscall-based approach.

So a multi-sig to require more than one signer to approve transactions before funds move. This is common on project treasuries. It used to be called Gnosis Safe. It is the main multi-sig that people use. It's now called Safe Wallet. And you can create your own with multiple hardware wallets to make it harder to compromise your cold storage. You can maybe make inheritance instructions and put little rules on there about how much can be withdrawn every day or every week, et cetera. I'm now going to go through some hardware devices that are going to be used for an example I'm doing at the end of the presentation. The first is the Grid Plus Lattice Hardware Wallet. This is a desktop hardware wallet. It sits on your desktop, and it has the ability to have multiple Ethereum and Bitcoin accounts, including your staking node, if you have an Ethereum staking node. They have a lot of really cool features I like. I use this as my day-to-day wallet. Inside of the actual machine is a security mesh. And if you're trying to open the Grid Plus, there is an electrical current going through the security mesh on the inside, and if it's interrupted by someone trying to open it, it actually deletes everything in the system. So even if someone grabs this from your desk and runs off, they can't really access anything, which is true of other hardware wallets as well, but I just haven't seen it done and implemented in such a way that is that advanced. Another cool thing is they have these backup safe cards that you can insert into here. I'm going to be using those to be giving to my family for backups, so if, like, I happen to pass away, my family can just take the safe card, plug it in, use the pin, and they don't have to know a lot about what's going on with the device. They can just have that little card with them. And that seems a little bit easier than having all these words on paper. It just feels nicer than having the words on paper that you're having to give your family members. The Ledger Nano X is a popular crypto wallet. Most people here probably know what a Ledger is, but for those who don't, it is a USB device that can be used to hold cryptocurrency. It has a secure chip inside of it, depending on which version of the Ledger you have. And it also now has Bluetooth capability. There's now ones with screens on them that are really nice to use. So the Ledger Nano X is one of the most widely used hardware wallets and one that I recommend a lot of people who are just getting started in crypto to use if they need a wallet, especially for portability. Lastly, there is a series of two apps on your phone called AirGap Vault and AirGap Wallet. So there is something called an AirGap machine that is – or how would you say it? You basically can AirGap a machine, which means you have a machine that is totally offline and is only used to sign transactions. So what this – I guess AirGap, I think, is the company has done is they've made an Android and iPhone app that you can have the AirGap Vault on, and that is the offline component. So once you install it, you put your phone in airplane mode and never connect to the internet again, and then you have the AirGap Wallet. So every time you need to do a transaction, you have to actually physically, like, scan a QR code from one phone to the other. That's the AirGap part. Basically, it doesn't touch the internet. That means hackers can't get to it. And then once it signs the transaction on the Vault phone, you can then do a scan to put it back to the wallet phone. So I thought it was a really neat idea. This has been a thing for years. Parity Technologies did an AirGap – an AirGap dApp – dApp and app solution years ago with MyCrypto that was the kind of de facto AirGap Ethereum case until we have this here. So for this talk, I did an example advanced setup scheme where I had a few different devices that I need to find in here. Oh, here. It is a used Pixel 8a purchased overseas at a really sketchy place on the side of the road with a bunch of used phones. I'll tell you in a second why I did it that way. And it's running GrapheneOS, which is a hardened Android operating system that, like, does a lot to help prevent, like, attackers from getting through weird, like, side channel attacks on an Android phone. And then AirGap Vault is on here. I have a GridPlus Lattice desktop hardware wallet at home, and then I have a fresh Ledger Nano X right here that I also labeled and have used for this experiment. Again, this is overkill for 99% of people, and I'm not even a target for this, but I wanted to do this because I thought it would be a lot of fun, and it actually was. I just – this was like an excuse for me to, like, live out my cypherpunk dreams of getting AirGap wallet devices from sketchy places and stuff like that, and it was a lot of fun. So, I talked a little bit about inheritance, but not deeply. The reason for that is I could go on an entire new presentation on crypto inheritance. That's something everybody seems to worry about nowadays for good reason. This book by Pamela Morgan, Crypto Asset Inheritance Planning, a Simple Guide for Owners, is one I highly recommend. I believe it's from 2018, so there's some stuff that is a little bit dated, but overall, it's a really, really good book to get your mind in the right place on what to do with crypto asset inheritance and making sure that, you know, even though you're trying to protect yourself from attackers and whatever your threat model says to protect yourself from, you still have, you know, your family and others who might need to recover your stuff in the event that you pass away. So, be always thinking about crypto inheritance. There are new tools coming out all the time that can help with that. And in general, not keeping it too complicated and being realistic about your threat model is really the biggest thing to take away today. Just have a good threat model. Don't overthink everything. Don't do what I did unless you're Vitalik or like someone actually important. And yeah, keep it simple. Thank you. I'll take questions now. Thank you, Hudson. We'll have to do Q&A. When you clear a hard drive and delete it, or, like, let's say you reformat it or do the little format option, all that does is – the data is still on your hard drive. They just put a zero at the very beginning of it, so it says, from here on out, act like all of that is blank. And then as you use your hard drive, it overwrites it. I just don't feel intelligent enough to speak on it compared to Ledger and GridPlus and some of the ones I'm more familiar with. transcripts.summary: Hudson from Polygon discusses operational security (OPSEC) and threat modeling in the context of cryptocurrency. The talk covers identifying critical information and implementing protective measures against exploitation, emphasizing the increasing risks of kidnapping and loss of cryptocurrency. Hudson presents a three-question quiz to assess the level of paranoia one should have, categorizing users as either 'advanced' or 'general' crypto users, exemplified by Vitalik Buterin and Hudson's mother, respectively. For general users, a hardware wallet is recommended for holdings over $500. Advanced users should use hardware wallets, consider advanced wallet and recovery schemes like Shamir's Secret Sharing, and separate personal and multi-sig wallets. While acknowledging the complexity of MPC solutions, smart contract multi-sigs such as Gnosis Safe (Safe Wallet) are presented as an alternative. Hudson then reviews several hardware devices like the Grid Plus Lattice, Ledger Nano X, and AirGap Vault/Wallet. The talk concludes with a discussion on crypto inheritance planning, emphasizing the importance of a good threat model and keeping things simple.

name: IPFS: A Decade in Browsers
description: Over the past decade, the IPFS public network has grown into millions of documents providing an alternative, resilient, and self-certifying web. But what is web without browsers? This talk will covers our efforts getting ipfs:// handler support directly into browsers and the challenges we've faced. Looking into the future, we'll also preview our upcoming plans to reduce reliance on centralized HTTP <> IPFS gateways, including Helia's verified fetch, AutoTLS for libp2p, and how we think browsers and p2p will evolve in the coming years.

transcripts.text: Hello everyone. Thank you so much for coming today and thank you to the organizers of this fantastic event. There's lots we could say about IPFS. It's 10 years old, so basically middle-aged in Web3 terms. But today I want to share our adventures in IPFS and web browsers. So please raise your hand if you used a web browser this week. All right. Keep your hand up if you've written an application for a web browser. And now put your hand up or keep your hand up if you've tried to make a web browser do things it's not really supposed to do. I see a lot of hands still up. And now put your hand up if you've written a web browser or contributed to a web browser. All right. This is going to be fun. Let me figure out the clicker. Thank you. Thank you. All right. Before we start, my name is Michelle Lee, or Mosh online, and I'm with the IPFS Foundation. We are an independent organization formed after 10 years of Protocol Labs incubation, and we act as a connective tissue for the project and community. We're a deliberately lean organization. We contribute to protocol stewardship. We drive real-world adoption and feedback loops, and we integrate with web standards like IETF, W3C, and more. I'm here with my colleagues Robin Bergeon and Bumblefudge. So IPFS launched in 2015, and a lot has happened since then. I think in that 10 years, it's fair to say we've made the web and computing more open, more efficient, more credible, and also more fun. And all of this took place through a heavily consolidating browser landscape. So this chart is of 2012 to 2024, and you can kind of guess who the blue on this chart is, right? And so we're trying to make peer-to-peer happen right as the browsers are consolidating and expanding their footprints. This has been a fun adventure. And so IPFS implementations have also evolved along with the web landscape. So in 2015, Go IPFS and JS IPFS, the goal is feature parity across the languages. So literally we had a table with check marks. Did this match that one, and did that one match this one? In 2022, the implementation fund was created to support new clients. And in 23, we made some pretty major changes within the project to encourage more client diversity. So Go IPFS was renamed Kubo, this is a simple rename to free up the namespace of what was officially a Go client. And JS IPFS went through a much more major change that became Helia, or it was deprecated in favor of Helia, which was a brand new browser-first implementation that is the foundation of some really cool stuff we're going to get to see today. In 2024, we saw a rise in mini-libraries, and community members from AppPro and other communities started writing a lot of modular IPLD tools, and in response, IPFS Foundation created Dazzle, which is a streamlined IPLD and CID spec meant to work really well with any networking stack or protocol, including HTTP, and we've built on that project again through Razzle, which is for retrieval, Mazzle for metadata, the puns write themselves, you can check it out at dazzle.ing. But I want to go back to these community-driven mini-libraries, because everywhere in these library descriptions, the words you see are fast and tiny, tiny and fast, tiny and small, don't be a full client, so we really start to see that users are taking modularization into their own hands, writing their own tools. You might come because you want content addressing, you want building blocks for content to, you know, to content address the whole internet. We're continuing to build on that, there's a whole list of projects in that focus area, and the goal is to make everything small, fast, extremely performant, and interoperable. The second one, which maybe this room is most familiar with, is the public network. The third bucket of IPFS users are coming because they want to build private or permissioned  So we have users ranging from scientists sharing datasets across a few research universities to a Korean civil engineering firm that's using IPFS to make a local network of monitoring devices for bridge wear and care. So to me, this is like a really fascinating kind of below the surface of the water iceberg of IPFS users, and we're going to explore that more later this year. But today, I want to focus on the public network, because I think that's maybe the one that's most familiar to this audience, and the one that's going through a lot of really cool changes. So by design, your IPFS node talks to other nodes using the IPFS protocol to find, fetch, and then verify content by CID. Some of it driven by AI, but others just driven by other community and networking needs. So we are going to design for the browsers we have today, and we're also going to be looking at the future. And I think this more modular approach, this local verification, will put us in a really good position to do that, and it will be great tools for the developer community. I want to end with three design principles. Because, like I said, you know, our mission at the IPFS Foundation is to take us from, hey, it really works in, you know, a lot of these fantastic case studies, to it's seamless and invisible, and it's upgrading the whole Internet. transcripts.summary: Michelle Lee from the IPFS Foundation discusses the organization's journey with IPFS and web browsers over the past 10 years, focusing on making the web more open, efficient, credible, and fun despite the consolidation of browsers. She explains the evolution of IPFS implementations from Go IPFS and JS IPFS to Helia, and the creation of Dazzle for streamlined IPLD and CID specifications. The talk highlights three types of IPFS users: those seeking content addressing, those using the public network (currently hosting five billion files), and those building private/permissioned networks. A major challenge is getting web users to adopt IPFS nodes, leading to the use of gateways as an interim solution, which inadvertently caused re-centralization. The presentation then explores strategies to integrate IPFS more directly with browsers, including new browsers, adding IPFS handlers to existing browsers, and leveraging service workers for verified content retrieval, specifically highlighting the Helia verified fetch library. The long-term vision includes running experiments on gateways to push more traffic to P2P and eventually rate-limiting gateways to reposition them as a true public common. The talk concludes with three design principles for IPFS development: drop-in replacements, easy defaults with clear upgrade paths, and prioritizing performance.

name: A Functional VM for Verifiable Computing over Binary Fields
description: This talk presents a new system for verifiable computing using the Binius proof library. Binius implements a hash-based SNARK built on towers of binary fields, which unlocks huge gains in computational efficiency compared with traditional SNARKs, particularly when using specialized hardware.

transcripts.summary: Jim from Irreducible discusses verifiable computing, a cryptographic technique for verifying computation integrity, crucial for scaling blockchain and peer-to-peer systems. He touches on potential applications like combating deep fakes and verifying machine learning model safety, including zero-knowledge proofs for privacy. He then dives into the PetraVM, a SNARK-optimized virtual machine, detailing its design, compiler stack, and early performance results. He contrasts it with other VMs like RISC-V, highlighting its efficient control flow and memory handling. The talk covers SNARK basics, emphasizing the prover-verifier model and finite field arithmetic. PetraVM, utilizing the Binius SNARK and its binary field tower data types, balances program flexibility with proving efficiency. Key design aspects include read-only memory arguments, inspired by the Cairo VM, and a functional programming paradigm with a write-once memory model. This model enables efficient memory management by eliminating garbage collection and general-purpose registers. The system uses XOR for pointer arithmetic and allows non-deterministic allocation. The presentation touches on a language named PetraML, a subset of standard ML that compiles to optimized assembly code. Early benchmarks comparing PetraVM to RISC-V VMs show promising performance. Future work involves compiler completion, optimization, recursive proof implementation, and the addition of optional read-write memory.

name: Bluesky, atproto, how to hack on it and why it matters
description:
In 2019 Twitter asked a team of crypto and p2p devs to design a protocol for the next generation of permissionless social media. The protocol escaped Twitter and now drives Bluesky, the fast-growing social media site. It can do a lot more.

This talk will cover: the principles underlying the design of atproto, why those principles matter, Bluesky and the unbundling of feeds, blocklists, curation and tagging, how the protocol works (Dag-cbor, Merkle Search Trees, DID:PLC), and how to make bots to make stuff happen on-chain.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses AppProto and BlueSky, clarifying they aren't speaking on behalf of BlueSky and weren't involved in AppProto's creation, but they like them. Links to information about AppProto from its creators are available on the speaker's BlueSky profile (goat.navy). The talk contrasts the early internet's decentralized nature with Web 2.0's centralization, highlighting the issues of editorial control and the need for decentralized protocols to fully address user needs. Jack Dorsey's vision of decentralizing Twitter led to the creation of AT Proto and BlueSky, aiming for scalability and a familiar user experience. AT Proto's core is the PDS (Personal Data Server), which stores structured, signed, and content-addressed data. The PDS is different because it stores structured data that follows a lexicon, it's attached to an identity, it contains social graphs, and it is content stressed and cryptographically signed. The architecture involves relays for aggregating changes from PDSs and app views for client backends. Identity is managed through did-web and did-plc standards. The speaker covers content creation, curation, moderation in BlueSky, where users can create feeds and moderate content. They highlight the potential of AppProto beyond BlueSky, allowing everyone to have a self-sovereign, cryptographically verifiable data store for various applications, contrasting it with blockchain's limitations for user-controlled data. The speaker concludes with a call to action to explore the provided links for more information and then answers questions about why the crypto community hasn't embraced AppProto more, the differences between AppProto, BlueSky, and Farcaster, and then touches on the differences between BlueSky and Mastodon.

name: Redesigning Governance: Trust Networks, Decentralization, and the Dichotomy of Extremes in Politics
description: In a world increasingly divided by extremes, the traditional structures of governance and political ideology no longer seem to offer the solutions we need. This talk will explore the potential of decentralized systems and cryptography to create new models for governance that break away from conventional dichotomies.

transcripts.summary: The speaker discusses decentralization, trust networks, and the dichotomy of extreme politics. Decentralization involves distributing power away from centralized authorities and has technical, monetary, governance, social/community, and cultural aspects. The speaker notes that the promise of breaking free from institutions to distributed networks has not been fully realized and calls for a holistic approach to decentralization, considering all aspects. They discuss how extreme capitalism and socialism both fail to empower people due to centralized control and suggests a need for new models that embrace what works in both systems, focusing on decentralized, resilient, radically collaborative, and human-centric approaches. They emphasize the importance of trust networks in decentralized systems for secure peer-to-peer interactions without intermediaries. Trust networks enable transparent governance where individuals can verify decisions and ensure inclusive processes. The speaker suggests rethinking governance models to be meritocratic and not capital-centric. They respond to audience questions about preventing chaos in decentralized systems, creating new forms of money embodying trust, decentralizing culture, and decentralized AI. The speaker is ultimately advocating for a future where technology empowers individuals and fosters collaboration.

name: Beyond the Ledger: JAM and the Future of Scalable Decentralized Computing
description: Blockchain tech can be more than just a ledger: it can be a scalable global computing network, moving away from transaction-centric blockchain design into a decentralised computer one, changing usage patterns, development patterns and tooling. The Join-Accumulate Machine (JAM) is a new protocol aiming to make the usage of blockchain core radically un-opinionated, and to enhance the scalability and efficiency of blockchain networks.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker discusses the security mechanism for Jam, a blockchain project combining Polkadot and Ethereum elements. Jam uses ELLs (based on divide and conquer) to scale security, which is much cheaper than ZK proof-based methods. ELLs involves splitting validator work and auditing, with clever rules to prevent attackers from bypassing audits. Validators announce audits beforehand to avoid DOS attacks. The speaker contrasts this crypto-economic scaling with ZK proofs, highlighting the cost and latency advantages of ELLs. He presents data showing ELLs can handle significantly more Ethereum gas per dollar than ZK protocols with much lower latency. 

The second topic covers consensus VMs, examining why they're slow compared to native execution. Key characteristics include determinism, the ability to limit work, and agreement on work done (gas). These requirements slow down VMs because they don't use native ISA and wall clock execution time isn't easily predictable. 

To address this, the speaker introduces Economically Sound Augmented Metering as a hybrid approach to improve gas estimations. This involves applying a metering factor based on staking, where malicious code triggers slashing. He outlines a mechanism involving subjective measurement by validators, statistical consolidation of measurements, and thresholding to determine if the ratio was intentionally breached, resulting in a slashing penalty based on the likelihood of the intentional breach. This brings objectivity over the amount of gas used.
This transcript discusses the performance and efficiency of different virtual machine implementations, specifically comparing Ethereum's EVM with the PVM used in the Jam project. It presents metrics for native execution time versus execution within these VMs, highlighting slowdowns and factors contributing to them, such as ISA changes and protocol overhead. The discussion covers native wall clock time compared to running it on Solidity, emphasizing the differences between ETHONE and GET. PVM shows a much smaller slowdown compared to EVM. The transcript then shifts to a demonstration of Core VM, focusing on its architecture, how it uses refining and accumulation for smart contract logic, and its ability to run guest VMs. The demonstration attempts to showcase running Quake within a Core VM instance on a Jam testnet, but it is unsuccessful due to networking issues.

description: It's a wrap! As Protocol Berg v2 concludes, we reflect on two days of profound engagement with protocol research, decentralized infrastructure, and core-developer experiences. Held in Prenzlauer Berg, Berlin, the event brought together a diverse community of engineers, researchers, and stakeholders from various decentralized protocols. With 108 sessions across multiple stages and a dedicated workshop room, participants delved into technical workshops, in-depth discussions, and community gatherings.

transcripts.text: We're back. Hey, friends. I don't have the clicker either. You'd think we'd be organized for a technical conference, but apparently not. All right, so we'll make this quick because we're a bit over time and we know everybody wants to go home, us especially. But yeah, okay, so in this session, we're just going to go over a few things. We're going to talk about the ethos of Protocol Berg, what led us to organize a sponsorless non-profit donation-backed event that's free to attend. You're also going to hear a bit about the finances, how much it costs, et cetera, and our closing thoughts. So let's give you some Protocol Berg B2 facts. We started working in this event approximately 245 days ago. Our first meeting was in October 10th, 2024, last year. We counted 52 volunteers, 881 attendees, 107 talks, a total of 542 questions in all of the talks. This is a median of two questions per user, so well done, and a total of 903 upvotes counted, so that's great. We got 3,790 euros, jamón and donuts, in donations from 89 amazing attendees. Thank you to those who have donated. Big thank you. Just for you to know, we split the orders, so donations were not visible to us when we reviewed the applications to attend. This is really important for us. Regarding the application decision-making process, we had, from October last year, from the moment, also from this year, we got the talks and the attendees' applications, DOD weekly calls to go through all of the applicants and all of the speakers to make sure we had the best curated agenda for you. Now you may ask, why are they doing a donation-backed, sponsorless, non-profit event that is free to attend? That is a really, really good question. We want to stay credibly neutral. This is very important for us, for the Department of Decentralization. We believe that conferences and educational events are a common good that everyone should have access to. We focus on the tech only, as you can see in these past two days and last year in East Berlin and the year before in our first edition of Protocol Berg. We try to include everyone, all people from all backgrounds. We do not restrict access based on financials, so very important again, and I know you've seen the signs all over, but please donate if you have the means to support us. This is really, really important for us. It keeps us going. It's also a content-first curation. What we like as core organizers, what we find interesting, regardless of what projects or companies are coming, is what motivates us to keep going and do this event. Our passion is to bring people together, to discuss ideas with the right mindset, the right intentions together, and to create also a breeding ground for new ideas like we did also last year in East Berlin. In short, we're trying to organize a conference that doesn't suck. You can see from some of the responses that we had for the applications that everybody loves Protocol Berg. You may also wonder how much an event like this costs. We're here to give you a bit of the financials as well, to be as transparent as possible. Protocol Berg version 2 this year costed €155,000, a bit more than that, actually. This includes all of the free food, all of the free drinks that you've enjoyed in these two days, the stage equipment, the furniture, the lighting, the decoration, the staff, security, the bar personnel, the cleaning personnel, all of the tech and stage managers, all of the roll-ups and the branding items that you see, our great photographer, Anton, who's been with us already since the very beginning. All of the swag that you got at the event. If you didn't get some swag, please make sure to get some before you leave. Very, very nice one. All of the volunteer swag as well, all of the T-shirts that you see, accounting and taxes for a non-profit organization here in Berlin, and of course, a safety buffer for any extra expenses. So who exactly supported us for this event specifically? Well, first of all, a big thank you to the Just Open Source Foundation who donated €100,000. As mentioned before, we also received almost 4K in community donations. Thank you so much, because without these donations, we wouldn't be able to make this happen. However, if you do the math, and I know some of you are very good at math in here, you will notice that there's over €50,000 of a gap, and we filled this with the reserve that we had from the Optimism Retrofunding Round and East Berlin Fall. So thanks to them too. But you see where we're getting at. This is not sustainable. We can't keep organizing these events without any kind of donations. So as Raul mentioned, if you can support us, we would really appreciate a small or large donation. Yes. Before you leave, a bit of housekeeping. Okay? Just for you to know, if you have a Protocol Bird ticket and you want to attend DAPCON this year, you can also get a discount with ZUPAS, which is TK-proof, so that's super great. Keep an eye on our channels to get more information about this. We want to give also a big, big shout-out to Toby for developing the Schedule app on Android. Thank you so much. There's a couple in the top corner that you might recognize. Big shout out to our collaborators as well, ZK AV Club, Meerkat and Streamith. I don't know if any of you are here, but please join us too. And of course, you know, we're all volunteers here for this event and for all of the things we do at DoD. And we could never, ever do this without the help of our amazing volunteers. So we're asking all of them to also come on stage with us so we can take a quick photo. Come on, all of you, all of you. Thank you for all your hard work these last two days, honestly. Thank you. And with that, we want to officially close Protocol Berg V2. Thanks for coming! And with that, we're done. Thanks, everyone.
transcripts.summary: The organizers of Protocol Berg discuss the ethos behind the event: a sponsorless, non-profit, donation-backed, and free-to-attend conference focused solely on technology. They emphasize credibly neutral, inclusivity and the importance of community donations for sustainability. Protocol Berg v2 cost €155,000, supported by the Just Open Source Foundation (€100,000) and community donations (almost €4,000). A reserve from Optimism Retrofunding Round filled a €50,000 gap. They announced a discount for Protocol Berg ticket holders for DAPCON, shouted out the app developer, Toby and reminded attendees about the lost and found. The organizers and volunteers were thanked and celebrated, officially closing Protocol Berg V2.

name: Integrating Blockchain Data into AI Agents
description: AI agents are transforming how we interact with data, but their effectiveness depends on real-time, reliable information. In this workshop, we will explore how to integrate blockchain data into AI agents using a SubQuery Indexer SDK. Participants will learn how to query on-chain data from different networks, process it efficiently, and use it to enhance AI-driven decision-making.

transcripts.summary: The workshop aims to demonstrate a practical integration of open-source tools for data exploration with AI, specifically for querying complex blockchain data using natural language. The speaker uses open source components to create a proof-of-concept system for querying blockchain data. The setup involves running a local substrate node, indexing data from it into a relational database using Substrate Indexing as SQL, and creating an AI-powered tool using Ollama for hosting an LLM and LangChain as a framework. The tool translates natural language requests into SQL queries, executes them, and interprets the results. The speaker showcases the process, including spamming a smart contract with data, setting up the indexer, and demonstrating the AI agent's query capabilities with examples. The speaker then opens the floor to questions and discussions, also stating that the context can be set up such that the AI learns and provides responses based on it.

name: 25-Minute Solidity Fuzzer: Fuzzing Smarter, Not Harder
description: Fuzzing and Formal Methods** are often seen as competing approaches to smart contract security. In this **hands-on workshop**, we combine insights from both, allowing participants to build a **minimal EVM/Solidity smart contract fuzzer in Python within 25 minutes**.

transcripts.summary:
The speaker, Thomas, introduces a workshop on fuzzing, a technique for finding bugs by feeding random inputs into a program and observing if it breaks. He emphasizes that fuzzing, while theoretically a black box technique, requires a deep understanding of the fuzzer and the program being tested, especially in the context of smart contracts and the EVM. The workshop involves building a fuzzer from scratch using Python to explore Solidity and EVM intricacies. The initial fuzzer implementation generates random byte inputs, but it quickly becomes apparent that this approach is ineffective due to the need for well-formed inputs that adhere to the contracts expected input types. The discussion then shifts to the transition from dump fuzzing to structural bare fuzzing to generate valid inputs for different function arguments, such as addresses and integers. They encounter challenges such as the fact that there is often a race condition between mint and remove admin so they must make an adjustment for those functions to be more equally represented in the output.
The speaker discusses minting cars in a smart contract and observes that after one successful mint, subsequent mints often fail or mint decreasing amounts due to the uniform distribution of sampled UN256 values causing overflows when calculating the total supply. They then demonstrate writing a fuzzer to find bugs by first creating an invariant that is expected to fail to confirm the fuzzer is operational. The speaker uses GNU parallel to run multiple instances of the fuzzer. The presentation outlines how to find and fix vulnerabilities in the BERC token contract. Specifically, they address issues related to minting and transferring tokens directly to the contract address, which inflates the share price in staking contracts. The vulnerabilities are fixed by adding require statements to prevent such actions. Also addressed is how fuzzers cannot break cryptographic signature based checks and how to pre-compute signatures for fuzzing smart contracts utilizing signature based authorization. They emphasize that dump fuzzing doesn't work, the number of runs means nothing if the contract is not exercised, fuzzing is not a black box, always requires understanding what the tool is doing and involves making tradeoffs. Input distributions are tricky and to take fuzzing reports with a grain of salt. Finally mentioning things not covered, such as passing time, pre-compiles, receive and fallback functions, proxy contracts, contract upgrade attacks.

name: Designing Protocols for a New Social Fabric
description: How might we design protocols that shape behaviors and address real-world challenges? In this workshop, we will individually map behavioral patterns, prioritize key challenges, and merge our ideas to develop protocol concepts that encourage positive interactions. Borrowing from design principles used by companies like Google and Apple, this session will provide hands-on experience in structuring sociotechnical rules - without much discussion. No technical background is required—just curiosity and a willingness to be creative.

transcripts.summary:
The speakers introduce themselves and the session's focus: designing for Web3 and embedding social coordination into technical protocols, particularly in the employment infrastructure. They aim to explore behavioral protocols, their impact, and how technology can improve them. The session will be interactive, using a mirror board for collaboration. They plan to dissect protocols from a social perspective, focusing on behavioral aspects enabled by technology, and delve into friction points, design processes, and real-world examples within the labor economy. They emphasize the importance of aligning technological and behavioral protocols with principles and values. Examples include protocols in apocalyptic environments, health protocols, and existing protocols like dating/marriage and COVID responses. They discuss current workplace protocols, like scheduling meetings across time zones and onboarding processes, highlighting challenges like determining pay, lack of social time, and the undervaluation of care work. The discussion transitions to ideating solutions and considering technical trade-offs, stakeholder conflicts, and the overall usefulness of protocols, with a goal of creating sustainable social fabric. They emphasize the importance of recognizing expertise and balancing it with authority, discussing examples of expertise in coding versus organizational management.
The discussion revolves around the potential conflicts in designing and building a protocol, emphasizing the importance of stakeholder and user research to manage tensions and disagreements. Key points include: addressing expertise and authority conflicts, balancing technical ideals with practical considerations like product-market fit, managing disagreements, and negotiating authority. The importance of conversation, negotiation, and persuasion with stakeholders is highlighted to solve a bigger problem affecting everyone, ultimately making solutions cost-effective. Furthermore, principles underlying a protocol significantly influence decision-making and conflict points. Being explicit about these principles, such as attracting investment versus creating the best cryptographic system, is crucial for identifying and mitigating conflicts. The organizers encourage the audience to reach out with projects and ideas and mention their presence at DAPCON, offering office hours to jam on these topics. They also acknowledge adapting the workshop from small groups to a more shout-out format.

name: Not your vote, not your lawyer: Delegation and the Legal Challenges
description:
We will explore the dynamic intersection of delegation and DAOs, concepts driving the future of decentralized governance. Delegation enables more efficient decision-making and distribution of power within DAOs but comes with its risks and challenges both from the delegate and delegator sides. 

We will dive into how delegation structures work in DAOs and the challenges they pose to traditional hierarchical models from a legal perspective, examining possible legal risks in governance delegation and how to mitigate them.
